echoes.dimitri_c3_a: The families once approved every quotation before publication. This grandson is asking for the same courtesy.
echoes.dimitri_c3_b: The museum digitized photographs with credited owners. These negatives have never had a public credit at all.

chapters.objective: Choose how the photographs are presented.

choices.label: Name her as the photographer
choices.outcome: Every caption reads 'Photographs by Ada Renn, factory worker and documentarian.' Dimitri rewrites his own chapter around her sequence. The exhibition's title changes to one of her own captions.
choices.memoryHint: The photographer is credited by name.

choices.label: Let the family write the captions
choices.outcome: The grandson writes six captions in his grandmother's voice, as she might have. Dimitri labels them clearly as family interpretation, not quotation. The wall becomes an argument between evidence and inheritance, in the best sense.
choices.memoryHint: The family captions are labeled as interpretation.

chapters.title: The Stop That Never Was
chapters.setting: A pub with a folding map
chapters.intro: A local history group insists the station had a second platform for a summer that appears in no record. Dimitri finds one photograph that might support it, and three that contradict it. They want him to settle the question in a talk next week.

echoes.dimitri_c4_a: You built a walking route that invented nothing. The group wants a second platform added to it.
echoes.dimitri_c4_b: You marked every uncertainty in the chronicle. This crowd would prefer a confident answer.

chapters.objective: Decide what the talk will claim.

choices.label: Present the conflict itself
choices.outcome: Dimitri shows all four photographs and explains why they disagree. Half the room leaves disappointed. The other half stays for an hour, arguing about shadows, and the group's next meeting is standing room.
choices.memoryHint: The talk presents the conflict, not a verdict.

choices.label: Say what the evidence supports
choices.outcome: Dimitri states plainly: no second platform is documented, and one photograph is suggestive but insufficient. The group accepts it slowly, and revises their leaflet. On the last page they print his caveat in full.
choices.memoryHint: The leaflet prints the caveat.

chapters.title: The Next Reader
chapters.intro: Dimitri's book is finished, and the publisher wants a dramatic subtitle about a secret railway. The alternative is a plain title, a shorter book, and a final chapter that admits what he still cannot prove. The ticket is in a frame above his desk.

echoes.dimitri_c2_a: The clock tower led you to the platform. The publisher wants the tower on the cover, larger than it was.
echoes.dimitri_c2_b: The route sketch crossed a garden. That garden is now the most photographed part of your research.

chapters.objective: Choose how the story goes to print.

choices.label: Keep the honest title
choices.outcome: The book appears as 'Saint Orin: A Station Remembered'. It sells modestly and stays in print for years. Researchers cite the uncertainty chapter more than any other.
choices.memoryHint: The honest title outlasts the hype.

choices.label: Take the dramatic subtitle
choices.outcome: The book sells ten times as many copies, and Dimitri spends a year correcting people who believe the station was a spy route. He decides the corrections are part of the work now.
choices.memoryHint: The dramatic book needs constant correction.

title: The Garden in the Drawer
tagline: A tiny seed can carry an entire neighborhood.
premise: A misplaced seed tin reveals a community garden omitted from the conservatory records.

chapters.title: The Unlisted Tin
chapters.intro: Nora finds a brass tin behind a row of carefully numbered seed drawers. Its faded label names Lantern Court, a courtyard demolished before the conservatory opened. Inside are dry seed envelopes and a folded watering rota. Nothing has a species name.
chapters.objective: Choose which record to examine before disturbing the seeds.

choices.label: Read the watering rota
choices.outcome: The rota lists five neighbors sharing one garden tap. A handwritten note asks that every harvest leave seeds for the following spring. Nora records the names without assuming which plant they grew.
choices.memoryHint: Five neighbors shared the care of Lantern Court.

choices.label: Inspect the envelope marks
choices.outcome: Under a desk lamp, Nora sees a repeated stamp: a small lantern beside three leaves. She matches the mark to an old community collection book and preserves the envelopes intact.
choices.memoryHint: The lantern stamp connects the tin to a community collection.

chapters.title: The Empty Garden Bed
chapters.setting: A courtyard beneath the city plan
chapters.intro: A collection book confirms that Lantern Court supplied seeds to the conservatory. The final entry leaves the garden bed number blank. Nora brings a copy of the old plan to a public records room; the courtyard lies beneath what is now a paved passage.
chapters.objective: Find a careful way to reconnect the collection with its place.

choices.label: Compare the survey maps
choices.outcome: Overlaying two surveys reveals a strip of ground left outside the demolition boundary. Nora marks it as a lead, then requests access rather than treating the plan as permission to dig.
choices.memoryHint: A small strip of the original garden may survive.

choices.label: Read the donation letters
choices.outcome: One donation letter describes a shared wooden bench, a north wall and a lantern above the gate. Nora assembles these details into a location note and credits the original contributors.
choices.memoryHint: The donation letters preserve the garden layout and contributors.

chapters.title: Room for a New Spring
chapters.intro: The conservatory agrees to safeguard the tin and document its uncertain contents. There are too few seeds to promise a revived garden. Nora sets out two responsible ways to make the discovery useful without turning a fragile collection into a spectacle.
chapters.objective: Choose the first step in caring for the collection.

choices.label: Prioritize conservation
choices.outcome: Nora catalogs every envelope and arranges a specialist viability assessment. A small public display uses drawings and copies, leaving the original seeds in controlled storage. Hope becomes a plan with limits.
choices.memoryHint: The original seeds are protected while specialists assess viability.

choices.label: Create a community record
choices.outcome: Nora builds a clearly labeled history file from the rota and letters. Neighbors can contribute memories voluntarily, while the unidentified seeds remain protected in the collection. The garden returns first as a shared record.
choices.memoryHint: The garden history is reopened through voluntary community contributions.

chapters.title: A Place at the Table
chapters.intro: At an open afternoon, Nora lays copies of the old rota beside the carefully conserved tin. The collection can now support a lasting project. Its future does not depend on claiming that every seed will grow; it depends on choosing how people can care for it.
chapters.objective: Choose the collection’s lasting role.

choices.label: Found a stewardship shelf
choices.outcome: The conservatory dedicates a labeled shelf to community-donated seeds and their histories, with clear collection rules and credited contributors. Lantern Court becomes its first record. Nora closes the drawer knowing it now has a place and a purpose.
choices.memoryHint: Lantern Court anchors a permanent community stewardship collection.

choices.label: Make a garden field guide
choices.outcome: Nora publishes a modest guide to the lost courtyard, separating documented details from open questions. Copies go to the local library and conservatory desk. The final page invites readers to care for a garden of their own.
choices.memoryHint: A credited field guide preserves the lost garden without inventing its past.

chapters.title: The Viability Report
chapters.setting: A lab bench under grow lights
chapters.intro: The specialist report arrives: nine of the forty envelopes hold viable seed. Nine is enough to grow a garden and far too few to replace the collection. Nora has one season and a decision about what the Lantern Court seeds are for.

echoes.nora_c1_a: The rota asked every harvest to leave seeds for the following spring. Nine envelopes are that promise, arriving late.
echoes.nora_c1_b: The lantern stamp connected the tin to a community collection. The collection's rules are now the question.

chapters.objective: Decide what the viable seeds are for.

choices.label: Grow them for conservation
choices.outcome: Nora sows under controlled conditions, hand-pollinates, and returns every seed to storage. No one sees a flower this year. The collection doubles, quietly, and the conservatory's long patience holds.
choices.memoryHint: The seeds are grown for the collection.

choices.label: Grow them with the neighbors
choices.outcome: Nora gives half the viable seed to Lantern Court descendants and grows the other half herself. The courtyard garden returns in window boxes across the district, and every grower keeps a seed for next year.
choices.memoryHint: Half the seeds return to the neighborhood.

chapters.title: The Courtyard Beneath
chapters.intro: The strip of ground outside the demolition boundary turns out to sit above a service void. Engineers need to open the paving for repairs. For two weeks, the old courtyard will be a hole in the city — and then covered again.

echoes.nora_c3_a: You protected the originals and built a display from copies. The paving is about to offer the real ground, briefly.
echoes.nora_c3_b: You reopened the garden as a shared record. Here is the chance to record the actual soil.

chapters.objective: Choose what happens during the opening.

choices.label: Invite an archaeologist in
choices.outcome: A botanist and an archaeologist sift the fill for two weeks. They find a clay pipe, a button, and pollen from three of the nine species. Everything is labeled and nothing is claimed beyond the evidence.
choices.memoryHint: The opened ground yields pollen and small finds.

choices.label: Hold a soil ceremony
choices.outcome: Nora organizes a quiet gathering where former neighbors each pour a handful of garden soil into the void. There is no excavation and no scientific claim. The paving goes back, and the courtyard has been visited.
choices.memoryHint: Neighbors return soil to the courtyard.

chapters.title: The Family Who Kept the Key
chapters.setting: A front room full of tins
chapters.intro: A woman arrives at the conservatory with her grandmother's key to the courtyard gate and a demand: the family wants the seed tin back. They say it was never donated. The collection has the tin, the rota, and no paperwork either way.

echoes.nora_c4_a: Your stewardship shelf credited every contributor. This family's grandmother is not on the label.
echoes.nora_c4_b: Your field guide separated documented facts from open questions. The provenance of the tin is now an open question.

chapters.objective: Decide how the claim is answered.

choices.label: Offer shared custody
choices.outcome: Nora proposes the tin stay in the collection with a family label and a loan agreement for display. The family accepts, and adds a photograph of their grandmother to the shelf. The key goes into the case beside it.
choices.memoryHint: The tin becomes a shared custody record.

choices.label: Return the tin and keep the record
choices.outcome: Nora returns the original tin with a full digital copy of every note, rota and assessment. The family is surprised by how much the conservatory kept. They lend it back for one exhibition a year.
choices.memoryHint: The tin returns home and visits yearly.

chapters.title: A Garden With a Future
chapters.intro: Lantern Court has a shelf, a field guide, and nine plants in careful hands. The conservatory offers Nora a permanent post running community collections. The alternative is a smaller job, more time in the greenhouse, and fewer meetings.

echoes.nora_c2_a: A strip of ground survived the demolition. A permanent post would let you look for the next strip.
echoes.nora_c2_b: The donation letters preserved a bench, a wall, a lantern. The new post is a bench of a different kind.

chapters.objective: Choose the shape of Nora's next years.

choices.label: Take the permanent post
choices.outcome: Nora accepts and spends her first year building a process any family can use to bring a tin, a rota, or a name. Three more collections arrive before winter. Two of them are older than Lantern Court.
choices.memoryHint: A permanent post opens three new collections.

choices.label: Stay with the plants
choices.outcome: Nora declines the post and keeps her hands in the soil. She trains one successor carefully and writes down everything she knows. The greenhouse smells of damp clay and orange peel, and the nine plants set seed.
choices.memoryHint: Nora stays with the plants and trains a successor.

title: The Hour We Kept
tagline: Repair the clock without erasing its history.
premise: A town clock contains two different repair histories and a missing hour in its service log.

chapters.title: Two Sets of Teeth
chapters.intro: Theo removes a protective cover during a scheduled inspection and finds two maker marks on the same gear assembly. The service book names only one repair. He photographs the parts in place and sets the clock’s maintenance file beside his bench.
chapters.objective: Choose the first source to compare.

choices.label: Examine the maker marks
choices.outcome: The second mark belongs to a local workshop that closed decades ago. Wear around the mounting screws suggests its part was fitted carefully. Theo records the finding without dismantling the working assembly.
choices.memoryHint: An uncredited local workshop contributed to the clock.

choices.label: Study the service dates
choices.outcome: A service date falls on the day the tower was closed for a civic gathering. Theo compares the public notice with the log and finds an unexplained one-hour gap.
choices.memoryHint: The repair log omits one hour during a documented tower closure.

chapters.title: The Apprentice’s Note
chapters.intro: A workshop archive contains a note describing an emergency replacement made before the town gathering. The note is signed by an apprentice rather than the master named in the official service book. Theo needs stronger evidence before changing a public record.
chapters.objective: Choose how to verify the note.

choices.label: Compare workshop drawings
choices.outcome: A dated drawing shows the unusual tooth spacing of the installed part. Theo documents the match and keeps the drawing’s authorship separate from assumptions about who did every stage of the work.
choices.memoryHint: The apprentice’s dated drawing matches the installed gear.

choices.label: Trace the material invoice
choices.outcome: An invoice records the correct brass stock delivered to the local workshop before the gathering. Together with the note and marks, it gives the missing repair a credible timeline.
choices.memoryHint: A material invoice supports the previously unrecorded repair timeline.

chapters.title: Keep the Honest Scar
chapters.setting: A working object, an incomplete account
chapters.intro: The town accepts that its clock owes something to an overlooked repair team. A scratched cover plate could be polished smooth during maintenance, or carefully cleaned with its old tool marks intact. Both treatments can protect the mechanism when performed by the restoration team.
chapters.objective: Choose the restoration approach to document.

choices.label: Retain the tool marks
choices.outcome: Theo cleans and protects the plate while retaining the marks that reveal how it was serviced. The condition report explains the decision. The clock looks cared for, and its history remains legible.
choices.memoryHint: The restored plate retains its documented workshop tool marks.

choices.label: Display a replica cover
choices.outcome: Theo preserves the original plate in controlled storage and fits a clearly dated replica for daily use. A small display shows why the old cover mattered, without presenting the replacement as original.
choices.memoryHint: A dated replica protects daily use while the original plate is conserved.

chapters.title: The Next Hour
chapters.setting: The clock returns to the square
chapters.intro: The mechanism is ready and the maintenance record is complete. The newly credited repair team will be named in the town archive. Theo has one final choice about how the clock should share its recovered history with people passing beneath it.
chapters.objective: Choose the public record that accompanies the repaired clock.

choices.label: Install a concise history panel
choices.outcome: A small panel names the documented contributors and directs curious visitors to the archive. When the clock strikes, nobody has to know the whole story to benefit from the hour it keeps. Theo listens, then packs his tools.
choices.memoryHint: A permanent panel credits the repair team and links to the evidence.

choices.label: Create an open workshop record
choices.outcome: Theo prepares an illustrated maintenance booklet for the public library, including the drawings, dates and remaining uncertainties. Future restorers will inherit more than a working machine: they will inherit an honest starting point.
choices.memoryHint: A public workshop record preserves the clock’s evidence for future restorers.

chapters.title: The Escapement's Second Hand
chapters.setting: A bench under a work lamp
chapters.intro: The restored clock has run four minutes slow for a month. Theo traces the drift to a wheel he did not fit: a component from the small local workshop, quietly replaced during the war and never logged. Correcting it means altering a part someone else installed to keep the town on time.

echoes.theo_c1_a: You recorded the second maker's mark without dismantling the assembly. The drift is coming from that mark's wheel.
echoes.theo_c1_b: You found the missing hour in the service log. The unlogged repair is the reason the clock is slow.

chapters.objective: Decide how to correct the drift.

choices.label: Adjust the wheel, keep the part
choices.outcome: Theo files a tenth of a millimeter from the wheel and documents exactly where. The clock keeps time. The old repair survives, corrected, and the file records both hands that touched it.
choices.memoryHint: The old wheel is adjusted, not replaced.

choices.label: Fit a new wheel and keep the old
choices.outcome: Theo machines a new wheel and stores the war-era part with a condition report. The clock gains accuracy; the old piece gains a label. Some visitors ask why the replaced part is the more interesting one.
choices.memoryHint: A new wheel runs; the old one is labeled.

chapters.title: The Striking Hour
chapters.intro: The clock's strike is uneven on the third blow, and the town has noticed. Theo can silence the strike until the fault is found, or let it ring wrong while he works. A silent clock is safe and strange; a wrong one is honest and maddening.

echoes.theo_c3_a: You kept the honest scar on the cover plate. The strike is another honest scar, in sound.
echoes.theo_c3_b: You fitted a clearly dated replica so daily use could continue. A silent clock is the opposite bet.

chapters.objective: Choose what the town hears.

choices.label: Let it strike, warts and all
choices.outcome: The third blow rings flat for eleven days. People set their watches by the first two and complain about the third. Theo finds a cracked pallet and repairs it, and the town misses the flat note when it goes.
choices.memoryHint: The town learns the flat third strike.

choices.label: Silence it until it's right
choices.outcome: Theo stops the strike and posts a handwritten note on the tower door explaining why. The square feels wrong at noon for a week. When the bell returns, a small crowd applauds, and Theo pretends not to notice.
choices.memoryHint: A note explains the silent bell.

chapters.title: The Apprentice's Name
chapters.setting: A workshop archive with a lost ledger
chapters.intro: A historian argues that the apprentice who made the emergency repair was never formally qualified, and that crediting her overstates the record. Theo has her signed note, her dated drawing, and one line in a ledger that might be her name written by someone else.

echoes.theo_c2_a: Her dated drawing matched the installed gear. The drawing is the strongest thing you have.
echoes.theo_c2_b: The material invoice gave the repair a credible timeline. The historian says a timeline is not a qualification.

chapters.objective: Decide how the record should read.

choices.label: Credit the work, name the gap
choices.outcome: The panel credits the apprentice as the fitter of the part and states plainly that her training is undocumented. The historian signs the wording. It is a smaller claim, and it holds.
choices.memoryHint: The credit names both work and gap.

choices.label: Publish the evidence and let it stand
choices.outcome: Theo publishes the note, the drawing, and the ledger line with a careful transcription. He makes no argument. Readers draw their own conclusions, and most of them draw the generous one.
choices.memoryHint: The evidence is published without argument.

chapters.title: The Hour After
chapters.intro: The restoration is finished and the archive is complete. The town offers Theo a contract to maintain every public clock in the district. The other path is to train two young restorers and hand them the keys, knowing they will make choices he would not.

echoes.theo_c4_a: Your history panel sent visitors to the archive. A district contract would send them to you.
echoes.theo_c4_b: Your workshop record gave future restorers an honest starting point. Two of them are standing on the stairs.

chapters.objective: Choose how the work continues.

choices.label: Take the district contract
choices.outcome: Theo takes the contract and spends a year learning six more clocks, each with its own hidden repair. He keeps a single notebook for all of them, and his handwriting gets smaller.
choices.memoryHint: The district's clocks share one notebook.

choices.label: Train the two restorers
choices.outcome: Theo hands over the keys on a Tuesday, then stays on for a year without pay. They make three choices he disagrees with. Two of them are better than his, and the third keeps the clock honest in a way he had not considered.
choices.memoryHint: The keys pass to two young restorers.

title: Clouds Over Beacon Hill
tagline: Read the weather behind a forgotten warning.
premise: An old weather notebook records an unexplained warning on a night the official archive calls calm.

chapters.title: A Calm Night on Paper
chapters.intro: Amara opens a donated observation notebook and finds a warning circled beside a night labeled calm in the digital archive. The handwriting is careful, with instrument readings listed every half hour. A contradiction is worth investigating, but it is not yet proof of a hidden storm.
chapters.objective: Choose the first measurement to check.

choices.label: Compare the pressure readings
choices.outcome: The pressure values follow a plausible trend, but the notebook uses an older instrument scale. Amara converts the entries and documents the method before comparing them with the official record.
choices.memoryHint: The notebook’s older pressure scale must be converted before comparison.

choices.label: Check the instrument location
choices.outcome: A hand-drawn station plan places the observer above the harbor, while the digital archive uses a sheltered inland site. Amara notes that two valid stations may have experienced different conditions.
choices.memoryHint: The notebook and official archive describe different observation sites.

chapters.title: The Missing Margin
chapters.setting: A library table covered in weather charts
chapters.intro: The notebook includes a clipped newspaper notice asking harbor workers to secure loose equipment. Its edge hides the publication date. Amara has found a local warning, but she needs to establish when it was issued before drawing conclusions from it.
chapters.objective: Choose the strongest route to date the notice.

choices.label: Find the newspaper edition
choices.outcome: A bound newspaper volume contains the complete notice with its date and page number. Amara adds the citation to her notes. The warning preceded the recorded observations by several hours.
choices.memoryHint: A dated newspaper confirms the local warning was issued in advance.

choices.label: Compare the harbor ledger
choices.outcome: A harbor ledger records the same equipment notice and names the station that sent it. Amara photographs the relevant page with permission and records the archive reference.
choices.memoryHint: The harbor ledger independently records the warning and its source.

chapters.title: What the Record Can Say
chapters.intro: The sources describe a cautious local warning during conditions that differed across the coast. There is no need to invent a catastrophe or accuse the archive of concealment. Amara can now choose how to communicate the disagreement without flattening it into a dramatic headline.
chapters.objective: Choose the clearest way to explain the evidence.

choices.label: Build a site comparison
choices.outcome: Amara plots the two observation sites beside their surviving readings. The display explains exposure, instrument limits and gaps. Visitors can see why apparently conflicting records may both contain useful information.
choices.memoryHint: A site comparison explains the differences and limits of the records.

choices.label: Publish an annotated timeline
choices.outcome: Amara assembles the notice, observations and harbor ledger into a timeline, labeling every uncertain interval. The pattern becomes understandable without suggesting that a historical notebook can predict today’s weather.
choices.memoryHint: An annotated timeline separates documented observations from uncertainty.

chapters.title: A Clearer Horizon
chapters.setting: An open afternoon at Beacon Hill
chapters.intro: The station opens its archive exhibit. Amara has traced a forgotten warning to a real local practice: observers shared cautious information even when their records were incomplete. The discovery can now become either an ongoing archive project or a practical lesson in reading evidence.
chapters.objective: Choose what the station builds from the discovery.

choices.label: Open a community archive desk
choices.outcome: The station establishes a process for documenting donated weather records, with provenance checks and clear access rules. Amara files the notebook as the first case, still marked with its uncertainties. The archive has become easier to question and improve.
choices.memoryHint: A community archive desk preserves local observations with provenance checks.

choices.label: Create an observation workshop
choices.outcome: Amara prepares a workshop about historical instruments, measurement sites and uncertainty, with a clear reminder to use official services for current warnings. The last slide shows two places under one sky, each worth listening to.
choices.memoryHint: An observation workshop teaches careful evidence reading and official-warning awareness.

chapters.title: The Forecast Nobody Filed
chapters.setting: A station desk at first light
chapters.intro: Amara finds a box of warnings that were written, signed, and never issued. They are forty years old, local, and cautious. Her station is about to publish its first public archive, and these pages were meant for the people still living on the hill.

echoes.amara_c1_a: You converted an old instrument scale before comparing records. These warnings use a scale nobody has calibrated in decades.
echoes.amara_c1_b: You found two valid stations on one hill. These warnings come from a third site that no longer exists.

chapters.objective: Decide how the unfiled warnings are handled.

choices.label: Publish them with a full methods note
choices.outcome: Amara scans every page, footnotes the scale and the missing site, and states that none of it is current advice. The archive adds a warning banner above its own exhibit. Nothing is dramatized; everything is dated.
choices.memoryHint: The old warnings are published with methods.

choices.label: Trace the observer's family first
choices.outcome: Amara locates the observer's daughter, who still has the original logbook. Together they compare handwriting and find two warnings that were revised before filing. The archive gains a second source and a living collaborator.
choices.memoryHint: The observer's family supplies a second source.

chapters.title: The Hill Under Pressure
chapters.setting: A planning office with a model
chapters.intro: A developer proposes homes on the lower slope where the old station stood. Amara has no authority over planning and no current flood model. She has a notebook, a newspaper, and a hundred years of caution that may or may not apply.

echoes.amara_c3_a: You built a site comparison instead of a headline. The review needs exactly that, at exactly the wrong speed.
echoes.amara_c3_b: Your annotated timeline labeled every uncertain interval. The planning deadline allows two weeks.

chapters.objective: Choose how to contribute to the review.

choices.label: Submit the historical record
choices.outcome: Amara files the notebook and its limits in the planning record, with a note that it is not a flood assessment. An engineer requests a modern survey. The homes are delayed by a season and built on higher ground.
choices.memoryHint: The historical record prompts a modern survey.

choices.label: Organize a public reading
choices.outcome: Amara holds an evening where residents read the old warnings aloud and station staff explain what the records cannot tell them. The planning meeting is packed. Nobody is told to evacuate anything; everybody is told to ask better questions.
choices.memoryHint: A public reading raises better questions.

chapters.title: The Warning That Traveled
chapters.intro: A volunteer forwards one of Amara's archived warnings as a live alert on a neighborhood app. It spreads for six hours before anyone corrects it. The station's name is attached. Amara can issue a sharp correction, or use the moment to teach.

echoes.amara_c4_a: Your archive desk set access rules and provenance checks. The app ignored all of them.
echoes.amara_c4_b: Your workshop taught people to read evidence. Someone read it too fast, and that is not the same as reading.

chapters.objective: Choose how the station responds.

choices.label: Correct it plainly and repeatedly
choices.outcome: The station issues a short correction in the same channels, then a second one, then a third. The app adds a date stamp to shared records. Six people say they had already left the hill and are glad they did.
choices.memoryHint: Repeated corrections add a date stamp.

choices.label: Publish a 'how this spread' account
choices.outcome: Amara traces the six hours of forwarding step by step, with the station's own role included. The account is shared more widely than the warning was, and one app developer calls to ask about provenance labels.
choices.memoryHint: A spread account prompts provenance labels.

chapters.title: What the Hill Remembers
chapters.intro: The archive desk is funded for another year. Amara can expand it across the coast, or keep one hill, one desk, and one relationship with the families who still live below the station. The barometer on the wall has been falling all afternoon.

echoes.amara_c2_a: A dated newspaper confirmed a warning that once mattered. Multiply that by every harbor on the coast.
echoes.amara_c2_b: The harbor ledger independently recorded the same warning. Independence is the thing an archive cannot invent.

chapters.objective: Choose the archive's next shape.

choices.label: Expand across the coast
choices.outcome: Amara builds a shared catalog with three other stations, each keeping its own rules and its own families. The first joint record is a warning that never needed to be issued, which she counts as a success.
choices.memoryHint: Three stations share one catalog.

choices.label: Keep one hill, one desk
choices.outcome: Amara stays, and the desk becomes the kind of place people bring things to because they know who will answer. She writes the station's first plain-language guide to reading its own archive. The barometer keeps falling, and she notes it.
choices.memoryHint: One desk becomes a trusted local archive.

title: The Unfinished Set
tagline: Build a stage for a story left unfinished.
premise: A theatre model reveals an alternate final scene never built for a long-closed community production.

chapters.title: The Door Behind the Model
chapters.intro: Felix is clearing the model cupboard before a community theatre exhibition. Behind a painted miniature wall, he finds a second doorway and a folded plan for a different final scene. The production file contains no explanation for the unused design.
chapters.objective: Choose which source to inspect first.

choices.label: Unfold the alternate plan
choices.outcome: The plan shows an open public square instead of the closed room used in the final production. A revision date confirms that it was a genuine design proposal. Felix logs it as an unused alternative, not a lost definitive ending.
choices.memoryHint: A dated alternate plan proposed an open-square final scene.

choices.label: Read the rehearsal notes
choices.outcome: A note asks whether the audience could see the doorway from the side seats. Felix recognizes a practical design problem rather than evidence of a creative dispute and adds it to the exhibition research.
choices.memoryHint: The rehearsal notes identify a sightline problem with the alternate doorway.

chapters.title: A Seat at the Edge
chapters.intro: The alternate set would have hidden an important entrance from several seats. Felix tests the old scale model with a small light and camera. The design still has something to offer, but reviving it will mean admitting why it failed the first time.
chapters.objective: Choose the first revision to test.

choices.label: Move the entrance forward
choices.outcome: Felix moves the model doorway toward the front of the stage and tests the view from both sides. The entrance becomes visible without adding height or blocking the main playing area. He records the change as a new design decision.
choices.memoryHint: Moving the doorway forward improves the side-seat view.

choices.label: Open the side wall
choices.outcome: Felix removes a non-structural model wall to create an open frame. The miniature test gives the audience a clearer view while retaining the suggestion of an interior. The exhibition can show both versions honestly.
choices.memoryHint: An open-frame revision improves sightlines while preserving the set’s idea.

chapters.title: Credit Where It Belongs
chapters.intro: The theatre can display the recovered plan and Felix’s new model together. Their relationship needs clear labels: one is an archived proposal, the other a present-day response. Felix considers how visitors might explore the design without confusing the two.
chapters.objective: Choose the exhibition format.

choices.label: Show the models side by side
choices.outcome: The original proposal and revised model sit on separate labeled plinths. Felix credits the documented designers and explains his own changes. Visitors can compare the decisions instead of being handed a story about an ending that never happened.
choices.memoryHint: Side-by-side models distinguish the archived design from Felix’s response.

choices.label: Build an illustrated process wall
choices.outcome: Felix arranges copies of the plans, sightline tests and revision sketches in order. Every contributor is credited where the records support it. The exhibit makes the work behind a stage visible.
choices.memoryHint: A process wall credits contributors and explains each revision.

chapters.title: The House Lights Rise
chapters.intro: The exhibition is ready. The unused design has become a complete, honestly credited project without pretending to be the original production. Felix can now give visitors a quiet way to look closely or a collaborative way to test how a stage changes with a point of view.
chapters.objective: Choose the exhibition’s closing experience.

choices.label: Offer a guided model viewing
choices.outcome: Small groups view the model from different seats while Felix explains the documented decisions. No one has to perform or share a personal memory. As the house lights rise, the once-hidden doorway becomes something everyone can see.
choices.memoryHint: A guided viewing makes the design accessible without demanding participation.

choices.label: Host a voluntary design table
choices.outcome: Visitors who wish to take part can sketch a doorway for an imaginary scene. Felix provides clear credit and display choices, with no collection of personal stories. The final table is full of different ways to make an entrance.
choices.memoryHint: A voluntary design table invites new ideas with clear consent and credit.

chapters.title: The Door That Was Cut
chapters.intro: The exhibition's success brings a proposal: rebuild the alternate set full-size for a one-night performance of the scene that was never staged. The script exists in fragments. The original designer's estate has opinions about the doorway.

echoes.felix_c1_a: You logged the alternate plan as an unused proposal. A performance would make it used.
echoes.felix_c1_b: You found a sightline problem, not a creative dispute. The estate has read your note and disagrees with the framing.

chapters.objective: Decide how the scene is staged.

choices.label: Stage it as a documented experiment
choices.outcome: Felix bills the night as a reconstruction test, with the fragments performed as fragments and the gaps read aloud. The audience watches a scene fail and succeed in the same hour. The estate approves the program.
choices.memoryHint: The scene is staged as an experiment.

choices.label: Let the estate direct the doorway
choices.outcome: The estate's representative chooses the open-square ending and writes a short program note about the designer's intent. Felix builds it faithfully and adds his own name only to the construction drawings, which is where it belongs.
choices.memoryHint: The estate directs the ending.

chapters.title: The Audience in the Dark
chapters.intro: At the first run, three audience members cannot see the crucial entrance from the side seats. The old problem is back, at full scale, and the performance is tomorrow. Felix can move the door again, or move the seats.

echoes.felix_c2_a: In the model, you moved the doorway forward. Full-size, the same fix costs the scene its central sightline.
echoes.felix_c2_b: You opened the side wall to solve the view. At full scale, an open wall reads as a different play.

chapters.objective: Choose what gives way.

choices.label: Move the seats
choices.outcome: Felix takes out twelve seats and rebuilds the side rake. The house is smaller and every seat works. The box office is furious for a day, then sells the remaining seats at a premium nobody expected.
choices.memoryHint: Twelve seats give way to the sightline.

choices.label: Re-stage the entrance in view
choices.outcome: Felix keeps the set and stages the entrance twice, once in shadow for each side of the house. It reads as a deliberate doubling. The designer's estate calls it an invention, and the audience calls it the best moment of the night.
choices.memoryHint: The entrance is doubled for both sides.

chapters.title: Whose Ending Is It
chapters.intro: The fragments leave the final line unresolved. Two actors propose different endings. A descendant of the original cast asks that the play end where the script ends, in silence. Felix has one rehearsal left.

echoes.felix_c3_a: Your side-by-side plinths let visitors compare without a verdict. This is the same problem with a curtain.
echoes.felix_c3_b: Your process wall credited every contributor. The ending has three contributors and no agreement.

chapters.objective: Choose the ending the audience receives.

choices.label: End where the script ends
choices.outcome: The last line is spoken, and then nothing. The silence lasts long enough to become uncomfortable, then long enough to become the point. The descendant weeps in the second row, and the cast holds the stage.
choices.memoryHint: The play ends in the script's silence.

choices.label: Stage all three endings
choices.outcome: The performance runs the final scene three times, each with a different ending, and the audience votes with light sticks. The result is chaotic, generous, and exactly what a community theatre is for. The descendant abstains.
choices.memoryHint: Three endings are staged and voted on.

chapters.title: The House Lights
chapters.setting: An empty auditorium, house lights up
chapters.intro: The one-night performance becomes a three-week run. The theatre offers Felix a permanent design post with a budget and a mandate to stage 'recovered works'. He can build an institution around rediscovery, or go back to building one set at a time.

echoes.felix_c4_a: Your guided viewings let people look closely without performing. An institution would need to protect that quiet.
echoes.felix_c4_b: Your voluntary design table gave everyone a doorway and a credit. A mandate would decide whose doorways get built.

chapters.objective: Choose what Felix builds next.

choices.label: Take the recovered-works post
choices.outcome: Felix builds a small program with strict rules: every recovered work is labeled, every contributor credited, no ending invented. Three seasons in, the theatre has a reputation for honesty that outlasts any single hit.
choices.memoryHint: A recovered-works program opens honestly.

choices.label: Keep building one set at a time
choices.outcome: Felix declines and returns to the scene shop. He takes a job on a new play by a first-time writer, with a doorway nobody can see from the side seats. He knows exactly how to fix it, and he waits to be asked.
choices.memoryHint: Felix returns to one set at a time.

title: A Window for the Rain
tagline: Make room for light without putting anyone on display.
premise: A community hall commissions a new window that must balance daylight, privacy and a view of the courtyard.

chapters.title: Light on the Workbench
chapters.intro: Sylvie sets a clear blue sample beside a softly textured pane. The community hall needs daylight for its reading tables, while the room beside the courtyard needs privacy. One beautiful window will have to answer more than one request.
chapters.objective: Choose the first question the design should answer.

choices.label: Test the daylight
choices.outcome: The clear sample carries a bright patch across the model reading table. Sylvie records when the light becomes uncomfortable and keeps the textured sample available for areas facing the courtyard.
choices.memoryHint: The clear sample carries a bright patch across the model reading table.

choices.label: Test the privacy
choices.outcome: The textured sample softens silhouettes while allowing a gentle blue glow. Sylvie records where it works, leaving a clear upper strip in the model so the hall can still see the sky.
choices.memoryHint: The textured sample softens silhouettes while allowing a gentle blue glow.

chapters.title: The Color of a Cloud
chapters.intro: A visit to the empty hall shows how quickly its light changes. The window will need to work on gray afternoons as well as bright evenings. Sylvie arranges removable sample panels so the committee can compare them without committing to an installation.
chapters.objective: Choose a sample arrangement for the review.

choices.label: Keep a quiet blue border
choices.outcome: A restrained blue border leaves most of the pane neutral. The committee can compare the sky and reading surfaces without strong color casts, while the border gives the hall a recognizable detail.
choices.memoryHint: A restrained blue border leaves most of the pane neutral.

choices.label: Use small scattered color
choices.outcome: Sylvie distributes small blue pieces across a neutral field. The room gains points of color rather than a full wash, and the review notes explain where each patch falls during the day.
choices.memoryHint: Sylvie distributes small blue pieces across a neutral field.

echoes.sylvie_c1_a: The clear sample carries a bright patch across the model reading table.
echoes.sylvie_c1_b: The textured sample softens silhouettes while allowing a gentle blue glow.

chapters.title: A Window at Sitting Height
chapters.intro: The sample review includes visitors who use the hall differently: seated readers, standing volunteers and people sensitive to glare. Sylvie has no reason to assume that one viewpoint represents them all. The mock-up can support another focused test.
chapters.objective: Choose the next review method.

choices.label: Compare seated views
choices.outcome: Sylvie places the mock-up at several sitting heights and records voluntary feedback. A lower band is adjusted so readers can look into the courtyard without being silhouetted from outside.
choices.memoryHint: Sylvie places the mock-up at several sitting heights and records voluntary feedback.

choices.label: Compare gentle light
choices.outcome: Sylvie arranges a low-glare comparison under different room lights. The team selects a softer transition between clear and textured areas and documents which questions still need an on-site check.
choices.memoryHint: Sylvie arranges a low-glare comparison under different room lights.

echoes.sylvie_c2_a: A restrained blue border leaves most of the pane neutral.
echoes.sylvie_c2_b: Sylvie distributes small blue pieces across a neutral field.

chapters.title: The First Rain
chapters.setting: The hall before its opening evening
chapters.intro: The approved design is installed by the qualified team. Rain beads against the new pane while the hall prepares to reopen. Sylvie can leave behind a record of how the window was made or a small way for visitors to explore its light.
chapters.objective: Choose the window’s lasting invitation.

choices.label: Keep the sample library
choices.outcome: The hall keeps labeled sample pieces in a secure display drawer, with the design decisions explained beside them. Visitors can see how privacy and daylight shaped the finished work. Sylvie leaves the room lit from within.
choices.memoryHint: The hall keeps labeled sample pieces in a secure display drawer, with the design decisions explained beside them.

choices.label: Make a light-study booklet
choices.outcome: Sylvie prepares an illustrated booklet showing the mock-ups, feedback and final adjustments. The window becomes a readable example of a shared decision, and the reading table remains a place to sit rather than a stage.
choices.memoryHint: Sylvie prepares an illustrated booklet showing the mock-ups, feedback and final adjustments.

echoes.sylvie_c3_a: Sylvie places the mock-up at several sitting heights and records voluntary feedback.
echoes.sylvie_c3_b: Sylvie arranges a low-glare comparison under different room lights.

chapters.title: The Room That Wants a Copy
chapters.setting: The hall's north day room, mid-morning
chapters.intro: Three months after the hall reopened, Sylvie stands in the north day room holding a level against the sill. Her window is on the cover of the annual report, and the committee has raised money on one plain promise: the same window, matched, for the room where the stroke group meets on Tuesdays. This room is half the height and faces west. By eleven the room is bright with reflected light; by four the sun will be low enough to reach people's eyes. Nadia, who chairs the hall, has the fabricator's quote in one hand and a donor dinner on Thursday. The group's coordinator has asked twice whether the room will be brighter.
chapters.objective: Choose how to answer the committee's promise of a matching window.

choices.label: Measure the north room
choices.outcome: Sylvie books a week of readings and pays for the meter herself. The west light comes in low and hard; the textured band that protected the hall's courtyard readers would sit exactly at seated eye level here. On Friday she tells Nadia the room needs a different answer. The donor dinner happens without a design, and the fabricator holds the quote for thirty days.
choices.memoryHint: Book a week of west-light readings before answering the committee.

choices.label: Reuse the hall pattern
choices.outcome: Sylvie carries the hall's proportions across to the smaller opening and orders the glass in the same blue. The sample drawer gives up its exact batch number. In the mock-up, the clear upper strip falls where the afternoon sun crosses a seated face; she marks it, asks the group's coordinator for one afternoon of testing, and signs the order so the deposit is not lost.
choices.memoryHint: Reuse the hall batch number for a smaller west opening.

echoes.sylvie_c1_a: You tested daylight first, following the clear sample's bright patch until it turned uncomfortable, and the committee now promises the same answer next door.
echoes.sylvie_c1_b: You began with privacy, softening silhouettes while keeping a clear strip of sky, and the annex budget now assumes that answer.

chapters.title: The Photograph at Dusk
chapters.setting: The hall, half an hour before sunset
chapters.intro: The hall is shortlisted for a civic building award, and the assessor's visit lands on the shortest evening of the month. He wants the window photographed at dusk with the reading tables occupied, because an empty room, he says, tells a funder nothing. For three months Sylvie has kept the room's users out of the glass's argument. The award money would pay for the north room's second fabrication. Nadia has already asked four volunteers to stay late, and the photographer is setting up at the courtyard end, where the pane turns the whole room into a lit box.
chapters.objective: Decide what the award photograph is allowed to show.

choices.label: Stage the dusk photograph
choices.outcome: Sylvie agrees, on paper: four signed consent forms, no faces in close-up, and a caption she writes herself. The image runs across two pages of the trust's report with the caption cut to six words. The grant is confirmed in March. In April a volunteer's daughter emails the hall to ask why her mother's window, as she calls it, is on a recruitment leaflet.
choices.memoryHint: Allow four signed volunteers inside the dusk award photograph.

choices.label: Submit drawings only
choices.outcome: Sylvie sends measured elevations, the light readings and the sample photographs, and declines the staged evening. The assessor's note calls the entry reticent. The shortlist decision slips to spring, and the north room's fabrication money goes unconfirmed through the winter. One volunteer offers, twice, to be photographed anyway. Nadia asks her to reconsider before Friday, not angrily.
choices.memoryHint: Send measured elevations and light readings instead of a staged evening.

echoes.sylvie_c2_a: You kept a quiet blue border around a neutral pane, and that edge is the detail the award assessor wants photographed at dusk.
echoes.sylvie_c2_b: You scattered small blue pieces across a neutral field, and those patches are what the assessor's photographer is asking to catch at dusk.

chapters.title: The Panel at Ruth's Chair
chapters.setting: The hall reading room, Tuesday afternoon
chapters.intro: Ruth Aldous helped raise the money for the window and has read at the same table for nineteen years. Glaucoma has narrowed her view to a bright smear at the edge of things, and she has two requests. She wants a clear panel set at her chair height, and she wants Sylvie to sign the hall's access statement, which describes the window as fully accessible to all visitors. The statement goes to the funder in nine days. Ruth has already told two trustees that the artist agrees. Sylvie has the mock-up photographs in her bag and no idea what a signature is worth here.
chapters.objective: Decide what to sign and what to change for Ruth.

choices.label: Sign with a qualifier
choices.outcome: Sylvie signs, having added a line that names what was tested, with whom, and what remains unknown. The funder's form will not accept the addition and returns it. The committee rewrites the sentence in its own words and resubmits. A clear panel is cut for Ruth's chair. She thanks Sylvie for the glass and does not mention the statement again.
choices.memoryHint: Sign the access statement only with a written qualifier.

choices.label: Decline the statement
choices.outcome: Sylvie refuses to sign and sends the test records instead, with the panel order attached. Ruth's daughter writes to the committee asking why her mother's request became a paperwork argument. The north room commission is put back on the agenda for review. On Tuesday Ruth sits two tables further from the courtyard, where the light is softer, and reads.
choices.memoryHint: Refuse the access statement and send test records to the funder.

echoes.sylvie_c3_a: You tested the mock-up at several sitting heights, taking voluntary feedback, so Ruth's request from her chair arrives as data rather than sentiment.
echoes.sylvie_c3_b: You chose the low-glare comparison under different room lights, and Ruth now reads that softness as the thing standing between her and the courtyard.

chapters.title: Two Rooms, Two Windows
chapters.setting: The glazing workshop, an hour before opening
chapters.intro: The north room money arrives in spring, smaller than promised and tied to a delivery date. Sylvie can take the second window on herself, which means a new study, a new pattern and a room that will not match the one on the annual report. Or she can hand the method to Colm Rees, the fabricator's glazier, who has cut every piece of the first window and has never designed anything. The sample drawer sits open between them. Outside, the van is waiting to take the first batch of glass to the north room.
chapters.objective: Choose who will design the north room's window, and how.

choices.label: Build the second window
choices.outcome: Sylvie takes the commission and spends the spring on the west light. The new pattern is narrower, denser at the top, and answers the afternoon properly. It also looks nothing like the window the donors paid for. One donor asks that her name be taken off the north room plaque. The room opens in September, four weeks late, and the stroke group sits in it without squinting.
choices.memoryHint: Take the north commission alone and redraw for west light.

choices.label: Hand over the method
choices.outcome: Sylvie writes the sequence down, hands Colm the drawer, and stands behind him while he sets the first panel. His window is rougher, brighter, and finished on the day it was promised. At the opening he thanks her by name and then answers every question himself. She stands at the back of the room, in the part of the floor where the old window throws its border.
choices.memoryHint: Write the method down and stand behind Colm at the bench.

echoes.sylvie_c4_a: You left labeled samples in a drawer, decisions explained beside them, and that drawer is now the north room's only teacher.
echoes.sylvie_c4_b: You wrote the light-study booklet, mock-ups, feedback and final adjustments, and a copy of it now sits in the annex's funding file.

title: The Bowl with Two Histories
tagline: A repair can be honest and beautiful at the same time.
premise: A donated bowl contains two old repair styles and one fragment that may belong to another object.

chapters.title: The Unmatched Curve
chapters.intro: Mateo lays the donated bowl on a padded support. An older repair joins most of its body, while a pale fragment sits loosely beside the rim. The donor’s note calls it complete, but the material does not yet support that claim.
chapters.objective: Choose the first non-invasive comparison.

choices.label: Compare the surfaces
choices.outcome: Under even light, Mateo records a different glaze texture on the loose fragment. He keeps it beside the bowl rather than fitting it, giving the uncertain piece its own entry in the condition report.
choices.memoryHint: Under even light, Mateo records a different glaze texture on the loose fragment.

choices.label: Compare the profiles
choices.outcome: A tracing shows that the loose fragment curves more tightly than the surviving rim. Mateo documents the mismatch with a scale drawing and keeps the fragment safely separate for further study.
choices.memoryHint: A tracing shows that the loose fragment curves more tightly than the surviving rim.

chapters.title: An Older Kind of Care
chapters.intro: The older repair appears stable, and a dated photograph shows that it has been part of the bowl for decades. Mateo can preserve that evidence during treatment without assuming it represents the original maker’s intention. The client asks what should remain visible.
chapters.objective: Choose how to explain the treatment plan.

choices.label: Keep the repair visible
choices.outcome: Mateo proposes cleaning and stabilizing the object while retaining the old join as a documented part of its history. The client understands that visible repair is a conservation decision, not a defect being ignored.
choices.memoryHint: Mateo proposes cleaning and stabilizing the object while retaining the old join as a documented part of its history.

choices.label: Make a treatment diagram
choices.outcome: Mateo prepares a diagram distinguishing original ceramic, old repair and uncertain additions. It supports a cautious treatment plan and gives the client a clear record without promising an invisible restoration.
choices.memoryHint: Mateo prepares a diagram distinguishing original ceramic, old repair and uncertain additions.

echoes.mateo_c1_a: Under even light, Mateo records a different glaze texture on the loose fragment.
echoes.mateo_c1_b: A tracing shows that the loose fragment curves more tightly than the surviving rim.

chapters.title: A Place for the Fragment
chapters.intro: The uncertain fragment cannot responsibly be attached to the bowl. That does not make it useless. Mateo considers how an exhibit could show the difference between a coherent object and a convenient story about completeness.
chapters.objective: Choose the fragment’s display context.

choices.label: Use a separate support
choices.outcome: A small independent support places the fragment near the bowl without suggesting a join. The caption explains what is known and what remains uncertain, allowing visitors to compare their curves for themselves.
choices.memoryHint: A small independent support places the fragment near the bowl without suggesting a join.

choices.label: Use an illustrated comparison
choices.outcome: The bowl is displayed with a drawing of the loose fragment and the profile comparison. The fragment stays in protected storage, while the exhibit still explains why it was excluded from the treatment.
choices.memoryHint: The bowl is displayed with a drawing of the loose fragment and the profile comparison.

echoes.mateo_c2_a: Mateo proposes cleaning and stabilizing the object while retaining the old join as a documented part of its history.
echoes.mateo_c2_b: Mateo prepares a diagram distinguishing original ceramic, old repair and uncertain additions.

chapters.title: What Complete Can Mean
chapters.intro: The stabilized bowl is ready to return to the collection. Mateo has preserved its repairs and kept the uncertain fragment distinct. The final record can emphasize the object’s documented journey or the careful decisions that prevented a misleading reconstruction.
chapters.objective: Choose the final interpretation.

choices.label: Tell the material history
choices.outcome: The collection record follows the surviving ceramic, dated repair and separate fragment without filling the gaps with invented owners. The bowl remains incomplete in form, but its account is more complete than before.
choices.memoryHint: The collection record follows the surviving ceramic, dated repair and separate fragment without filling the gaps with invented owners.

choices.label: Show the decisions
choices.outcome: Mateo creates a concise display of the questions asked during treatment, with photographs and clear limits. Visitors leave knowing that a good restoration can include choosing not to add a piece.
choices.memoryHint: Mateo creates a concise display of the questions asked during treatment, with photographs and clear limits.

echoes.mateo_c3_a: A small independent support places the fragment near the bowl without suggesting a join.
echoes.mateo_c3_b: The bowl is displayed with a drawing of the loose fragment and the profile comparison.

chapters.title: A Letter from Bellhaven
chapters.intro: Four months after the exhibit closed, a letter arrives from the county museum in Bellhaven. Their own repaired bowl has a gap along one side, and the curator has measured it against the profile drawing published in Mateo's exhibit catalogue. The curve agrees to within two millimetres. She asks whether the loose fragment might travel for a supervised fitting test, and whether the donor's family has been consulted. Mateo reads the letter twice, then lifts the fragment's box from the shelf and sets it under the lamp. The fragment is kept in its own box, labeled as an uncertain addition, and has not been part of anything since the exhibition closed.
chapters.objective: Choose how the fragment meets the Bellhaven bowl.

choices.label: Send it for fitting
choices.outcome: The fragment travels by courier in a padded box, with a condition report and two sets of photographs. At Bellhaven it settles into the gap without pressure and without quite seating. The curator calls the result encouraging and asks to keep it for a season of further study. Mateo agrees to six weeks, then spends the six weeks wondering what encouraging will become in her board's minutes.
choices.memoryHint: Send the fragment to Bellhaven with a condition report.

choices.label: Request a profile cast
choices.outcome: Mateo asks Bellhaven to send a silicone profile cast and a set of measured photographs instead. The comparison is suggestive, no more; two curves agreeing is not a join. Bellhaven's director reads the request as a refusal and says so in a letter copied to the donor's family. The family asks Mateo, reasonably, why he will not simply look at the thing.
choices.memoryHint: Ask Bellhaven for a silicone profile cast instead of the bowl.

echoes.mateo_c1_a: You compared the surfaces, recording a different glaze texture on the loose fragment, and that separate entry is what the other museum's letter now cites.
echoes.mateo_c1_b: You traced the fragment's profile and found it curved more tightly than the surviving rim, and someone now claims their own bowl explains that curve.

chapters.title: The Sentence in the Grant
chapters.setting: The lab director's office, Friday afternoon
chapters.intro: Director Alcott has a grant application on the desk and one sentence highlighted. It describes the fragment as likely part of the Bellhaven bowl, and the acquisition funding depends on the phrase. She wants Mateo's co-signature as the conservator who examined it. His condition report, three lines down, says only that the fragment is consistent with the bowl's profile. The application closes Friday. Alcott points out, kindly, that his contract comes up for renewal in the autumn. The fragment sits in its box three metres away, and the sentence has already been read by two people who will never examine it.
chapters.objective: Decide whether to co-sign the grant's central claim.

choices.label: Sign the softer wording
choices.outcome: Mateo signs after changing likely part of to consistent with, and the grant advances to a second round. The museum's press release quotes the original phrase anyway, having taken it from the draft. Alcott apologises and asks him to stand in a photograph with both bowls. He stands where the light shows the gap in each of them, and the photographer asks him to move left.
choices.memoryHint: Change likely part of to consistent with before co-signing.

choices.label: Refuse to co-sign
choices.outcome: Mateo declines and submits his measured drawing in place of a signature. The application goes forward without him and stalls in the second round. Alcott stops copying him on correspondence about the fragment. In September his contract renewal is listed as under review, and the fragment's box stays on the shelf, opened every few weeks for the humidity check.
choices.memoryHint: Submit a measured drawing where the grant expects a signature.

echoes.mateo_c2_a: You argued for keeping the old join visible as documented history, and now you are asked to smooth a different uncertainty into one clean sentence.
echoes.mateo_c2_b: You made a treatment diagram separating original ceramic from old repair and uncertain additions, and the director wants only its most definite line.

chapters.title: What Clara Wants Written
chapters.setting: The gallery loading bay, after hours
chapters.intro: Clara Wexford donated her grandmother's bowl and has come to the loading bay with the exhibition catalogue under her arm. She has read what Mateo wrote about the bowl, the notes that follow ceramic, dated repair and separate fragment without filling the gaps. She says the family name is now attached, permanently, to a word she has come to hate: incomplete. She asks him to write, for the Bellhaven file, that the fragment belongs with the other bowl, so the family can be finished with the question. The bay doors are open and the evening air smells of wet stone.
chapters.objective: Decide how far to go in accommodating Clara's request.

choices.label: Write only compatibility
choices.outcome: Mateo writes three lines stating that the fragment is materially consistent with the Bellhaven profile and that no join has been demonstrated. He sends Clara a copy before anyone else sees it. She reads it at the loading door, folds it once, and says it is a very careful piece of paper. The family withdraws its support for the loan, and Clara stops coming by the lab on Fridays.
choices.memoryHint: Write compatibility without a demonstrated join for the family file.

choices.label: Record her reading
choices.outcome: Mateo adds a paragraph to the file, in the family's own words and clearly attributed, saying that the donor's family reads the fragment as belonging with the Bellhaven bowl. Clara cries a little and then laughs at herself. The paragraph does its work. Eighteen months later a dealer quotes it in a sale listing with the attribution quietly gone, and Mateo has to write to the auction house.
choices.memoryHint: Add the family reading as an attributed paragraph in the file.

echoes.mateo_c3_a: You gave the fragment its own support, near the bowl without suggesting a join, and Clara now asks you to write the join into words.
echoes.mateo_c3_b: You kept the fragment in storage and let a drawing carry the comparison, and Clara wants the family's reading to travel beside it.

chapters.title: Two Bowls, One Case
chapters.intro: The comparison leaves the question where Mateo found it: consistent, unproven, and now shared between two institutions. Bellhaven proposes a joint technical note, signed by both conservators, publishing both profiles and the test photographs. Their board proposes something else as well, a single case for a season, both bowls side by side with the fragment on its own support between them. The case is already being measured. Mateo is asked which proposal he will put his name to. Both institutions have sent a courier schedule, and neither has sent a lawyer.
chapters.objective: Choose what the two bowls become to each other.

choices.label: Publish the joint note
choices.outcome: Mateo signs the note. Both profiles are printed at the same scale, the test photographs run unretouched, and the conclusion says what it can. The fragment stays in its own collection. A small ceramics journal reprints the note, and for a year it is cited in exactly the way he hoped. The Bellhaven case is built anyway, holding one bowl and a great deal of empty space.
choices.memoryHint: Publish both profiles at one scale with unretouched test photographs.

choices.label: Agree the joint display
choices.outcome: Mateo agrees to the case, on condition that each bowl keeps its own label and the fragment keeps its own support. Visitors call it a reunion within a week; the labels are read by almost nobody. He spends an afternoon on the lighting, angling it so each bowl's gap stays visible to anyone who looks up. On the last day he watches a child point at the space between them.
choices.memoryHint: Share one case while keeping separate labels and support.

echoes.mateo_c4_a: You let the record follow ceramic, dated repair and separate fragment without invented owners; the joint note now asks for that discipline from two institutions.
echoes.mateo_c4_b: You showed the questions asked during treatment, including choosing not to add a piece; a joint display now risks reading those as reunion.

title: The Untranslatable Invitation
tagline: Find the welcome inside an ambiguous sentence.
premise: An old festival invitation can mean either an invitation to arrive or a promise to leave a place for someone.

chapters.title: Two Ways to Begin
chapters.intro: Ines places a facsimile invitation beside two draft translations. The sentence is short, but its purpose is uncertain: it could ask someone to attend or tell them that a place is already waiting. A festival exhibit needs a responsible English version.
chapters.objective: Choose which evidence to examine first.

choices.label: Read the surrounding notes
choices.outcome: A planning note describes welcoming returning residents rather than recruiting an audience. Ines marks it as context supporting the reserved-place reading, while keeping the alternative visible in her working draft.
choices.memoryHint: A planning note describes welcoming returning residents rather than recruiting an audience.

choices.label: Compare repeated phrases
choices.outcome: Other invitations in the same file use the phrase before a named place setting. Ines records the comparison as support for a welcoming formula rather than claiming that the phrase has only one possible meaning.
choices.memoryHint: Other invitations in the same file use the phrase before a named place setting.

chapters.title: The Intended Reader
chapters.intro: A reply survives beside the invitation, thanking the organizers for remembering an absent friend. It supports the idea of keeping a place, but the exhibit audience will not have that private context. Ines needs a translation that can carry its meaning without exposing unnecessary details.
chapters.objective: Choose how to provide context.

choices.label: Add a short translator’s note
choices.outcome: Ines writes a brief note explaining that the invitation reassured a returning guest. It uses only details cleared for display and separates contextual evidence from the translated sentence itself.
choices.memoryHint: Ines writes a brief note explaining that the invitation reassured a returning guest.

choices.label: Pair the two readings
choices.outcome: The exhibit draft shows both defensible readings with a plain explanation of the reply’s relevance. Ines leaves the audience room to see the choice rather than presenting a single English sentence as inevitable.
choices.memoryHint: The exhibit draft shows both defensible readings with a plain explanation of the reply’s relevance.

echoes.ines_c1_a: A planning note describes welcoming returning residents rather than recruiting an audience.
echoes.ines_c1_b: Other invitations in the same file use the phrase before a named place setting.

chapters.title: A Welcome That Travels
chapters.intro: The draft now reaches readers unfamiliar with the festival’s customs. A phrase that felt warm in the source can sound possessive in English. Ines asks the review team to compare an explicit invitation with a gentler expression of welcome.
chapters.objective: Choose the main display wording.

choices.label: Make the invitation explicit
choices.outcome: The display uses clear language about a place being available to the returning guest. The translator’s note records the ambiguity, preserving the evidence without making visitors decode the exhibit to understand its welcome.
choices.memoryHint: The display uses clear language about a place being available to the returning guest.

choices.label: Keep the gentle ambiguity
choices.outcome: The display preserves the image of a place being kept, followed by a readable explanation. Ines makes clear that this is a considered literary choice, not the only correct version of the original.
choices.memoryHint: The display preserves the image of a place being kept, followed by a readable explanation.

echoes.ines_c2_a: Ines writes a brief note explaining that the invitation reassured a returning guest.
echoes.ines_c2_b: The exhibit draft shows both defensible readings with a plain explanation of the reply’s relevance.

chapters.title: Names Beneath the Words
chapters.intro: The translated invitation is ready, and the necessary permissions are recorded. Ines can end the project by documenting the translation process or by inviting visitors to compare clearly labeled alternatives. Neither choice needs to turn private correspondence into public spectacle.
chapters.objective: Choose the exhibit’s closing element.

choices.label: Publish the translation record
choices.outcome: A concise record credits the source, permissions and translation decisions. Future readers can trace why the English wording was chosen. Ines files her working notes knowing that clarity has not required pretending away uncertainty.
choices.memoryHint: A concise record credits the source, permissions and translation decisions.

choices.label: Offer a comparison card
choices.outcome: Visitors receive a card with the two readings, their supporting context and a clear credit to the translation team. The exhibit ends with an invitation to read carefully, not a contest to discover a secret correct answer.
choices.memoryHint: Visitors receive a card with the two readings, their supporting context and a clear credit to the translation team.

echoes.ines_c3_a: The display uses clear language about a place being available to the returning guest.
echoes.ines_c3_b: The display preserves the image of a place being kept, followed by a readable explanation.

chapters.title: The Line in the Stone
chapters.setting: The festival gateway, three weeks before opening
chapters.intro: The revived festival has commissioned a stone threshold for its east gate, and the committee's designer has taken the invitation's welcome as the inscription. The masons are cutting next week. Ines sees the proof on a Tuesday: one reading, cut clean, no note, no second face. The sentence she spent a season keeping uncertain is about to become civic furniture, fixed in a place where nobody will ever ask what else it might have meant. The committee chair calls it the heart of the project. The proof is a rubbing on thin paper, and the letters are already the right size for a doorway.
chapters.objective: Decide what the stone is permitted to say.

choices.label: Approve the carved line
choices.outcome: Ines approves the inscription on one condition: a second, smaller line on the reverse face, naming the source and the other reading. The masons cut both. At installation the reverse face goes into the footing, against the drainage bed, and the second line is unreadable without a torch and a reason. The chair promises a plaque in the spring. The gate opens on schedule, and the sentence is already permanent.
choices.memoryHint: Approve one line with a second reading cut on the reverse.

choices.label: Hold the stone
choices.outcome: Ines withholds approval until the committee agrees to cut both readings, one above the other, each attributed. The masons stand down for a week and the gate opens with a painted plywood panel over the gap. A donor who paid for the stone asks to be introduced to her. The program is already printed with the single line, and the chair stops returning her calls for four days.
choices.memoryHint: Withhold approval until both readings are cut and attributed.

echoes.ines_c1_a: You read the surrounding notes first and marked the reserved-place reading, keeping the alternative visible, and the masons are now cutting only one of them.
echoes.ines_c1_b: You compared repeated phrases before a named place setting and recorded them as support, not proof; the festival now wants the phrase on stone.

chapters.title: A Name for the Recipient
chapters.setting: The archive reading room, Thursday morning
chapters.intro: A woman named Maren Fenwick writes to the archive with a photograph of the same invitation, kept in her family since the festival. The recipient, she says, was her great-aunt, who left the coast at twenty and came back at sixty-one. The archive director wants the name in the exhibit before a funding bid on the theme of return, and the bid language is already drafted. Ines has the translation, the note and the permissions, and none of them covers a living family's private letter. The letter is two pages, polite, and certain of its facts.
chapters.objective: Decide whether the recipient gets her name back.

choices.label: Ask the family to consent
choices.outcome: Ines drafts the label with Maren, gives her the final wording, and waits three weeks for the family's written consent. The name goes in, with a sentence about the letter's privacy that the director finds excessive. The bid succeeds. A cousin writes to the archive asking how a letter to one woman became a public exhibit, and the label has to be reprinted in the second week.
choices.memoryHint: Draft the label with Maren and wait for written consent.

choices.label: Keep the recipient unnamed
choices.outcome: Ines describes the recipient only as a returning resident and thanks Maren in the acknowledgements, without the name. The director asks for a memo explaining the decision and forwards it to the bid committee. The bid is rewritten with a weaker theme and comes in second. Maren sends a short, correct email saying she had hoped her great-aunt would be more than a category.
choices.memoryHint: Describe the recipient as a returning resident and thank Maren only.

echoes.ines_c2_a: You wrote a short translator's note from cleared details only, and the archive now wants a name where that note deliberately kept one out.
echoes.ines_c2_b: You paired both readings with a plain explanation of the reply, and the archive now wants a single name to sit under them.

chapters.title: The Second Name
chapters.setting: The exhibit office, late on a Wednesday
chapters.intro: Dara Osei translated the first draft of three labels, including the sentence that eventually became the exhibit's opening. Ines cut her looser rendering in review and rewrote the line herself. Now Dara has a residency application due Friday and asks to be credited as co-translator, because a research assistant credit will not open the door. The archive's house style allows one named translator per exhibit. The application form has a single line for it.
