Ines has the drafts in a folder, and the folder is the entire argument for either answer.
chapters.objective: Decide whose name the translation carries, and in what words.

choices.label: Credit her as co-translator
choices.outcome: Ines adds Dara's name to the label and a line in the record naming which passages began as hers. The archive's editor objects to a two-name credit and asks for a memo. The residency panel writes back asking who translated what, exactly. Dara answers the letter herself, at length, and sends Ines a copy. The label is reprinted once, in a smaller font, above the fold of the case.
choices.memoryHint: Add Dara to the label and name the passages she began.

choices.label: Offer a separate credit
choices.outcome: Ines offers a research assistant credit, a reference letter and her own draft pages as work samples. Dara says the panel will not count any of it, takes the letter anyway, and stops coming to the Wednesday reviews. The label keeps one name. Ines reads her own sentence on the wall the following week and hears it in Dara's rhythm, which is the part she cannot record.
choices.memoryHint: Offer a research assistant credit, reference letter and draft pages.

echoes.ines_c3_a: You made the display explicit about a place being available and recorded the ambiguity in a note, and Dara asks which of those counts.
echoes.ines_c3_b: You kept the gentle image of a place being kept with a readable explanation, and Dara wants her looser line named in that choice.

chapters.title: The Sentence After the Festival
chapters.setting: The archive basement, the week after closing
chapters.intro: The festival is over and the exhibit comes down on a Monday. Two offers remain on Ines's desk. The archive would publish the whole translation dossier: every draft, Dara's marked passages, both readings, the correspondence in redacted form, as an open teaching text with her name on the introduction. The committee would rather she help them settle the gate for good, cover the threshold with a bronze plate naming the text as a historical quotation, and let the festival write a welcome of its own. Neither offer includes the other, and the basement is cold enough to see breath.
chapters.objective: Choose what the invitation becomes once the exhibit closes.

choices.label: Publish the whole dossier
choices.outcome: Ines spends the winter annotating. The dossier runs to ninety pages, including drafts she would not have chosen to show, and a seminar in another city adopts it. The carved line stays on the gate, now supported by a page reference. Maren reads the redacted reply and writes that the gaps are in the wrong places. Ines agrees, and the second printing carries her objection as a footnote.
choices.memoryHint: Publish every draft and marked passage as an open teaching text.

choices.label: Cover the carved line
choices.outcome: Ines helps draft the bronze plate, arguing for the words historical quotation and one date. The stonemason returns with a drill and sets four bolts; the plate sits proud of the stone. The festival writes a new welcome, plainer and better suited to a gate. The invitation goes under glass in the archive, where visitors lean close, and where the sentence finally has a room small enough for both readings.
choices.memoryHint: Set a bronze plate over the line, calling it historical quotation.

echoes.ines_c4_a: You published the translation record with source, permissions and decisions, and it is the only thing that could hold a dossier together now.
echoes.ines_c4_b: You handed visitors a comparison card with both readings and a clear credit, and the festival now wants one reading printed six metres wide.

title: The Crossing at Dusk
tagline: A crossing matters most when people can actually make it.
premise: A revised ferry timetable leaves a gap between the last bus and the final boat.

chapters.title: The Neat Timetable
chapters.intro: Silas compares a proposed ferry timetable with the evening bus service. The final connection fails by several minutes, even though each operator has met its own target. The harbor committee asks him to bring a practical recommendation rather than a dramatic complaint.
chapters.objective: Choose the first connection to examine.

choices.label: Trace the arriving route
choices.outcome: Silas follows the published bus arrival and the permitted walking route to the terminal. The connection needs more time than the timetable allows, and he records the gap without relying on an unrealistically fast walk.
choices.memoryHint: Silas follows the published bus arrival and the permitted walking route to the terminal.

choices.label: Compare boarding needs
choices.outcome: The operations records show that passengers need different amounts of boarding time. Silas documents the range with the crew and makes clear that a useful connection cannot be planned around the fastest passenger.
choices.memoryHint: The operations records show that passengers need different amounts of boarding time.

chapters.title: The Wait by the Water
chapters.intro: The committee can consider a later final sailing or an earlier connecting bus. Both require agreement from the operators and a safety review. Silas lays out the consequences for crews and passengers without promising that a timetable change is already approved.
chapters.objective: Choose the proposal to develop first.

choices.label: Propose a later sailing
choices.outcome: Silas prepares a limited later-sailing proposal with crew, operating and connection questions listed openly. It creates a plausible transfer window while leaving approval and safety checks with the responsible operators.
choices.memoryHint: Silas prepares a limited later-sailing proposal with crew, operating and connection questions listed openly.

choices.label: Propose a coordinated bus
choices.outcome: Silas asks the bus team to examine an earlier terminal connection and a clearer transfer notice. The proposal may solve the gap without extending ferry operations, but it needs evidence about other affected stops.
choices.memoryHint: Silas asks the bus team to examine an earlier terminal connection and a clearer transfer notice.

echoes.silas_c1_a: Silas follows the published bus arrival and the permitted walking route to the terminal.
echoes.silas_c1_b: The operations records show that passengers need different amounts of boarding time.

chapters.title: More Than a Departure Time
chapters.intro: A revised connection is ready for a supervised trial. Some passengers need a quiet place to wait; others need a route they can identify without asking a stranger. Silas has enough time to improve one part of the terminal before the trial begins.
chapters.objective: Choose the trial’s supporting improvement.

choices.label: Clarify the transfer route
choices.outcome: A simple route notice identifies the approved terminal approach and the correct boarding point. The team reviews it for readability and access, so the trial measures a usable connection rather than a confusing race between services.
choices.memoryHint: A simple route notice identifies the approved terminal approach and the correct boarding point.

choices.label: Improve the waiting area
choices.outcome: The committee prepares a sheltered, clearly identified waiting point within its approved facilities. Silas includes it in the trial information and records remaining access questions for the operator’s review.
choices.memoryHint: The committee prepares a sheltered, clearly identified waiting point within its approved facilities.

echoes.silas_c2_a: Silas prepares a limited later-sailing proposal with crew, operating and connection questions listed openly.
echoes.silas_c2_b: Silas asks the bus team to examine an earlier terminal connection and a clearer transfer notice.

chapters.title: A Crossing People Can Use
chapters.intro: The supervised trial produces useful feedback and operational records. A final timetable will still need formal approval. Silas can recommend a longer monitored trial or present a phased coordination plan that names the work still required.
chapters.objective: Choose the next accountable step.

choices.label: Extend the monitored trial
choices.outcome: The operators agree to review a longer limited trial under their own rules. Public notices clearly state its dates and limits. Silas leaves the cabin with a timetable that finally acknowledges the journey between its printed lines.
choices.memoryHint: The operators agree to review a longer limited trial under their own rules.

choices.label: Publish the coordination plan
choices.outcome: The committee publishes a phased plan with named responsibilities and unresolved questions. Passengers can see what is proposed and what remains unchanged. The harbor has gained a clearer process as well as a possible new connection.
choices.memoryHint: The committee publishes a phased plan with named responsibilities and unresolved questions.

echoes.silas_c3_a: A simple route notice identifies the approved terminal approach and the correct boarding point.
echoes.silas_c3_b: The committee prepares a sheltered, clearly identified waiting point within its approved facilities.

chapters.title: The Boat That Made the Cut
chapters.setting: The ticket cabin, first winter meeting
chapters.intro: A season after the review, the later sailing runs whenever the timetable allows and fills most of those nights. The operator now wants it made permanent, and the arithmetic requires dropping the 18:10, which has carried the fish market and the kitchen staff home for nineteen years. Silas has the trial sheets in front of him. His recommendation carried weight last time, and the committee will read whatever he writes as the answer. Outside the cabin window, the 18:10 is loading in the rain, half full, on time. The crew roster is pinned above the desk with a pencil line through December.
chapters.objective: Decide what to recommend about the permanent evening service.

choices.label: Accept the trade
choices.outcome: Silas supports the trade and negotiates a later bus from the terminal for the 18:10 regulars, forty minutes after their old crossing. Two of them stop coming to the market altogether. The later boat runs full through the winter, the counts look healthy, and at the spring meeting the operator thanks him by name for a clear recommendation. The 18:10 comes out of the printed timetable in April.
choices.memoryHint: Trade the 18:10 for a later bus from the terminal.

choices.label: Argue a seasonal split
choices.outcome: Silas proposes the later boat three nights a week and the 18:10 on the other four, from October to March. Approval takes another month and the timetable becomes two columns with a footnote. In the changeover week a market trader reads the wrong column and watches the boat leave. The 18:10 survives the winter; the later sailing runs half empty on Tuesdays and the operator asks him to explain why.
choices.memoryHint: Split the week three nights later, four nights at 18:10.

echoes.silas_c1_a: You traced the published bus arrival and the permitted walking route, and the connection you timed is now the one the operator proposes to cut.
echoes.silas_c1_b: You compared boarding needs with the crew and refused to plan around the fastest passenger, and the permanent proposal now plans around the fullest boat.

chapters.title: The Consultation File
chapters.intro: The harbour authority opens a formal consultation on the evening service, and the operator's submission arrives with Silas's trial figures attached. The boardings are counted at the gangway, so they show a later boat whose weeknight loading is still unsettled. They do not show the eleven people who stopped walking down to the terminal when the connection became unreliable, or the ones who now leave work early. Written responses close on Friday, and the operator's manager has asked for a quiet word before then. Silas wrote the tally sheet himself and knows exactly what it leaves out.
chapters.objective: Decide how the trial's numbers enter the public record.

choices.label: File a correction
choices.outcome: Silas files a correction with the raw sheets, the walking-away count and a plain account of how the gangway tally was taken. The panel asks the operator to respond in writing. The manager stops copying him on scheduling emails and starts routing crew queries through the harbour office. The consultation is extended three weeks, and the later boat's future is argued in public instead of decided in a room.
choices.memoryHint: Attach the raw sheets and the walking-away count to the consultation.

choices.label: File a joint addendum
choices.outcome: Silas drafts one paragraph with the manager, conceding that the counts measure boardings and not demand, and both names go on it. The panel accepts the addendum without comment. The manager agrees to fund a second trial in the spring and puts it in an email. The frame around the numbers stays as the operator wrote it, and Silas keeps the meeting he needs to get anything changed at all.
choices.memoryHint: Co-write one paragraph conceding the counts measure boardings only.

echoes.silas_c2_a: You built a limited later-sailing proposal with crew, operating and connection questions listed openly, and the operator is now quoting it back without those questions.
echoes.silas_c2_b: You asked the bus team for an earlier terminal connection and clearer transfer notice, and the consultation now treats that request as finished change.

chapters.title: What the Master Won't Write
chapters.setting: The ferry wheelhouse, after the last crossing
chapters.intro: Master Vance has run the evening boat for eleven years and asks Silas up to the wheelhouse after the last crossing, which is not a thing she does. In winter fog the turnaround at the outer pier leaves the crew twenty minutes against a schedule that assumes thirty. She wants the later sailing taken out of his recommendation. She will not put it in writing, because a written objection from the master goes to the operator as a refusal of duty. The vote is in nine days. The radar is on and the window is black.
chapters.objective: Decide how the master's objection reaches the record.

choices.label: Carry it as constraint
choices.outcome: Silas writes an operational constraint raised by crew into the recommendation, without a name. The panel asks which crew. There is one crew, and the question goes to the operator, who asks Master Vance directly whether she raised it. She does not deny it. The recommendation keeps its warning. On the next foggy Tuesday she takes the later boat out on the longer approach and says nothing at the gangway.
choices.memoryHint: Record the fog turnaround as an unnamed crew constraint.

choices.label: Attach a private note
choices.outcome: Silas leaves the recommendation clean and files the objection as a note to the safety review, which meets two days before the vote with a full agenda. The note is item nine. The vote proceeds on the timetable as written and the review endorses it in principle. Master Vance reads the minutes, finds her objection recorded as a crewing matter for the operator, and stops asking him to the wheelhouse.
choices.memoryHint: File the objection as a note to the safety review.

echoes.silas_c3_a: You clarified the transfer route so the trial measured a usable connection, and the master asks you now to leave one thing out.
echoes.silas_c3_b: You improved the sheltered waiting point and logged the access questions you could not answer, and the master's objection is one more of those.

chapters.title: The Winter Column
chapters.setting: The ticket cabin, the night before the vote
chapters.intro: The panel votes tomorrow and Silas has one page. One version keeps two evening crossings all year and writes a winter exception into the timetable: the 18:10 runs from April to September, the later boat all year, with the changeover printed in both columns. The other makes the later boat permanent and puts the saved money into a booked minibus for the 18:10 regulars, eight seats, telephone booking, no standing. Both fit on the page. The pencil is blunt. He has been awake since four and the harbour is quiet in the way it gets before a decision.
chapters.objective: Choose the evening the harbour will actually get.

choices.label: Write the winter exception
choices.outcome: Silas writes the winter exception and the panel passes it by one vote. The printer needs two editions of the timetable and the changeover week produces three arguments at the gangway. The crossing survives the fog, the crew gets its thirty minutes from October, and a woman who has used the 18:10 since she was nineteen tells him she will not trust a timetable with a season in it.
choices.memoryHint: Print both columns, with the 18:10 running April to September.

choices.label: Fund the booked minibus
choices.outcome: Silas writes the minibus and the operator takes the saving. The later boat runs all year, full by February. The minibus holds eight, leaves at 18:25, and needs booking by four; two regulars do not have a phone that takes the confirmation text. He drives the first week himself, in his own time, and the panel records the arrangement as a pilot with no named successor.
choices.memoryHint: Put the saving into eight booked seats leaving at 18:25.

echoes.silas_c4_a: You recommended a longer monitored trial with dates and limits posted, and the permanent decision now has to be made without one.
echoes.silas_c4_b: You published a phased plan with named responsibilities and unresolved questions, and the harbour now expects you to close the questions rather than name them.

title: The Rooftop Agreement
tagline: Make a rooftop plan that leaves room for neighbors.
premise: A rooftop apiary proposal needs the agreement of neighbors who use the building in very different ways.

chapters.title: Before the First Hive
chapters.intro: Tessa brings an apiary proposal to a building meeting. Some adults welcome the idea; others worry about using the roof and its access route. No hives have been installed. The first task is to understand concerns without treating them as obstacles to dismiss.
chapters.objective: Choose the first source of guidance.

choices.label: Invite voluntary concerns
choices.outcome: Tessa offers a private way to submit practical concerns without asking for medical histories. The responses identify access and communication needs that the site assessment must address before any installation is considered.
choices.memoryHint: Tessa offers a private way to submit practical concerns without asking for medical histories.

choices.label: Review the site assessment
choices.outcome: Tessa shares the qualified assessor’s site review in plain language. It identifies limits, responsibilities and unanswered questions, giving residents a common starting point without claiming that an assessment guarantees everyone’s comfort.
choices.memoryHint: Tessa shares the qualified assessor’s site review in plain language.

chapters.title: A Boundary That Means Something
chapters.intro: The assessment supports a smaller proposal with a clearly separated working area. Tessa can prioritize a revised placement or a stricter access agreement. Either approach must leave the shared roof usable and keep actual hive management with qualified staff.
chapters.objective: Choose the next revision.

choices.label: Rework the placement
choices.outcome: A qualified team revises the proposed location to improve separation from shared access. Tessa records the change and returns it for review, rather than treating a new drawing as permission to begin work.
choices.memoryHint: A qualified team revises the proposed location to improve separation from shared access.

choices.label: Define the access agreement
choices.outcome: Tessa drafts clear responsibilities, contact routes and limits for the proposed working area. Residents can review what the project would require, including how concerns would be raised and how the trial could be ended.
choices.memoryHint: Tessa drafts clear responsibilities, contact routes and limits for the proposed working area.

echoes.tessa_c1_a: Tessa offers a private way to submit practical concerns without asking for medical histories.
echoes.tessa_c1_b: Tessa shares the qualified assessor’s site review in plain language.

chapters.title: Learning Without Pressure
chapters.intro: The revised proposal is ready for a decision about a limited season. Tessa wants residents to understand what is being considered without pressuring anyone to visit a hive or take part. Two optional supporting activities could make the project easier to evaluate.
chapters.objective: Choose a low-pressure way to share information.

choices.label: Create a project information board
choices.outcome: A concise board explains the proposed scale, responsible staff and review dates. It avoids personal stories and medical claims, making it possible to follow the project without participating in an activity.
choices.memoryHint: A concise board explains the proposed scale, responsible staff and review dates.

choices.label: Offer a separate garden session
choices.outcome: An optional session discusses shared rooftop planting with the relevant specialists. It remains separate from hive access, allowing residents to explore the roof’s ecology without being asked to approach bees.
choices.memoryHint: An optional session discusses shared rooftop planting with the relevant specialists.

echoes.tessa_c2_a: A qualified team revises the proposed location to improve separation from shared access.
echoes.tessa_c2_b: Tessa drafts clear responsibilities, contact routes and limits for the proposed working area.

chapters.title: The Agreement in Writing
chapters.intro: The building has enough information to decide on a limited project. Tessa has promised neither universal support nor a permanent installation. She can recommend a small reviewed season or keep the roof focused on the shared garden while the apiary questions remain open.
chapters.objective: Choose the proposal Tessa takes forward.

choices.label: Recommend a reviewed season
choices.outcome: Tessa recommends a limited season only if the responsible parties approve the site and written conditions. Clear review dates and a route for concerns stay part of the plan. The project begins with accountability rather than a promise to stay forever.
choices.memoryHint: Tessa recommends a limited season only if the responsible parties approve the site and written conditions.

choices.label: Keep the garden first
choices.outcome: Tessa recommends postponing the apiary and advancing the shared garden work that already has agreement. The proposal remains documented for future review. Choosing a smaller project becomes a responsible outcome, not a failed ending.
choices.memoryHint: Tessa recommends postponing the apiary and advancing the shared garden work that already has agreement.

echoes.tessa_c3_a: A concise board explains the proposed scale, responsible staff and review dates.
echoes.tessa_c3_b: An optional session discusses shared rooftop planting with the relevant specialists.

chapters.title: The Second Roof
chapters.setting: A neighbouring tenants' hall, early evening
chapters.intro: Nine months after the rooftop review, Tessa is asked to repeat it. The tenants' association two streets east has read the building's written agreement and wants the same thing on their own roof: a smaller terrace, one stair, a shared laundry. They have a grant deadline and no coordinator. Tessa's hours come from a green-spaces budget that now carries a condition, a second site before the financial year closes. Saying yes keeps the first roof funded and splits her attention. Saying no means explaining to the first roof's volunteers why their monthly checks might shorten anyway.
chapters.objective: Decide whether the second roof gets her hours.

choices.label: Take the second roof
choices.outcome: Tessa accepts on paper: a six-month scope, the same private concern route, and a written cap of two visits a month. The first roof's volunteers get a rota instead of her. By the third week the new committee has forwarded eleven emails about a swarm under the laundry vent, and the qualified team's next free visit is five weeks out.
choices.memoryHint: Promise the east roof two visits each month.

choices.label: Renegotiate the grant
choices.outcome: Tessa writes back that the second site needs its own coordinator, and offers the first roof's agreement as a template with her name taken off it. The budget officer replies within the day. The condition stands, her hours are cut by a third, and the first roof's monthly checks become quarterly.
choices.memoryHint: Trade a third of your hours for a second coordinator.

echoes.tessa_c1_a: You invited voluntary concerns before any hive was installed, and that private route is exactly what the second roof's committee has asked you to copy.
echoes.tessa_c1_b: You shared the assessor's review in plain language, and the second roof's committee quotes its limits back to you as reason to trust the plan.

chapters.title: A Visit from the Ward
chapters.setting: The building's stair landing, Wednesday morning
chapters.intro: The borough's pollinator officer arrives with a laminated map and a photographer booked for the seventeenth. A half-day open roof would anchor a green corridor launch and release four thousand pounds for equipment and insurance. The building's agreement says no public access to the working area without a vote of residents, and the stair is the only way up. Tessa has three weeks and one meeting. The officer is friendly, the money is real, and the residents who signed the concern route are already asking her which way she is leaning.
chapters.objective: Choose how to answer the borough's open-day request.

choices.label: Put it to a vote
choices.outcome: Tessa books the meeting room, prints the route with the stair head marked as the turnaround, and states the cap in the notice: twenty visitors, one hour, no access above the third floor. The vote passes by four. On the day a resident stands at the landing counting people and does not smile once.
choices.memoryHint: Let residents vote on twenty visitors for one hour.

choices.label: Decline the open day
choices.outcome: Tessa sends the officer the annual report instead, with the review dates and the insurance figure, and offers to speak at the launch without the roof. The four thousand pounds goes to a community orchard three wards over. The first roof keeps its quiet, and the officer's follow-up email is polite enough that Tessa reads it twice looking for the cost.
choices.memoryHint: Send the annual report instead of opening the stair.

echoes.tessa_c2_a: You reworked the hive placement for separation from shared access, and that separation is the argument you now use against opening the stair.
echoes.tessa_c2_b: You wrote the access agreement with contact routes and limits, and the officer's request runs straight into your own clause about public visits.

chapters.title: The Name on the Sign
chapters.setting: The stair notice board, before inspection
chapters.intro: The stair notice board holds a laminated sheet listing who does what above the third floor, and Priya Nandakumar wants her line changed. She has done the reading, kept the log, and carried equipment up in the rain; her practical assessment is booked for October. The draft annual report, which the whole building will read, lists her as a volunteer assistant. Priya asks Tessa to write beekeeper instead, because it is the word her family will see, and because she is tired of being described by what she has not finished.
chapters.objective: Decide how Priya is described in the report.

choices.label: Keep the exact wording
choices.outcome: Tessa keeps volunteer assistant and adds a line naming the tasks Priya actually performs, with the assessment date beside it. Priya reads the draft at the bench, thanks her, and does not come to the next two inspection days. The board goes up on a Thursday with both names spelled correctly.
choices.memoryHint: Keep volunteer assistant and list the tasks beside it.

choices.label: Change the title
choices.outcome: Tessa writes rooftop beekeeper and adds a footnote about supervised work. The assessor, reading the report before it goes to the building, asks which of the two beekeepers holds the current certificate. Tessa answers the email twice and sends the second version. Priya brings a cake to the next inspection.
choices.memoryHint: Write beekeeper on the board with a footnote.

echoes.tessa_c3_a: You put up an information board naming the scale, staff and review dates, and Priya's request concerns the one line on it she cannot control.
echoes.tessa_c3_b: You offered a garden session kept separate from hive access, and residents could explore the roof's ecology there without being asked to approach bees.

chapters.title: The September Review
chapters.setting: The roof at dusk, review date
chapters.intro: The review date arrives with the site folder, the insurance quote, and the same residents in the same room. Two recommendations are drafted. One carries the apiary into a three-year agreement with an annual public report, a named contact and a review each September. The other closes the apiary question at this meeting, returns the marked area to planting, and lodges the whole file with the city's green-spaces team as a worked example. Tessa has promised to recommend one and not to campaign for it. The stair door is propped open behind her, and the roof smells of cold brick and cut thyme.
chapters.objective: Recommend what the building decides at the review.

choices.label: Recommend the three years
choices.outcome: Tessa reads the three-year terms aloud, including the insurance figure and the September review, and sits down before the vote. It passes with two abstentions. Afterwards she stands at the parapet while the caretaker folds the chairs. The roof is louder than the room was: wind in the water butt, a bus three streets off, someone laughing on the stair.
choices.memoryHint: Tie the apiary to a public review each September.

choices.label: Recommend closing the question
choices.outcome: Tessa recommends closing it, and reads the handover: the folder, the key safe code, the assessor's unanswered questions, all lodged with the green-spaces team by Friday. The marked area becomes four raised beds in spring. She carries the folder down herself rather than leave it on the table, and the stair light clicks off behind her.
choices.memoryHint: Hand the whole folder to the green-spaces team.

echoes.tessa_c4_a: You recommended a reviewed season with written conditions and review dates, and this meeting is that review arriving on the day you named.
echoes.tessa_c4_b: You kept the garden first and left the apiary documented for later, and tonight's paper asks whether later has arrived.

title: The Unplayed Note
tagline: Give an old instrument a new way to be heard.
premise: A community orchestra receives an unfinished instrument whose intended sound was never documented.

chapters.title: An Instrument in Pieces
chapters.intro: Owen opens a donated case containing an unfinished instrument and a small packet of parts. There is no reliable account of the maker’s intended setup. The community orchestra hopes it can become useful, but Owen first needs to understand what survives.
chapters.objective: Choose the first careful comparison.

choices.label: Document the construction
choices.outcome: Owen records dimensions, materials and unfinished surfaces without assigning an undocumented maker. The resulting file identifies which parts appear to belong together and which questions require a specialist examination.
choices.memoryHint: Owen records dimensions, materials and unfinished surfaces without assigning an undocumented maker.

choices.label: Compare the surviving parts
choices.outcome: Owen lays the loose components beside the body and checks their documented condition. Several appear compatible, but he labels the finding as provisional. The orchestra receives a useful inventory rather than a story about a lost masterpiece.
choices.memoryHint: Owen lays the loose components beside the body and checks their documented condition.

chapters.title: A Purpose Before a Finish
chapters.setting: A meeting with the adult orchestra
chapters.intro: The instrument can be completed under a documented repair plan, but its intended use will shape the work. The orchestra needs both an occasional performance instrument and a practical instrument for its adult learning group. Owen asks which purpose should guide the first proposal.
chapters.objective: Choose the purpose to develop.

choices.label: Support the learning group
choices.outcome: Owen develops a durable, clearly documented setup proposal with the qualified repair team. The adult learning group can evaluate its usability, while the original unfinished state remains recorded in photographs and drawings.
choices.memoryHint: Owen develops a durable, clearly documented setup proposal with the qualified repair team.

choices.label: Support small performances
choices.outcome: Owen prepares a proposal for modest ensemble use and a supervised listening session. It includes the instrument’s limitations and avoids claiming to recover a sound that nobody documented. The orchestra can judge the result on what it actually offers.
choices.memoryHint: Owen prepares a proposal for modest ensemble use and a supervised listening session.

echoes.owen_c1_a: Owen records dimensions, materials and unfinished surfaces without assigning an undocumented maker.
echoes.owen_c1_b: Owen lays the loose components beside the body and checks their documented condition.

chapters.title: The Room Has a Voice
chapters.intro: The completed work is ready for a controlled rehearsal review. Sound changes with the room and the listener’s position, so a single enthusiastic comment will not settle every question. Owen offers two ways to make the feedback more useful.
chapters.objective: Choose the listening review.

choices.label: Compare different seats
choices.outcome: Adult volunteers listen from several positions and describe differences without ranking one perspective as correct. Owen documents the room conditions so the comments remain useful instead of turning into conflicting verdicts about the instrument.
choices.memoryHint: Adult volunteers listen from several positions and describe differences without ranking one perspective as correct.

choices.label: Compare different ensembles
choices.outcome: Two small adult ensembles try the instrument under the agreed supervision. Owen records how it fits their different arrangements, keeping the discussion focused on practical use rather than searching for a universally ideal sound.
choices.memoryHint: Two small adult ensembles try the instrument under the agreed supervision.

echoes.owen_c2_a: Owen develops a durable, clearly documented setup proposal with the qualified repair team.
echoes.owen_c2_b: Owen prepares a proposal for modest ensemble use and a supervised listening session.

chapters.title: A Case That Opens Again
chapters.intro: The instrument has a documented finish, a clear repair record and an agreed role. Owen can help the orchestra create a lending process or leave a public account of the work. Either ending gives the instrument a future without inventing a glorious past.
chapters.objective: Choose what accompanies the instrument.

choices.label: Create a lending record
choices.outcome: The orchestra establishes a responsible lending record with condition checks and clear care instructions from the specialists. Owen places the file inside the case. The instrument’s next chapter belongs to the adults who will actually play it.
choices.memoryHint: The orchestra establishes a responsible lending record with condition checks and clear care instructions from the specialists.

choices.label: Create a listening exhibit
choices.outcome: A small exhibit pairs the unfinished-state photographs with approved recordings and the treatment record. Visitors hear a present-day instrument with an honest history. Owen leaves the final listening seat open for the next person.
choices.memoryHint: A small exhibit pairs the unfinished-state photographs with approved recordings and the treatment record.

echoes.owen_c3_a: Adult volunteers listen from several positions and describe differences without ranking one perspective as correct.
echoes.owen_c3_b: Two small adult ensembles try the instrument under the agreed supervision.

chapters.title: The Second Case
chapters.setting: The workshop bench, a wet Tuesday
chapters.intro: Three months after the orchestra settled the first instrument's future, a second case arrives at the workshop, delivered by the same clerk who handled the donation. Inside is another unfinished body, a bag of parts, and a delivery note with no name on it. The orchestra's committee assumes it is a pair with the first and wants them shown together; the learning group assumes it is a spare. Owen looks at the neck joint, cut and then abandoned, and at the photographs already pinned above the bench. He has one bench, no budget for a second file, and a letter asking him to say what the thing is.
chapters.objective: Decide whether the second instrument enters the workshop.

choices.label: Take it into the file
choices.outcome: Owen starts a second record the same week: measurements, photographs, a provisional parts list, and a page of questions for the specialist. It costs him four evenings he had promised to the learning group. The committee is delighted and asks, in the same email, when both instruments will be ready to play.
choices.memoryHint: Open a second file before touching the neck.

choices.label: Refer it onward
choices.outcome: Owen writes a referral with the measurements he has and the name of a workshop with a second bench and a conservator on call. The committee reads the letter as a refusal and asks whether the first instrument was only interesting because nobody else wanted it. The case goes back into the solicitor's van before lunch.
choices.memoryHint: Send the case to a bench with a conservator.

echoes.owen_c1_a: You recorded dimensions and materials without naming an undocumented maker, and this new body has arrived with the same blank where a name should be.
echoes.owen_c1_b: You laid the loose parts beside the body and labelled the fit provisional, and the second case's bag of parts waits for the same test.

chapters.title: The Story They Want
chapters.setting: The orchestra's instrument room, before rehearsal
chapters.intro: The orchestra's funder sends a producer to make a short film for its annual appeal. The brief asks for the rediscovered instrument and a maker's story. The instrument has no documented maker, and the first page of Owen's file says so in his own hand. The producer is pleasant and specific: ninety seconds, one close-up of the unfinished surface, one line from Owen about what the instrument has become. The orchestra needs the appeal money before the season opens. Owen is handed an editorial approval form that gives him two weeks and no say over the final cut.
chapters.objective: Choose what Owen signs before the filming starts.

choices.label: Sign with the record attached
choices.outcome: Owen signs, then attaches the file's first page as a condition and asks for the sentence about the unknown maker to be read aloud. The producer agrees in the room. The rough cut keeps the close-up and drops the sentence, and the appeal page describes the instrument as almost certainly from a named period.
choices.memoryHint: Attach the unknown-maker page to the release form.

choices.label: Decline the film
choices.outcome: Owen declines, and the appeal runs with photographs of the orchestra instead. The development officer is quiet with him for a month. In September the funder's next round opens with a line about projects that can tell their own story, and the orchestra's application is shorter than last year's by a page.
choices.memoryHint: Refuse the ninety seconds rather than edit the file.

echoes.owen_c2_a: You built a documented setup with the repair team and kept the unfinished state on record; the producer now wants to edit around that record.
echoes.owen_c2_b: You proposed modest ensemble use and a supervised listening session; the film's ninety seconds now do that work without the limits.

chapters.title: The Donor's Daughter
chapters.setting: The workshop, after closing, one lamp on
chapters.intro: Elin Marsh, the donor's daughter, comes to the workshop with a folder of her own. She has seen the photographs of the instrument in pieces and asks Owen to take them out of the public file before the exhibit or the lending record is shown again. Her father spent his last working years starting things; she does not want a photograph of the bare neck joint to be what outlives him. Owen's file is the only honest account of what the instrument was. Her folder holds three alternatives: a portrait, a letter, and the finished instrument in better light.
chapters.objective: Decide what the unfinished photographs are allowed to show.

choices.label: Withdraw them to the archive
choices.outcome: Owen removes the photographs from the public file and seals them in an envelope with the date and Elin's request written across the flap, to be opened by the next conservator. The exhibit's first panel now begins with the finished instrument. Elin sends a card in November. The envelope sits in the drawer beside the specialist's unanswered questions.
choices.memoryHint: Seal the bare-neck photographs for the next conservator.

choices.label: Keep them, add her letter
choices.outcome: Owen keeps the photographs and gives them a facing page with Elin's letter, unedited, in her own words. She reads the proof at the bench, asks for one sentence about her father's temper to be cut, and signs the rest. That panel runs longer than the others, and visitors stand at it longer.
choices.memoryHint: Face the bare photographs with her written letter.

echoes.owen_c3_a: You compared listening positions and recorded the room instead of crowning one verdict, and Elin's request asks you to do the same with a photograph.
echoes.owen_c3_b: You let two ensembles test it and kept the talk on practical use; Elin now asks you to weigh a use that is not musical.

chapters.title: What the Case Holds
chapters.setting: The instrument room, the night before the season
chapters.intro: The funder's money arrives with a condition: a case study, the file published in full, and the second instrument finished for the learning group by spring. The alternative is smaller and slower. The file stays a working document that travels in the case, the second instrument stays unfinished as a comparison piece the group can examine, and the orchestra finds the difference from its own ticket income. The second instrument is unfinished, its neck joint still open, wherever the case now sits. The choice is really about which object the orchestra is going to be known for.
chapters.objective: Choose what the orchestra does with the second instrument.

choices.label: Finish it for the group
choices.outcome: Owen writes the plan, the repair team signs it, and the neck joint closes in March. The case study appears with the file quoted in full, including the page where nobody is named. The two instruments end up side by side in the room, one playable, one a photograph on the wall, and the group stops asking which is the real one.
choices.memoryHint: Close the second neck joint by spring.

choices.label: Keep it unfinished
choices.outcome: Owen mounts the second body on a stand with its parts in a shallow tray and a card listing what is known and what is not. It becomes the thing the group handles before they play anything. The grant is smaller, ticket prices rise by a pound, and the open neck joint is the first thing anyone sees through the door.
choices.memoryHint: Mount the open neck joint on a handling stand.

echoes.owen_c4_a: You put a lending record in the case with checks and care notes, and the orchestra measures decisions by what can be lent and returned.
echoes.owen_c4_b: You built a listening exhibit from the unfinished photographs and the treatment record, and visitors now expect the orchestra to explain rather than display.

title: The Book That Would Not Close
tagline: Make a book that has room to keep growing.
premise: A community collection has grown beyond its binding, forcing a choice about what a finished book can be.

chapters.title: Too Many Pages
chapters.intro: Leonie receives a community collection whose latest pages prevent the cover from closing. The original contributions must remain intact, and new adult contributors still want to add material. A larger cover alone may not solve the problem.
chapters.objective: Choose the first part to document.

choices.label: Collate the pages
choices.outcome: Leonie records the order, dimensions and condition of every approved contribution. The list reveals several different paper formats, giving her a clear basis for a new structure without deciding which contributions matter most.
choices.memoryHint: Leonie records the order, dimensions and condition of every approved contribution.

choices.label: Examine the binding
choices.outcome: Leonie documents the stressed seams and the cover’s current movement. The old structure was never designed for this volume, so she explains that protecting it may require changing the format rather than forcing it shut.
choices.memoryHint: Leonie documents the stressed seams and the cover’s current movement.

chapters.title: One Volume or Several
chapters.intro: The contributors agree that their pages should remain accessible. Leonie prepares two reversible mock-ups: an expandable structure and a small boxed series. Each offers a different balance between continuity, handling and future additions.
chapters.objective: Choose the mock-up to develop.

choices.label: Try an expandable structure
choices.outcome: The expandable mock-up keeps the collection together while making its capacity visible. Leonie records a practical limit and explains how additions would be managed, so growth becomes an agreed process rather than another overloaded spine.
choices.memoryHint: The expandable mock-up keeps the collection together while making its capacity visible.

choices.label: Try a boxed series
choices.outcome: The boxed-series mock-up gives each section enough room and allows future volumes to join it. Leonie proposes a shared index so the collection still reads as one project even when its pages live in several bindings.
choices.memoryHint: The boxed-series mock-up gives each section enough room and allows future volumes to join it.

echoes.leonie_c1_a: Leonie records the order, dimensions and condition of every approved contribution.
echoes.leonie_c1_b: Leonie documents the stressed seams and the cover’s current movement.

chapters.title: Who Finds the Next Page
chapters.intro: The preferred structure works, but visitors need a way to find their way through the collection. Leonie can develop a readable shared index or a simple contribution record. Neither should reveal more about an adult contributor than that person has agreed to share.
chapters.objective: Choose the navigation aid.

choices.label: Build a shared index
choices.outcome: A plain-language index groups approved contributions by topic and format. Contributors choose their public credit, and private contact details stay outside the book. The collection becomes easier to explore without turning its makers into a directory.
choices.memoryHint: A plain-language index groups approved contributions by topic and format.

choices.label: Build an additions record
choices.outcome: A clear record shows when approved pages were added and where they can be found. Leonie separates public credits from private administration, giving future binders a useful history without publishing personal information.
choices.memoryHint: A clear record shows when approved pages were added and where they can be found.

echoes.leonie_c2_a: The expandable mock-up keeps the collection together while making its capacity visible.
echoes.leonie_c2_b: The boxed-series mock-up gives each section enough room and allows future volumes to join it.

chapters.title: A Finished Place to Begin
chapters.intro: The rebound collection opens comfortably and has a documented limit for additions. Its final presentation can emphasize the craft of keeping it usable or the practical process that allows future contributions. Leonie knows that finished need not mean permanently closed.
chapters.objective: Choose the collection’s final presentation.

choices.label: Show the binding decisions
choices.outcome: The reading table includes a small display of the mock-ups and their tradeoffs. Visitors can understand why the format changed. Leonie closes the cover easily, leaving a collection that can be handled rather than merely admired.
choices.memoryHint: The reading table includes a small display of the mock-ups and their tradeoffs.

choices.label: Leave an additions guide
choices.outcome: Leonie prepares a concise guide for future approved additions, with capacity limits and preservation responsibilities. The project has a clear next step without promising unlimited growth. Its last page points toward a process, not an empty placeholder.
choices.memoryHint: Leonie prepares a concise guide for future approved additions, with capacity limits and preservation responsibilities.

echoes.leonie_c3_a: A plain-language index groups approved contributions by topic and format.
echoes.leonie_c3_b: A clear record shows when approved pages were added and where they can be found.

chapters.title: Thirty-One Waiting Pages
chapters.setting: The reading table, a Saturday in March
chapters.intro: Five months after the collection was rebound, thirty-one approved contributions sit in a lidded crate beside the reading table. The documented limit allows four more pages this year. The contributors' committee is pleased and expects Leonie to solve it the way she solved the last problem. The crate is not the difficulty. The difficulty is that two of the thirty-one come from people who were told no in January, and one of them has since been told yes by a committee member who never read the limit. Leonie lifts the lid and counts the different paper formats inside: six.
chapters.objective: Decide how the collection handles the waiting pages.

choices.label: Hold the written limit
choices.outcome: Leonie binds the four pages the limit allows, numbers them, and publishes the queue for the rest with dates. Two contributors withdraw rather than wait. The committee member who made the promise stops attending. The cover closes without strain for the first time in its life, and the lidded crate stays under the table where visitors can see it.
choices.memoryHint: Bind four pages and publish the queue with dates.

choices.label: Open a companion sequence
choices.outcome: Leonie proposes a companion binding: the same cloth, a shared index, a stated capacity of its own, joined to the first by a linen spine strip. It takes six weeks and two committee meetings. The crate empties. The shelf now holds two volumes that must be lifted together, and the reading table needs a second stand.
choices.memoryHint: Join a second volume with a linen spine strip.

echoes.leonie_c1_a: You collated order, dimensions and condition before deciding anything, and the crate's six different paper formats are the first thing you count.
echoes.leonie_c1_b: You documented the stressed seams and the cover's movement, and that reading is why the limit exists and why it is now being tested.

chapters.title: The Digitisation Offer
chapters.setting: The community centre's back office, midweek
chapters.intro: The centre's director brings an offer from a heritage fund: a scanner, a photographer, and a web edition, if the collection is online by autumn. The money would cover the room's heating for two winters. The fund's form requires the whole collection to be published, not a selection, and the contributors chose their credit lines one at a time, some as initials, two as nothing at all. Leonie reads the form twice. The director watches her and says, reasonably, that a book nobody can reach is only half a book.
chapters.objective: Choose what Leonie puts in the grant application.

choices.label: Apply for a partial edition
choices.outcome: Leonie applies with a consent-gated edition: only pages whose contributors sign again go online, the rest listed by title and shelf number. The fund returns the form asking for a percentage. She sends sixty-one per cent. The award comes in reduced, enough for one winter, and the director stops copying her on the heating emails.
choices.memoryHint: Put online only pages whose contributors consent again.

choices.label: Decline the fund
choices.outcome: Leonie declines and writes the refusal into the collection's administration file so the next binder inherits the reasoning. The director finds the money elsewhere with a condition about public events instead. The reading table gets a second lamp, and the queue for the scanner becomes a queue for the photocopier at the library.
choices.memoryHint: Write the refusal into the administration file.

echoes.leonie_c2_a: You chose the expandable structure and recorded a practical limit, and the fund's form is the first thing to test whether that limit was real.
echoes.leonie_c2_b: You chose the boxed series and a shared index so the collection could live in several bindings; the fund wants it all under one address.

chapters.title: A Page to Take Back
chapters.setting: The bench, with the volume open
chapters.intro: Hana Osei sits at the bench with her hands flat on the open volume and asks Leonie to take out the page she contributed nine years ago. It describes a family argument in enough detail that a cousin recognised himself at a reading. The page sits in the third gathering, sewn through, and the finding aid already points to it in four places. Removing it means reopening a section, renumbering eight pages, and reprinting the index. Keeping it means Hana stops coming to the reading table. The kettle clicks off and neither of them moves.
chapters.objective: Decide how the collection should answer Hana's request.

choices.label: Remove and resew
choices.outcome: Leonie lifts the gathering, cuts the threads, and sews the section back with a cancellation slip in place of the page and a note in the administration file. Eight page numbers change and the index is reprinted at her own cost. Two contributors ask why their references have moved. Hana returns the following month and reads from a different page.
choices.memoryHint: Cut the threads and leave a cancellation slip.

choices.label: Keep it, add a note
choices.outcome: Leonie keeps the page and sets a facing note, in Hana's words, saying that she asked for its removal and why. The note is shorter than the page and set in a smaller type. Hana reads it twice, agrees to it, and does not come back to the reading table. The gathering keeps its original sewing and the index stays as printed.
choices.memoryHint: Set the objection facing the page, in small type.

echoes.leonie_c3_a: You built a plain-language index by topic and format with public credits chosen by contributors, and Hana's page sits in four of its entries.
echoes.leonie_c3_b: You kept an additions record that separated public credit from private administration, and Hana's request now belongs in exactly that second file.

chapters.title: What the Shelf Holds
chapters.setting: The reading table, the night of the annual meeting
chapters.intro: At the annual meeting the collection has a year of handling behind it, a queue of approved pages, and two futures on the table. One is a deposit with the county archive: climate-controlled, catalogued, accessible by appointment, and no longer on the reading table. The other is a keeper's rota, four volunteers, an annual binding, and the collection staying exactly where it is. Leonie has the volume in front of her with the cover closed and her thumb in the gutter. The room smells of paste and the radiator, and someone has left a coat on the chair.
chapters.objective: Choose where the collection should live next year.

choices.label: Recommend the archive
choices.outcome: Leonie recommends deposit, with the companion volume and the administration file going together, and a reading copy made for the table. The transfer takes a morning and two signatures. The shelf is empty by noon. She stands in front of it with the docket in her hand and the room suddenly larger than she remembers it.
choices.memoryHint: Send book and file to the county archive.

choices.label: Recommend the rota
choices.outcome: Leonie recommends the rota: four names, a rota sheet, a key in a biscuit tin, and an annual binding each March. Two of the four are over seventy and one is Hana. The collection stays on the table. By the second year the rota has a waiting list and the cover has a new scuff on the corner.
choices.memoryHint: Put the key in a biscuit tin for four keepers.

echoes.leonie_c4_a: You displayed the mock-ups and tradeoffs so visitors could see why the format changed, and the annual meeting asks you to justify another change.
echoes.leonie_c4_b: You left a concise additions guide with capacity limits and preservation duties, and the meeting's question is whether that guide travels with the book.

title: The Bridge at Walking Pace
tagline: A bridge is also the walk that leads to it.
premise: A pedestrian bridge renewal looks complete on paper but leaves its approaches difficult to use.

chapters.title: Beyond the Span
chapters.intro: Zane reviews a renewal plan for a pedestrian bridge. The structural assessment belongs to the qualified project team, but the public-space review shows a separate problem: the approaches offer little room to pause or understand the route. The drawing needs a user’s pace.
chapters.objective: Choose the first review source.

choices.label: Review the approved walking route
choices.outcome: Zane studies the permitted public route with the access team, keeping clear of restricted works. Their notes identify a confusing turn before the bridge rather than treating the span itself as the whole journey.
choices.memoryHint: Zane studies the permitted public route with the access team, keeping clear of restricted works.

choices.label: Review the consultation notes
choices.outcome: The consultation file repeatedly mentions the approach and the lack of resting space. Zane organizes the comments by practical need without collecting personal health details, giving the design review a clearer question to answer.
choices.memoryHint: The consultation file repeatedly mentions the approach and the lack of resting space.

chapters.title: A Place to Pause
chapters.setting: A scale model of the approach
chapters.intro: The team can examine a rest area proposal or a clearer approach layout. Both need the responsible specialists’ review before any site work. Zane prepares a comparison that distinguishes an appealing concept from a technically approved design.
chapters.objective: Choose the concept to develop first.

choices.label: Develop a rest-area concept
choices.outcome: The model gains a clearly separated place to pause outside the main flow. Zane lists the access, maintenance and engineering checks still required, allowing the team to assess a real proposal without presenting it as ready to build.
choices.memoryHint: The model gains a clearly separated place to pause outside the main flow.

choices.label: Clarify the approach layout
choices.outcome: Zane revises the model’s route cues and removes an unnecessary visual detour. The access team can evaluate whether the approach becomes easier to understand, while the technical review remains with the qualified project team.
choices.memoryHint: Zane revises the model’s route cues and removes an unnecessary visual detour.

echoes.zane_c1_a: Zane studies the permitted public route with the access team, keeping clear of restricted works.
echoes.zane_c1_b: The consultation file repeatedly mentions the approach and the lack of resting space.

chapters.title: Reading the Crossing
chapters.intro: The revised concept is ready for another public-space review. Visitors could compare a physical model or examine a clear sequence of route diagrams. Zane wants feedback that helps the project rather than a vote about who can walk fastest.
chapters.objective: Choose the review format.

choices.label: Use a physical route model
choices.outcome: The team presents a labeled model with the current and proposed routes kept distinct. Adult participants can point out confusing transitions without sharing personal histories. Zane records the questions that the model cannot resolve.
choices.memoryHint: The team presents a labeled model with the current and proposed routes kept distinct.

choices.label: Use a route sequence
choices.outcome: A sequence of plain diagrams shows the approach, crossing and exit. Reviewers can discuss each transition separately, and the team records where an on-site check is still needed. The crossing becomes a sequence of experiences rather than a line on paper.
choices.memoryHint: A sequence of plain diagrams shows the approach, crossing and exit.

echoes.zane_c2_a: The model gains a clearly separated place to pause outside the main flow.
echoes.zane_c2_b: Zane revises the model’s route cues and removes an unnecessary visual detour.

chapters.title: A Plan with Its Limits
chapters.intro: The review identifies a practical improvement and a list of required approvals. Zane can recommend a limited, supervised wayfinding trial or a phased design review. The bridge remains subject to official access rules throughout the process.
chapters.objective: Choose the recommendation to publish.

choices.label: Recommend a limited trial
choices.outcome: The team proposes a reversible wayfinding trial in an approved public area, subject to the responsible authorities’ permission. The update states its limits clearly. Zane’s plan now makes room for learning before permanent change.
choices.memoryHint: The team proposes a reversible wayfinding trial in an approved public area, subject to the responsible authorities’ permission.

choices.label: Publish a phased review plan
choices.outcome: A public plan separates the access concept, technical checks and approval stages. It names unresolved questions without burying them in optimistic language. The bridge project gains an honest route toward improvement, measured at a human pace.
choices.memoryHint: A public plan separates the access concept, technical checks and approval stages.

echoes.zane_c3_a: The team presents a labeled model with the current and proposed routes kept distinct.
echoes.zane_c3_b: A sequence of plain diagrams shows the approach, crossing and exit.

chapters.title: The Permanent Brief
chapters.setting: The project office, a bright cold morning
chapters.intro: Eleven months after the review closed, the authority issues the permanent design brief and attaches a second crossing to it: a footbridge behind the market, narrower approaches, a shorter consultation window. The first bridge's public spaces appear in the brief as items subject to value engineering. Zane reads the phrase three times. The bundle saves a procurement round and gives the second crossing a budget it would not get alone. It also means one public meeting for two places, and nobody in this office has ever walked the second approach.
chapters.objective: Choose how Zane should answer the combined brief.

choices.label: Accept both crossings
choices.outcome: Zane accepts and splits the meeting into two halves, with the second bridge given the last forty minutes. Half the room leaves before it starts. The resting place survives value engineering as a bench and a widened kerb, and the second crossing's approach is still only a line on a plan when the brief is signed.
choices.memoryHint: Give the second crossing the last forty minutes.

choices.label: Ask for the first alone
choices.outcome: Zane writes back asking to separate the schemes and to walk the second approach before any brief is agreed. The authority agrees and moves the second crossing to next year's programme. The first bridge keeps its full review and its place in the queue. The market traders write to the authority asking why their crossing has gone quiet.
choices.memoryHint: Walk the second approach before signing any brief.

echoes.zane_c1_a: You walked the permitted route with the access team and found a confusing turn before the bridge, and this brief still begins at the span.
echoes.zane_c1_b: You sorted the consultation notes by practical need without collecting health details, and the second bridge has no such notes at all.

chapters.title: The Number in the Bid
chapters.setting: A meeting room with a projector and no windows
chapters.intro: The authority's communications lead projects a chart: pedestrian counts up eighteen per cent across the review area. The figure includes the service lane, which was never part of the approved route and which Zane's own notes flagged as unresolved. The number goes into a funding bid on Friday. The lead asks Zane to sign the summary as the review's author. The bid would pay for the resting place and settle what happens to the second crossing. The chart is not wrong. It is measuring a route the design does not serve, and Zane can already hear the panel's question in spring.
chapters.objective: Decide what Zane signs before the bid closes.

choices.label: Sign with the caveat
choices.outcome: Zane signs and adds two lines: the figure includes an unapproved shortcut, and the split between the two routes is not yet surveyed. The lead keeps the caveat in the annex and the headline number on the slide. The bid goes in. In April the panel asks about the shortcut, and the annex is the only place with an answer.
choices.memoryHint: Put the shortcut caveat in the bid annex.

choices.label: Hold the figure
choices.outcome: Zane refuses to sign until the second count closes in three weeks. The lead submits the bid with last year's numbers and a note that the review is ongoing. It is shortlisted anyway, at a lower amount. The resting place survives. The lead stops inviting Zane to the Monday meeting.
choices.memoryHint: Wait for the second count before signing the figure.

echoes.zane_c2_a: You developed a rest-area concept and listed every check still outstanding, and this chart is the same problem in a different suit.
echoes.zane_c2_b: You clarified the approach layout and removed a visual detour, and the service lane is the one detour your revision could not remove.

chapters.title: The Flower Stall
chapters.setting: The market approach, six in the morning
chapters.intro: Ivy Tan has run the flower stall at the market end of the approach for nineteen years. Her deliveries arrive at twenty past six, and the only place a van can stand is the strip the permanent design turns into the resting place. The alternative bay is thirty metres on, behind the refuse store, and the refuse truck is there until half past. She asks Zane to keep the strip as it is, or to write delivery access into the design as a timed exception. She has a petition with forty-one names and photographs of the strip in all weathers.
chapters.objective: Answer Ivy Tan's request about the delivery strip.

choices.label: Write a timed exception
choices.outcome: Zane drafts a timed exception: loading before seven, bollards out at quarter past, the resting place in use for the rest of the day. It needs a traffic order and adds four months. Ivy hands the petition over for the file. The design team asks who will enforce quarter past seven on a Saturday.
choices.memoryHint: Allow loading before seven with bollards out after.

choices.label: Keep the design clean
choices.outcome: Zane keeps the strip as a resting place and offers Ivy the bay from half past six, with a written note to the refuse contractor about the truck's schedule. The note is not a guarantee, and he says so. Ivy's deliveries move to the bay for a fortnight, then return to the strip at a quarter past six, and nobody stops them.
choices.memoryHint: Offer Ivy the bay behind the refuse store.

echoes.zane_c3_a: You used a labeled model that kept current and proposed routes distinct, and Ivy has brought photographs of the same strip in every season.
echoes.zane_c3_b: You used a sequence of diagrams to discuss each transition separately, and Ivy's request is aimed at the one transition the sequence made invisible.

chapters.title: One Package or Two
chapters.setting: The approach at eight in the morning
chapters.intro: The permanent scheme is ready for its statutory stage, and the authority wants one submission before the financial year ends. Zane can put the resting place and the route cues in as a single package, which keeps them tied together in the approval and in the budget. Or he can split them: cues first, resting place held back for a second phase with the delivery strip still under negotiation. The first is faster and harder to unpick later. The second keeps Ivy's strip alive as a question. Traffic comes off the bridge in a steady line.
chapters.objective: Choose what Zane should send for statutory approval.

choices.label: Submit one package
choices.outcome: Zane submits the package with the timed exception attached and the shortcut listed as an unresolved item. Approval takes nine months and comes back with the resting place intact and the exception reduced to three days a week. Ivy reads the notice at the stall and puts the petition in a drawer. The strip has a bench on it by summer.
choices.memoryHint: Keep bench and route cues in one submission.

choices.label: Submit the cues first
choices.outcome: Zane submits the cues alone, with the resting place named in the covering note as the next phase. Approval comes in eleven weeks. The approach is easier to read by June and there is still nowhere to stop. The second phase enters next year's programme at position nine, and the strip keeps its vans and its puddles through another winter.
choices.memoryHint: Submit the route cues and hold the bench back.

echoes.zane_c4_a: You recommended a reversible trial in an approved area with its limits stated, and this submission is the point where reversible stops being available.
echoes.zane_c4_b: You published a phased plan that named the unresolved questions, and the resting place is the question you now have to place in a phase.

title: The Pattern of the Tide
tagline: Turn shared observations into a pattern people can use.
premise: A public-room textile commission must express a neighborhood without turning its residents into decorative material.

chapters.title: Before the First Thread
chapters.setting: A loom beside the evening window
chapters.intro: Freya is commissioned to design a textile for a shared public room. The brief asks for a local feeling but supplies no agreed source material. She proposes beginning with public observations rather than borrowing motifs or personal histories without permission.
chapters.objective: Choose the first design reference.

choices.label: Observe the evening light
choices.outcome: Freya sketches the changing bands of light across the room’s windows. The first swatch uses an original rhythm of pale and dark blue, with the observation date recorded instead of an invented cultural explanation.
choices.memoryHint: Freya sketches the changing bands of light across the room’s windows.

choices.label: Observe the daily routes
choices.outcome: Freya traces the public paths visible from the room and turns their intersections into a new geometric study. The pattern comes from her own observation, and the design notes clearly identify that limited source.
choices.memoryHint: Freya traces the public paths visible from the room and turns their intersections into a new geometric study.

chapters.title: A Pattern at Room Scale
chapters.setting: Swatches on the public room wall
chapters.intro: A small swatch can feel very different when repeated across a large surface. Freya prepares two mock-ups, one with an even rhythm and one with generous quiet areas. The room’s users need to judge the textile in context.
chapters.objective: Choose the larger mock-up.

choices.label: Keep an even rhythm
choices.outcome: The even mock-up creates a steady visual field without a single dominant emblem. Freya records how the repeat meets the room’s edges so the full textile can be reviewed as an environment rather than a tiny decorative sample.
choices.memoryHint: The even mock-up creates a steady visual field without a single dominant emblem.

choices.label: Leave quiet areas
choices.outcome: The second mock-up leaves larger stretches of plain blue between patterned sections. It gives the room calmer visual space and lets the original study remain legible without covering every surface in detail.
choices.memoryHint: The second mock-up leaves larger stretches of plain blue between patterned sections.

echoes.freya_c1_a: Freya sketches the changing bands of light across the room’s windows.
echoes.freya_c1_b: Freya traces the public paths visible from the room and turns their intersections into a new geometric study.

chapters.title: Made to Be Lived With
chapters.intro: The design is ready, but the public room needs a textile that can be maintained responsibly. Freya can prioritize replaceable sections or a companion repair record. The qualified fabricators will still determine the final materials and installation.
chapters.objective: Choose the maintenance idea to develop.

choices.label: Design replaceable sections
choices.outcome: Freya proposes clearly documented sections that can be replaced individually if the fabricators approve the structure. The pattern’s joins become intentional, turning maintenance into a planned part of the design instead of a hidden afterthought.
choices.memoryHint: Freya proposes clearly documented sections that can be replaced individually if the fabricators approve the structure.

choices.label: Create a repair record
choices.outcome: Freya prepares a record of the repeat, colors and approved material choices. The room’s caretakers will have a reliable reference, while the final treatment and cleaning guidance remains with the qualified fabricators.
choices.memoryHint: Freya prepares a record of the repeat, colors and approved material choices.

echoes.freya_c2_a: The even mock-up creates a steady visual field without a single dominant emblem.
echoes.freya_c2_b: The second mock-up leaves larger stretches of plain blue between patterned sections.

chapters.title: The Cloth in the Room
chapters.intro: The approved textile is ready for its shared room. Its source studies, fabrication credits and care responsibilities are complete. Freya can accompany it with an accessible account of the pattern or keep a useful set of approved spare materials for the caretakers.
chapters.objective: Choose the handover’s emphasis.

choices.label: Explain the pattern
choices.outcome: A concise display shows the original observations and the decisions that turned them into cloth. The design belongs to this project without claiming to represent every resident. Freya watches it become part of a room people actually use.
choices.memoryHint: A concise display shows the original observations and the decisions that turned them into cloth.

choices.label: Keep a practical care kit
choices.outcome: The caretakers receive approved spare material, the fabrication record and specialist care guidance. The textile’s future becomes a shared responsibility with clear limits. Its story continues through ordinary use, not an invented legend about its symbols.
choices.memoryHint: The caretakers receive approved spare material, the fabrication record and specialist care guidance.

echoes.freya_c3_a: Freya proposes clearly documented sections that can be replaced individually if the fabricators approve the structure.
echoes.freya_c3_b: Freya prepares a record of the repeat, colors and approved material choices.

chapters.title: The Lobby Across the Street
chapters.setting: The public room, six months after handover
chapters.intro: Six months on, the cloth has settled into the room: the blue has gone slightly duller where the sun reaches it, and the caretakers vacuum along the joins every Thursday. Freya comes to check a loose thread and finds a stranger photographing the repeat with his phone held flat against the wall. He represents a residence hotel across the street. Its lobby is being refurbished, and he wants the same pattern at twice the width, with her name on a brass plate. He has a budget and a deadline. Freya looks at the cloth, then at the plastic chairs and the noticeboard with its swim timetable, and asks him to wait while she works out what exactly he would be buying.
chapters.objective: Decide whether the pattern can leave this room

choices.label: Ask the room's users first
choices.outcome: Freya puts the offer to the Thursday caretakers and the swim club and tells the hotel she will abide by whatever they decide. Two weeks pass. The caretakers argue about money, then about whether a lobby is a room at all, and vote no. The hotel withdraws. The cloth stays singular, and Freya has handed her own authorship to a vote she cannot call back.
choices.memoryHint: The pattern's future put to the room's users.

choices.label: License it with conditions
choices.outcome: Freya negotiates a narrow license: the pattern may be woven for one lobby, credited as after a design by Freya Linden for a public room, with a fee that pays a second weaver for a year. The hotel agrees quickly. By spring a photograph of the lobby appears in a property brochure, cropped so the credit falls outside the frame.
choices.memoryHint: One lobby, one credit line, one funded weaver.

echoes.freya_c1_a: You drew the pattern from recorded bands of evening light, dated in the margin, and a hotel now wants that light for its lobby.
echoes.freya_c1_b: You built the repeat from public routes you traced and labeled as your only source, and a hotel now wants to buy those crossings.

chapters.title: What the Shortlist Wants
chapters.setting: A civic awards office above the bus station
chapters.intro: The commission is shortlisted for a civic design award. The organizers want a two-hundred-word statement about what the pattern means to the neighborhood, a photograph of residents standing in front of it, and someone to accept at a lunch. The press officer has already drafted a line about the community's shared story, woven in blue. Freya reads it twice. The cloth was made from a dated observation study and a fabrication record, not from anybody's story, and the residents in that photograph would be chosen by a photographer who has never been in the room. The statement is due Friday. The fabricators are counting on the citation for their own portfolio.
chapters.objective: Choose what the award submission is allowed to claim

choices.label: Submit the source ledger
choices.outcome: Freya sends the observation dates, the swatch decisions, the fabricators' names and one sentence about what the pattern is not. The entry is compliant and visibly cold. The judges shortlist it anyway but move it into a craft category, not community. The fabricators get their citation. Freya spends the lunch explaining a chart to a table of people who wanted a story.
