choices.memoryHint: Dates and named hands instead of a community story.

choices.label: Withdraw and teach instead
choices.outcome: Freya withdraws the entry and offers the same hour to the fabricators' guild as a paid workshop on documented sourcing. Twelve people come, mostly students, and the fee covers a month of studio rent. The award goes to a mural. In the room nothing changes, and a caretaker asks her, not unkindly, why the cloth never gets to be on a poster.
choices.memoryHint: A paid sourcing workshop replaces the award entry.

echoes.freya_c2_a: You chose the even mock-up, a steady field with no dominant emblem, and now a jury wants one emblem to put on a poster.
echoes.freya_c2_b: You left wide stretches of plain blue between patterned sections, and now the award wants those quiet areas cropped out.

chapters.title: A Mark for Deniz
chapters.setting: The caretaker's office behind the pool
chapters.intro: Deniz Aydin has looked after the room for eleven years. She comes to Freya with a sheet of graph paper on which she has copied a small shape her mother used to draw on the backs of envelopes: a fish with three fins. She wants it worked into the next round of maintenance. She does not want it explained on a label. She wants it in the cloth, where her mother's neighbors will see it and know. Freya thinks about the pattern's premise. Everything in it comes from something observed and documented. Deniz's fish is not less real for being undocumented. It is simply private, and it would change what the whole surface is claiming.
chapters.objective: Decide how a private mark enters public cloth

choices.label: Weave it, credited plainly
choices.outcome: Freya redraws the fish at the scale of the repeat and weaves it into one section, with a line in the maintenance record: Fish motif, drawn by Deniz Aydin, used with permission. Within a year two other caretakers ask for their own marks. The cloth begins to carry names the room cannot see, and Freya is no longer certain what the pattern is made of.
choices.memoryHint: A private fish shape joins the weave under Deniz's name.

choices.label: Frame it beside the cloth
choices.outcome: Freya declines the weave and has the graph paper mounted in an oak frame at the end of the room, captioned with Deniz's name and nothing else. Deniz says thank you and does not come to the mounting. The pattern stays a record of what was observed. The corridor smells faintly of the pool, and the fish hangs close enough to the cloth that visitors assume it belongs.
choices.memoryHint: The fish hangs framed, close enough to seem part of it.

echoes.freya_c3_a: You designed replaceable sections with documented joins, and Deniz now wants one of those sections to hold something undocumented.
echoes.freya_c3_b: You wrote a repair record of the repeat, colors and materials, and Deniz wants a shape that record cannot account for.

chapters.title: The Annexe in Plaster
chapters.setting: An empty annexe with new plaster
chapters.intro: The building is extending into the old storage annexe, and the committee has asked Freya to decide what the textile becomes there. The annexe will hold a smaller, quieter room used mostly in the evenings. She can specify a fixed edition: one design, closed after approval, archived with its evidence and never altered. Or she can leave the annexe a written palette and a set of rules, so the caretakers and whoever follows them can make new cloth from the same observations without her. The committee will approve either. The plaster is still damp. Freya unrolls a sample and holds it against the wall to see how the new light falls.
chapters.objective: Choose whether the pattern closes or stays open

choices.label: Specify one fixed edition
choices.outcome: Freya designs a single smaller panel for the annexe and writes a closing note: this is the last addition, and the file goes to the archive with its dates and permissions. The committee is relieved to have an answer. The panel goes up in a morning. Afterwards the caretakers stand in front of it with their hands behind their backs, as if at a window.
choices.memoryHint: One last panel closes the file for good.

choices.label: Leave a palette and rules
choices.outcome: Freya writes four pages: the observed palette, the permitted repeats, the credit line, and the rule that nothing enters the cloth without a documented source and a named hand. The committee hesitates, then signs. By autumn the annexe holds a first test panel woven by a caretaker Freya has never met, slightly wrong, unmistakably the same family of blue.
choices.memoryHint: Four pages let strangers weave the same blue.

echoes.freya_c4_a: You hung a panel explaining the observations and decisions behind the cloth, and now an empty annexe asks what else that explanation should carry.
echoes.freya_c4_b: You left the caretakers a care kit, spare material and clear limits, and now they are asking for a different kind of instruction.

title: The Loaf Before Dawn
tagline: Let a small bakery welcome more than one kind of morning.
premise: A bakery’s proposed early opening needs a plan that balances freshness, waste and the people doing the work.

chapters.title: A Window Before Sunrise
chapters.intro: Malik’s bakery is considering an early opening for adult neighbors whose schedules miss the usual service. The idea sounds generous, but the team needs a manageable plan. A counter full of unsold bread would not count as a successful welcome.
chapters.objective: Choose the first planning source.

choices.label: Review existing demand
choices.outcome: Malik compares voluntary requests with the bakery’s existing sales records, using no personal work or health details. The notes support a modest early offering rather than an impressive display that the team cannot sustain.
choices.memoryHint: Malik compares voluntary requests with the bakery’s existing sales records, using no personal work or health details.

choices.label: Review the team’s capacity
choices.outcome: The bakers review their current workload and identify what could fit without assuming extra unpaid time. Malik records a clear limit for the proposal, keeping the people making the bread inside the story of the opening.
choices.memoryHint: The bakers review their current workload and identify what could fit without assuming extra unpaid time.

chapters.title: One Batch or Two
chapters.setting: The planning board by the oven
chapters.intro: The team agrees on a limited trial. Malik can offer a small consistent range or a narrower service with advance reservations. Both need clear ingredient information and an honest explanation that the trial may change after review.
chapters.objective: Choose the trial’s format.

choices.label: Keep a small regular range
choices.outcome: The trial offers a small, clearly described range within the team’s agreed capacity. Malik explains the limits before opening, making the service predictable without promising that every possible preference can be met immediately.
choices.memoryHint: The trial offers a small, clearly described range within the team’s agreed capacity.

choices.label: Use limited reservations
choices.outcome: A simple reservation process lets adults request from a fixed range without sharing unnecessary personal details. Malik caps the trial at the agreed capacity and keeps a small walk-in allowance so the opening does not become an exclusive club.
choices.memoryHint: A simple reservation process lets adults request from a fixed range without sharing unnecessary personal details.

echoes.malik_c1_a: Malik compares voluntary requests with the bakery’s existing sales records, using no personal work or health details.
echoes.malik_c1_b: The bakers review their current workload and identify what could fit without assuming extra unpaid time.

chapters.title: The Shape of a Queue
chapters.setting: A mock-up of the early counter
chapters.intro: The opening plan needs an arrangement for collecting bread. Some guests will be passing quickly; others may want a quiet place to wait. Malik can improve the collection instructions or arrange a modest sheltered waiting point within the approved premises.
chapters.objective: Choose the next practical improvement.

choices.label: Clarify the collection steps
choices.outcome: A readable notice explains the opening time, reservation limits and available range. Ingredient and allergen information stays explicit. Malik removes confusing extra steps so a quick visit does not require a conversation about someone’s private routine.
choices.memoryHint: A readable notice explains the opening time, reservation limits and available range.

choices.label: Prepare a calm waiting point
choices.outcome: The team arranges a clearly identified waiting point within the bakery’s approved space. The trial information explains how collection works, giving guests a place to pause without turning a bread pickup into a crowded event.
choices.memoryHint: The team arranges a clearly identified waiting point within the bakery’s approved space.

echoes.malik_c2_a: The trial offers a small, clearly described range within the team’s agreed capacity.
echoes.malik_c2_b: A simple reservation process lets adults request from a fixed range without sharing unnecessary personal details.

chapters.title: A Morning Worth Keeping
chapters.intro: The trial produces a manageable amount of feedback and a clearer picture of waste and workload. Malik can recommend a regular limited service or a revised trial with fewer opening days. Neither outcome needs to pretend that generosity means endless availability.
chapters.objective: Choose the bakery’s next commitment.

choices.label: Keep the limited service
choices.outcome: The bakery keeps the service at its reviewed scale, with clear days, limits and ingredient information. The team knows what it has agreed to provide. Malik closes the review book beside a counter prepared for an ordinary, useful morning.
choices.memoryHint: The bakery keeps the service at its reviewed scale, with clear days, limits and ingredient information.

choices.label: Revise before expanding
choices.outcome: The bakery shortens the schedule and reviews the offering before making a longer commitment. Guests receive a clear explanation. Malik leaves the light on for a smaller morning that the team can sustain rather than a grand opening it cannot.
choices.memoryHint: The bakery shortens the schedule and reviews the offering before making a longer commitment.

echoes.malik_c3_a: A readable notice explains the opening time, reservation limits and available range.
echoes.malik_c3_b: The team arranges a clearly identified waiting point within the bakery’s approved space.

chapters.title: The Extra Tray
chapters.setting: The bakery at four in the morning
chapters.intro: Three months into the limited service, the morning has found its shape: the same nine or ten faces, the same two loaves held back, the same twenty quiet minutes before the first bus. Malik is doing the accounts at four and finds the waste column has crept up. He has been slipping an extra tray into the oven each night, just in case, and the just-in-case bread has been going into the bin at nine. Worse, the minutes it takes are on nobody's rota. Priya has started staying late without writing it down. The service still works. The plan that made it work no longer describes it.
chapters.objective: Decide what to do with the extra tray

choices.label: Cut it, post numbers
choices.outcome: Malik drops the extra tray and pins the week's bake-and-sell figures on the board where the team and the guests can both read them. Two regulars arrive at half past eight to crumbs. One of them, Hana, says she will come earlier, and does. Waste falls to almost nothing. Priya studies the board for a long time and asks whether the numbers are for the team or the customers.
choices.memoryHint: Bake-and-sell figures pinned where guests can read them.

choices.label: Formalize a last-hour table
choices.outcome: Malik keeps the tray and writes a rule for it: whatever is left at half past eight goes on a small table at half price, no reservations, no names. He adds the twenty minutes to the rota and takes them out of his own prep time. The table empties by nine. He is now baking for a discount he invented, and the night is longer than the plan says.
choices.memoryHint: Leftover loaves at half price, paid for with prep time.

echoes.malik_c1_a: You based the trial on voluntary requests and existing sales records, deliberately modest, and the morning has quietly outgrown the numbers you wrote down.
echoes.malik_c1_b: You set the opening's limit from the team's real capacity, and the extra tray has pushed past it without anyone deciding to.

chapters.title: The Box Contract
chapters.setting: The bakery office, blinds half down
chapters.intro: A facilities manager from the office block on the corner sits in the office with a folder. Her building has two hundred night staff and a canteen that closes at ten. She wants a standing order: one hundred and twenty breakfast boxes, five mornings a week, delivered by half past six, at a price she has already circled. Rosa, who owns the bakery, has done the arithmetic on the back of the folder and likes it. It would pay for a second night shift and a used proving cabinet. It would also make the early window's bread the thing left over after the boxes. The facilities manager waits with her pen uncapped.
chapters.objective: Choose how the bakery answers the box contract

choices.label: Take two capped mornings
choices.outcome: Malik counters with forty boxes, two mornings, and a trial that ends in eight weeks. The facilities manager accepts because she has no other supplier, and Rosa signs. The bakery buys the cabinet and hires a second night baker. The early counter now opens forty minutes later than before, because the boxes come first. The regulars adjust. Nobody complains out loud.
choices.memoryHint: Forty boxes, two mornings, eight weeks, then review.

choices.label: Offer only the surplus
choices.outcome: Malik refuses the standing order and offers the building whatever is unsold at half past eight, at cost, no promised quantity. The facilities manager takes the numbers away and never calls back. Rosa is quiet for a week. The window keeps its hours and its bread. At four in the morning the oven sounds the same, and he listens as if he had won something small, expensive.
choices.memoryHint: No promised quantity, only what is unsold at cost.

echoes.malik_c2_a: You opened with a small range and limits stated up front, and now someone wants a promise it was never built to keep.
echoes.malik_c2_b: You capped reservations but kept a walk-in allowance so the trial stayed open, and the box contract would make it a delivery schedule.

chapters.title: The Sheet with No Name
chapters.setting: The counter at ten past six
chapters.intro: Hana has come since the first week, always at twenty past six, always the dark rye. This morning she asks Malik to hold a loaf past the collection window until eight, and to let her settle up at the end of the week. She says it quickly and looks at the till rather than at him. Then she asks him not to write her name on the hold sheet, because the sheet is clipped to the board and anyone waiting can read it. The holds began as a favor in the second month and now carry eleven names. Malik made a rule about that sheet so the board would never become a list of who needed what. The rule was easier before he knew why.
chapters.objective: Decide what the hold sheet is actually for

choices.label: Keep a tab, no name
choices.outcome: Malik starts a tab on a folded card behind the till, marked with a number, and tells Hana the loaf will be there. By the third week there are four cards. He has begun keeping a private ledger of who is short this month, which is the thing he said it would not do. The bread is never wasted. He checks the cards before he checks the oven.
choices.memoryHint: A numbered card behind the till, no names.

choices.label: Change the rule for everyone
choices.outcome: Malik takes the names off the sheet and moves the last two loaves to a shelf stocked until half past seven, first come, no holds. Hana gets her loaf without asking. So does everyone else, and two regulars who relied on named holds arrive to an empty shelf and say nothing. The board is blank. Malik writes the new hour on it in chalk and underlines it twice.
choices.memoryHint: The hold sheet goes blank; a shared shelf replaces it.

echoes.malik_c3_a: You wrote a plain notice so a quick visit would not require explaining a private routine, and Hana asks for hers to stay unwritten.
echoes.malik_c3_b: You made a calm waiting point inside the approved space so nobody had to hurry, and Hana asks to wait without being seen waiting.

chapters.title: A Name for the Morning
chapters.setting: The bakery, an hour before opening
chapters.intro: The lease is renewed for five years, and Rosa wants to print the early service properly: a card in the window, a name, a fixed five-day week, the hours set in the same type as the rest of the shop. She has left the design on the counter for Malik to approve. The morning has never had a name. It has had a rota line, a chalk note, and nine or ten people who know when the door is unlocked. A printed card would let it survive a change of staff, a bad month, a new owner. It would also make it a product with hours, and products are judged against their hours.
chapters.objective: Choose whether the morning gets a public name

choices.label: Print the card, fix hours
choices.outcome: Malik approves the card: five mornings, six until nine, bread until it is gone. The first week brings strangers and two complaints about the nine o'clock close. The regulars keep coming, a little earlier now, and Priya pins the rota beside the card so the two documents can be compared. In the window the type is small and blue, and it stays there through the winter.
choices.memoryHint: A printed card puts the morning's hours in public.

choices.label: Keep it in the rota
choices.outcome: Malik leaves the design on the counter unsigned. The morning keeps its chalk note and its unlocked door. Rosa calls it a mistake and does not raise it again. When Priya takes three weeks off in March, the service runs short two mornings because nothing on the wall says so. Malik covers both, badly. The chalk note is rewritten each Sunday in his hand and rubbed out each night.
choices.memoryHint: The chalk note stays, rewritten each Sunday in his hand.

echoes.malik_c4_a: You kept the reviewed service with its days and limits, and the shop wants those limits printed where strangers can hold you to them.
echoes.malik_c4_b: You shortened the schedule and promised a smaller morning the team could sustain, and the question is whether it can survive being advertised.

title: The Path Beyond the Map
tagline: Draw a map that admits where its knowledge ends.
premise: A visitor map shows an old path as open even though its current access status has never been verified.

chapters.title: A Line Too Confident
chapters.intro: Celia receives an old visitor map marked for reprint. One path appears as an ordinary open route, but the supporting file contains no current access record. She cannot responsibly send it back to print just because the old line looks clear.
chapters.objective: Choose the first verification source.

choices.label: Compare official records
choices.outcome: Celia compares the map with current land-management records and finds that access status is unresolved. She marks the line for review and keeps the old edition as evidence of what visitors were previously told.
choices.memoryHint: Celia compares the map with current land-management records and finds that access status is unresolved.

choices.label: Consult the access team
choices.outcome: The responsible access team confirms that the route needs an updated review. Celia records the contact and the limits of the answer, removing any suggestion that an informal conversation has approved the path for use.
choices.memoryHint: The responsible access team confirms that the route needs an updated review.

chapters.title: The Space Around a Path
chapters.setting: A table of old and current plans
chapters.intro: The map can show the unresolved route distinctly or omit it from the visitor edition while preserving it in the archive. Celia explains that an attractive line is less important than a clear distinction between historical information and current access guidance.
chapters.objective: Choose the visitor-map approach.

choices.label: Mark the uncertainty clearly
choices.outcome: The revised draft separates the historical path from approved visitor routes and refers readers to current official information. Celia tests the legend for clarity so an uncertain route cannot be mistaken for a quiet alternative.
choices.memoryHint: The revised draft separates the historical path from approved visitor routes and refers readers to current official information.

choices.label: Keep it in the archive only
choices.outcome: The visitor draft omits the unverified route and records why it was removed. The historical line remains available in the documented archive, preserving the evidence without promoting a route whose access status is unresolved.
choices.memoryHint: The visitor draft omits the unverified route and records why it was removed.

echoes.celia_c1_a: Celia compares the map with current land-management records and finds that access status is unresolved.
echoes.celia_c1_b: The responsible access team confirms that the route needs an updated review.

chapters.title: A Legend People Can Read
chapters.intro: The revised draft needs a readable legend. Celia can test a high-contrast layout or a companion tactile model with the relevant specialists. Neither will turn the map into a substitute for current conditions or official instructions.
chapters.objective: Choose the next accessibility review.

choices.label: Review the visual legend
choices.outcome: The team compares line styles, symbols and plain labels rather than relying on color alone. Celia records feedback and makes the uncertain-status category easier to distinguish from an approved visitor route.
choices.memoryHint: The team compares line styles, symbols and plain labels rather than relying on color alone.

choices.label: Review a tactile companion
choices.outcome: A specialist team examines a tactile model that distinguishes the main areas and the limits of the information. Celia keeps it paired with current official guidance, treating accessibility as a review process rather than a claim she can certify alone.
choices.memoryHint: A specialist team examines a tactile model that distinguishes the main areas and the limits of the information.

echoes.celia_c2_a: The revised draft separates the historical path from approved visitor routes and refers readers to current official information.
echoes.celia_c2_b: The visitor draft omits the unverified route and records why it was removed.

chapters.title: The Date Beside the Map
chapters.intro: The visitor map is ready for the responsible authority’s final review. Its sources and limits are documented, but any printed map will age. Celia can emphasize a visible update record or a clear process for collecting corrections without inviting people to test uncertain routes.
chapters.objective: Choose the map’s future safeguard.

choices.label: Publish the update record
choices.outcome: The map carries a clear publication date, source summary and route to current official notices. Celia hands over a drawing that makes its age visible instead of borrowing certainty from clean printing.
choices.memoryHint: The map carries a clear publication date, source summary and route to current official notices.

choices.label: Create a correction process
choices.outcome: The visitor center establishes a review process for reported map errors, with corrections checked by the responsible team. Celia’s final file includes the unresolved questions. The map becomes something that can improve without asking visitors to take risks.
choices.memoryHint: The visitor center establishes a review process for reported map errors, with corrections checked by the responsible team.

echoes.celia_c3_a: The team compares line styles, symbols and plain labels rather than relying on color alone.
echoes.celia_c3_b: A specialist team examines a tactile model that distinguishes the main areas and the limits of the information.

chapters.title: Cairns on the Unverified Line
chapters.setting: The junction above the old bridge
chapters.intro: Two months after the visitor map goes out, Celia walks the corridor to see what the printing has done. The unverified path is being used. Brush has been cut back along the first four hundred meters, the saplings stacked in neat bundles, and someone has built cairns at the switchbacks where the ground is vague. A laminated card in a plastic sleeve is tied to a birch: a walking club's name, a date, an invitation to a Sunday work party. Celia photographs the cairns and writes the grid references in her notebook. The map was honest. The honesty has not made the ground any clearer, and the club's care is starting to look like a decision.
chapters.objective: Decide how the map should answer the cairns

choices.label: Log them through corrections
choices.outcome: Celia files the cairns and the cut brush through the visitor center's correction process, with photographs and dates, and states that maintenance is not an access decision. The note goes on the board by the toilets. The club's secretary writes back in a day and points out that the board is inside a building that closes at five. The cairns stay. The correction is correct and nobody reads it.
choices.memoryHint: The correction lives on a board behind a locked door.

choices.label: Walk it with the steward
choices.outcome: Celia arranges to walk the corridor with Ronan Pike, the club's steward, on a Tuesday, recording what has physically changed and taking no position on whether it should be walked. Six hours, two sandwiches, one washed-out culvert. Her notebook fills. The club posts a photograph of the two of them at the top cairn, captioned as a site visit, which is true and reads like an endorsement.
choices.memoryHint: Six hours walking with Ronan, recording change, endorsing nothing.

echoes.celia_c1_a: You checked the land-management records, found access unresolved, and marked the line for review rather than clearing it for print.
echoes.celia_c1_b: You asked the access team, recorded the limits of their answer, and refused to treat a conversation as approval for the route.

chapters.title: The Category They Want
chapters.setting: A meeting room with a broken blind
chapters.intro: The recreation office proposes a new category for the spring reprint: open, unmaintained. It would put the corridor on the visitor map as a real line with a real warning, and it would give the agency a defensible position when people walk it anyway. The catch is the survey. The category requires a condition assessment, updated annually, and nobody at the agency has the hours. The officer suggests, without quite asking, that Celia might do the first one. The visitor center needs the spring numbers, and a map with a new line on it sells more maps than a map with a gap.
chapters.objective: Choose whether to support the agency's new category

choices.label: Write the survey yourself
choices.outcome: Celia agrees to the assessment and spends four unpaid weekends on it, measuring tread, drainage and two collapsed culverts. The category goes on the spring map. Her name sits in the small print as surveyor, which makes the next annual update hers by habit. The line is real, the warning is real, and the corridor is busier by June than it has been in twenty years.
choices.memoryHint: Four unpaid weekends buy the corridor a category.

choices.label: Publish the evidence file
choices.outcome: Celia declines the survey and puts the whole corridor file on the visitor center's public shelf instead: records, photographs, unresolved questions, dates. It runs to four hundred pages and nobody asked for it. The reprint goes out with the gap still in it. Two councillors read the file. One of them asks the right question at the right meeting, six months later than a survey would have answered it.
choices.memoryHint: Four hundred pages on the public shelf instead of a survey.

echoes.celia_c2_a: You marked the uncertainty on the map and sent readers to official information, and the agency wants a category instead.
echoes.celia_c2_b: You kept the unverified route off the edition and recorded why, and the agency wants it back in a form you would endorse.

chapters.title: The Name at the Junction
chapters.intro: Ronan Pike, who stewards the walking club's work on the corridor, brings a folding map and a folded sheet of paper. The paper is a photocopy of a page from his father's notebook, describing the corridor by a name the family used: the Coffin Road, for the shape of the slope, or so he was told. He wants the name on the map at the junction, in the same lettering as the other features. He is not asking for a memorial and says so twice. He is asking for the ground to be called what the people who worked it called it. Celia looks at the photocopy: no date, no source, one hand, and a slope that may or may not carry the name.
chapters.objective: Decide how an unsourced name enters the map

choices.label: Print it as local usage
choices.outcome: Celia sets the name at the junction in italic, with a footnote: known locally as, source not verified. It is honest, and it is printed, and printed names travel. Within a season the club's route cards use it without the footnote, then a guidebook does, then a sign appears at the lay-by in routed oak. Ronan is delighted. Celia finds the italics doing less work than she hoped.
choices.memoryHint: The name goes in italic with an unverified footnote.

choices.label: Record it, do not print
choices.outcome: Celia takes the photocopy into the oral-history file with Ronan's account, his father's name and the date of the conversation, and leaves the map's lettering alone. The file is searchable and almost never searched. Ronan signs the form, shakes her hand, and does not come back to the archive room. In the drawer the name sits with its one source attached, waiting for a second that may never arrive.
choices.memoryHint: The photocopy enters the oral-history drawer unprinted.

echoes.celia_c3_a: You tested the legend so an uncertain route could not be mistaken for an approved one, and now a name needs the same test.
echoes.celia_c3_b: You paired the tactile model with official guidance and refused to certify accessibility alone, and this name arrives with less to certify it.

chapters.title: The Layer Under Review
chapters.intro: The visitor center has money for one new thing this year, and the manager wants it to be a routes-under-review layer: a quarterly-checked set of dashed lines, each with a date and a named reviewer, printed on a separate sheet that can be replaced without reprinting the map. She offers Celia the file. It would keep the corridor visible and keep it questioned, and it would mean Celia signs her name to a question four times a year for as long as she does it. The alternative is to close the corridor file, hand the evidence to the agency, and let the ordinary process decide.
chapters.objective: Choose what the corridor file should become next

choices.label: Take the quarterly layer
choices.outcome: Celia accepts and builds the layer outward from the corridor, one sheet, four dates a year, her initials in the margin. The first replacement sheet goes up in April. By the second she has begun dreading the quarter turning, and the drawer of unresolved questions has become a schedule. On the wall the dashes hold their uncertainty in public, and she checks them the way she checks weather.
choices.memoryHint: Dashed lines, four dates a year, her initials in the margin.

choices.label: Close it and hand over
choices.outcome: Celia writes a closing summary, boxes the corridor file, and delivers it to the agency with a note listing every question it cannot answer. The visitor center prints no layer. The map stays until the next full revision, which may be hers or may not. On the last afternoon she stands at the light table with the lamp off, looking at the shape of the gap.
choices.memoryHint: The boxed file goes to the agency with every open question.

echoes.celia_c4_a: You gave the map a visible publication date and a route to current notices, and the center asks whether a date is enough.
echoes.celia_c4_b: You built a process for reported errors, checked by the responsible team, and the corridor needs a standing layer, not a single correction.

title: The Last Reel, First Light
tagline: Give an unfinished screening an honest opening night.
premise: A community cinema finds a licensed archive print whose surviving version has no confirmed soundtrack.

chapters.title: The Canister in the Booth
chapters.intro: Nico inventories a fictional local film cleared for the cinema’s archive program. Its picture materials survive, but no verified soundtrack accompanies them. A penciled note mentions music without naming a recording, so the screening cannot responsibly advertise an original score.
chapters.objective: Choose the first record to examine.

choices.label: Review the print’s record
choices.outcome: Nico compares the materials with the archive’s condition and version records. The surviving print is documented clearly, while the missing soundtrack remains an explicit gap rather than an invitation to borrow unrelated music.
choices.memoryHint: Nico compares the materials with the archive’s condition and version records.

choices.label: Review the rights file
choices.outcome: Nico confirms the permissions for the surviving picture and separates them from any proposed new accompaniment. The cinema now has a clear boundary for the program instead of assuming that permission for one element covers every addition.
choices.memoryHint: Nico confirms the permissions for the surviving picture and separates them from any proposed new accompaniment.

chapters.title: What the Audience Hears
chapters.intro: The cinema can screen the surviving version silently or commission a newly licensed accompaniment that is clearly described as contemporary. Nico prepares both options without suggesting that either recovers a soundtrack whose contents are unknown.
chapters.objective: Choose the screening format.

choices.label: Keep the surviving silence
choices.outcome: The program explains that the verified version has no surviving soundtrack in the collection. Nico prepares the screening around that limitation, allowing the film’s present condition to be understood without turning an absence into a mystery he can solve.
choices.memoryHint: The program explains that the verified version has no surviving soundtrack in the collection.

choices.label: Commission new accompaniment
choices.outcome: The cinema proposes a clearly credited contemporary accompaniment with separate permissions and an explicit description. The new work will be a response to the film, not a replacement falsely advertised as its recovered original soundtrack.
choices.memoryHint: The cinema proposes a clearly credited contemporary accompaniment with separate permissions and an explicit description.

echoes.nico_c1_a: Nico compares the materials with the archive’s condition and version records.
echoes.nico_c1_b: Nico confirms the permissions for the surviving picture and separates them from any proposed new accompaniment.

chapters.title: A Seat in the Screening
chapters.intro: The program’s rights and format are clear. The access team identifies two useful additions: a readable introduction to the surviving version or a separately scheduled low-stimulation presentation. Nico asks which the cinema can support responsibly first.
chapters.objective: Choose the first access addition.

choices.label: Prepare a readable introduction
choices.outcome: A concise introduction explains the format, missing materials and any new contribution before the screening begins. The cinema makes the same information available in writing so visitors do not have to catch every spoken sentence.
choices.memoryHint: A concise introduction explains the format, missing materials and any new contribution before the screening begins.

choices.label: Plan a quieter presentation
choices.outcome: The cinema proposes a separately described low-stimulation presentation under its venue procedures. Nico records the features and limits plainly, allowing visitors to decide whether that version suits them without making a universal accessibility claim.
choices.memoryHint: The cinema proposes a separately described low-stimulation presentation under its venue procedures.

echoes.nico_c2_a: The program explains that the verified version has no surviving soundtrack in the collection.
echoes.nico_c2_b: The cinema proposes a clearly credited contemporary accompaniment with separate permissions and an explicit description.

chapters.title: The House Lights Return
chapters.intro: The screening gives the cinema a clearer account of the film and of its own choices. Nico can preserve the program as an archive case or develop a modest series about incomplete film materials. The audience’s attention need not become a demand for another event.
chapters.objective: Choose the program’s lasting form.

choices.label: Keep a complete screening record
choices.outcome: The cinema files the permissions, presentation notes and credited additions beside the print record. Future projectionists will know exactly what was shown. Nico turns up the house lights on a screening that has been honest about its missing pieces.
choices.memoryHint: The cinema files the permissions, presentation notes and credited additions beside the print record.

choices.label: Develop a limited archive series
choices.outcome: A small proposed series explores clearly documented film fragments and presentation choices, each subject to its own permissions. The cinema publishes the scope without promising endless discoveries. Nico leaves the booth ready for the next carefully chosen frame.
choices.memoryHint: A small proposed series explores clearly documented film fragments and presentation choices, each subject to its own permissions.

echoes.nico_c3_a: A concise introduction explains the format, missing materials and any new contribution before the screening begins.
echoes.nico_c3_b: The cinema proposes a separately described low-stimulation presentation under its venue procedures.

chapters.title: The Splice in Reel Three
chapters.intro: The second screening sells out, and on the second night the film jumps in the same place: a splice in reel three, old tape gone brittle, the frame lurching sideways before it catches. Nico has seen it coming since the condition report. The print is on loan and finite, and the archive's note allows no more than four projections without stabilization. He has two left. He can cut the damaged frames and re-splice, which is standard practice and would make the join invisible, or he can build a deliberate stop into the running order. Friday is already sold out.
chapters.objective: Decide how the damaged splice should be handled

choices.label: Cut and re-splice
choices.outcome: Nico takes the reel to the bench, removes nine frames and makes a clean join with fresh tape and a new leader. Friday runs without a hitch. Nobody in the audience knows anything happened, which is the point of the craft and of the problem: the surviving version is nine frames shorter and the program note still says what it said. He pencils the change into the condition record.
choices.memoryHint: Nine frames removed, the join made invisible.

choices.label: Build the stop in
choices.outcome: Nico leaves the splice and writes a ninety-second pause into the order: lights to half, one plain sentence about the damaged join, then back in. On Friday the room goes quiet in a way he has not heard. Two people leave. The rest stay, and afterwards a man in the second row says it is the first time a cinema told him the truth about what he watched.
choices.memoryHint: Ninety seconds of half-light and one honest sentence.

echoes.nico_c1_a: You checked the print against the archive's condition and version records, and those records set a limit on how often it can run.
echoes.nico_c1_b: You separated the picture rights from any added accompaniment, and the print's physical condition is now the thing setting the terms.

chapters.title: The Festival's Offer
chapters.setting: The cinema office, phone on speaker
chapters.intro: The regional archive festival wants the print for one night in autumn. Their programmer is careful and enthusiastic: a restored presentation, a commissioned score from a composer with a following, the cinema credited as co-presenter, and a fee that would cover the roof repair the venue has postponed for two years. She uses the word restored twice. Nico asks what she means by it and hears the answer he expected: cleaned, stabilized, and presented with new music, which is three things, only one of which is restoration. Bea, the venue manager, is already calculating the roof. The offer expires Monday.
chapters.objective: Choose the terms the cinema can live with

choices.label: Lend it with written terms
choices.outcome: Nico agrees on paper: no restored wording, the print's gaps stated in the festival's own program, the score billed as a new response, and the cinema's projection notes traveling with the reels. The festival accepts all four and then prints a poster that says restored anyway, in large type, with a small line about new music. The roof gets fixed. Nico spends the autumn writing letters about a poster.
choices.memoryHint: Four written terms travel with the reels.

choices.label: Decline and keep it here
choices.outcome: Nico declines, and Bea takes it badly for ten days. The roof is patched with a tar sheet that flaps. The print stays in the booth, where Nico can check the splices himself and where the program's terms are his to keep. The next screening draws twelve people. He knows every one of them by name, and the film runs exactly as the note says it runs.
choices.memoryHint: The print stays, the roof gets a tar sheet.

echoes.nico_c2_a: You kept the surviving silence and explained the absence rather than solving it, and the festival now wants to solve it on your behalf.
echoes.nico_c2_b: You commissioned a new accompaniment with separate permissions and its own credit, and the festival wants to fold that work into a restoration.

chapters.title: Fourteen Unsigned Bars
chapters.setting: The booth, under the bench lamp
chapters.intro: Marta Kest is the director's niece and has been to every screening. She brings a single sheet of manuscript found in a box of household papers: fourteen bars, treble clef, no title, no signature, a tempo mark in another hand. She is certain it is the missing theme. She wants it played on Friday, before the film, by anyone who can read it. Nico holds the paper by the corner and looks at the notation, which is competent and unremarkable and could be anybody's. His program says the soundtrack does not survive. A page is not a soundtrack, and it is also not nothing.
chapters.objective: Decide what should happen to the found page

choices.label: Exhibit it, unplayed
choices.outcome: Nico has the page mounted under glass in the lobby with a caption listing what is known: found among Kest's papers, undated, unsigned, purpose unknown. Marta reads it twice and says it makes her aunt sound like a suspect. It stays up for the run. People stop in front of it on their way in, and one of them asks Nico why he will not just play the thing.
choices.memoryHint: Under glass, captioned by four known facts, never played.

choices.label: Play it as curtain-raiser
choices.outcome: Nico books a violinist for twenty minutes and puts the page first, before the leader, with an introduction that states the four facts and no more. Fourteen bars, about forty seconds, played twice. The room listens hard. Afterwards three people tell him the film made more sense with it, the sentence his program was written to prevent. The page goes back in its box on Monday.
choices.memoryHint: Fourteen bars before the leader, played twice.

echoes.nico_c3_a: You wrote an introduction so nobody had to catch every spoken sentence, and a single sheet now needs a caption doing the same work.
echoes.nico_c3_b: You planned a separate low-stimulation presentation with its limits described plainly, and this page arrives with no description at all.

chapters.title: The Next Frame
chapters.intro: The run ends in November. The print goes back to the archive in a fitted case, and the cinema has to decide what the program leaves behind. Bea wants a small annual fixture: one film, one problem, one night, always with the gaps stated and the credits checked. It would give the venue a signature and a reason to keep the booth staffed. Nico has the alternative in a folder: close the case completely, file the notes, and let the next program start from nothing, unburdened by a format. The roof still leaks over the third row. The projector lamp is four hundred hours from its end.
chapters.objective: Decide what the archive program should leave behind

choices.label: Make it an annual night
choices.outcome: Nico writes the format down: one print, one documented gap, one guest with a claim to make, all terms approved before the poster. Bea books the first for next October. It is a good shape and it is now a shape, and by the third year the audience arrives knowing what to expect, which is the one thing the first screening never gave them. The roof gets a bucket.
choices.memoryHint: One print, one gap, one guest, every October.

choices.label: Close the case, file it
choices.outcome: Nico returns the print with a complete record: permissions, presentation notes, the splice, the found page, the attendance each night. The folder goes into the cabinet with the other closed cases. There is no series and no poster. On the last night he brings up the house lights himself and stands in the doorway while twelve people put on their coats and go out into the rain.
choices.memoryHint: A complete record in the cabinet, no series.

echoes.nico_c4_a: You filed the permissions, presentation notes and credited additions beside the print, and the cabinet asks whether a record is enough of a legacy.
echoes.nico_c4_b: You proposed a limited series on documented fragments, each with its own permissions, and the question is whether it should continue without you.

title: A Courtyard After Dark
tagline: Help a courtyard feel welcoming after dark.
premise: A courtyard lighting renewal must improve its public routes without flooding neighboring windows with light.

chapters.title: Where the Light Lands
chapters.intro: Ada reviews a lighting brief for a courtyard used by adult residents and evening visitors. The current proposal brightens the paths but also sends light toward nearby windows. Before choosing a fixture, she needs to understand what the space is asking the light to do.
chapters.objective: Choose the first review.

choices.label: Read the evening-use notes
choices.outcome: Ada organizes voluntary comments about routes, waiting points and unwanted glare without asking residents to describe private routines. The notes identify specific places to review instead of treating more brightness as a complete answer.
choices.memoryHint: Ada organizes voluntary comments about routes, waiting points and unwanted glare without asking residents to describe private routines.

choices.label: Study the existing light
choices.outcome: The qualified team’s survey shows uneven coverage and light spilling beyond the intended areas. Ada builds a model of those findings so the next design can be compared with the actual problem rather than a dramatic before-and-after image.
choices.memoryHint: The qualified team’s survey shows uneven coverage and light spilling beyond the intended areas.

chapters.title: A Smaller Circle of Light
chapters.intro: The qualified team can assess a shielded fixture proposal or an approach that uses reflected light from approved surfaces. Ada keeps both at concept stage while the necessary technical and environmental reviews are completed.
chapters.objective: Choose the concept to develop.

choices.label: Develop shielded lanterns
choices.outcome: The model directs warm light toward the intended route and away from nearby windows. Ada records the shielding idea and the checks still required, making the design legible without presenting a model as an installation specification.
choices.memoryHint: The model directs warm light toward the intended route and away from nearby windows.

choices.label: Develop reflected light
choices.outcome: The model tests a gentler reflected-light approach on suitable proposed surfaces. Ada documents its limits and asks the specialists to assess feasibility, keeping the design focused on useful light rather than a glowing courtyard spectacle.
choices.memoryHint: The model tests a gentler reflected-light approach on suitable proposed surfaces.

echoes.ada_c1_a: Ada organizes voluntary comments about routes, waiting points and unwanted glare without asking residents to describe private routines.
echoes.ada_c1_b: The qualified team’s survey shows uneven coverage and light spilling beyond the intended areas.

chapters.title: An Evening with an End
chapters.intro: The proposal needs an operating plan as well as a visual design. The responsible team can examine a consistent reviewed schedule or a limited supervised trial with clear feedback. Ada does not want a beautiful mock-up to conceal an unclear responsibility for later changes.
chapters.objective: Choose the operating proposal.

choices.label: Set a reviewed schedule
choices.outcome: Ada proposes a clear schedule for the authorities and specialists to assess, with responsibilities and adjustment rules stated openly. Residents can understand the proposal without assuming that lights will remain unchanged or on indefinitely.
choices.memoryHint: Ada proposes a clear schedule for the authorities and specialists to assess, with responsibilities and adjustment rules stated openly.

choices.label: Begin with a limited trial
choices.outcome: The team proposes a reversible trial under the required permissions and supervision. Ada defines the questions to be reviewed, including spill light and route clarity. The trial becomes a way to learn, not a disguised permanent installation.
choices.memoryHint: The team proposes a reversible trial under the required permissions and supervision.

echoes.ada_c2_a: The model directs warm light toward the intended route and away from nearby windows.
echoes.ada_c2_b: The model tests a gentler reflected-light approach on suitable proposed surfaces.

chapters.title: The Window and the Path
chapters.intro: The revised model shows a courtyard with readable routes and quieter edges. The technical approvals remain the responsibility of the qualified project team. Ada can leave a public explanation of the decisions or a clear maintenance and review brief for the operator.
chapters.objective: Choose the handover document.

choices.label: Explain the light’s boundaries
choices.outcome: A public design note shows where the proposal aims light and where it deliberately avoids it. The courtyard is described as a shared environment rather than a promise of safety through brightness. Ada’s final drawing includes the dark areas it respects.
choices.memoryHint: A public design note shows where the proposal aims light and where it deliberately avoids it.

choices.label: Prepare the operator’s brief
choices.outcome: The operator receives the approved design record, specialist specifications and review responsibilities. Changes must return through the agreed process. Ada leaves a courtyard plan whose future can be managed as carefully as its first evening.
choices.memoryHint: The operator receives the approved design record, specialist specifications and review responsibilities.

echoes.ada_c3_a: Ada proposes a clear schedule for the authorities and specialists to assess, with responsibilities and adjustment rules stated openly.
echoes.ada_c3_b: The team proposes a reversible trial under the required permissions and supervision.

chapters.title: The Second Courtyard
chapters.setting: The drying yard off Bellamy Court, January dusk
chapters.intro: Four months after the Bellamy Court lanterns went up, the operator's log records eleven complaints and none of them about light. Ada counts that as a kind of success. Then the building committee asks her to look at the drying yard behind the same block, where a laundrette vents warm air over three rotary lines and a fire escape. They want it lit by spring, using her drawings. The yard is four meters wide with windows on three sides. Her drawings describe a courtyard twice that width. Meret Osei, who chairs the committee, has already sent those drawings to a contractor for a price.
chapters.objective: Decide whether the second yard gets a new survey or a copy.

choices.label: Survey the yard at dusk
choices.outcome: Ada stands in the yard with a meter and the laundrette's evening keyholder, reading the walls rather than the drawings. The narrower space throws light back off the boiler flue, and the windows above the lines catch everything. She comes away with four measurements and no scheme. The contractor's price expires on Friday and Meret does not call to ask why.
choices.memoryHint: Measure the narrow yard yourself before reusing the drawings.

choices.label: Scale the first plan
choices.outcome: Ada takes the Bellamy Court record, subtracts a meter of width and hands over a scaled proposal with the shielding notes attached. The price holds and the committee is pleased. On the plan, the lantern over the fire escape sits within a meter of a bedroom window, which the drawing cannot show, because the yard has never been measured.
choices.memoryHint: Subtract a meter from the old courtyard plan.

echoes.ada_c1_a: You read the evening-use notes first, gathering comments about routes and glare without asking anyone to describe private routines.
echoes.ada_c1_b: You began with the survey, building a model from the team's findings so the design answered the actual problem rather than a dramatic image.

chapters.title: The Insurance Letter
chapters.setting: The committee room above the laundrette, February
chapters.intro: A bicycle is taken from the alley beside Bellamy Court in February, and a neighborhood bulletin runs the story under a headline about dark corners. The building's insurer responds with a renewal condition: a reduced premium if the courtyard and the alley reach a stated level of illumination. Meret Osei brings the letter to Ada with a pen already uncapped. The committee needs a signature by Friday to hold the premium, and the drying yard's funding sits in the same envelope. Ada has measurements showing the alley's problem is a broken gate latch and a blocked sightline, not a missing lantern.
chapters.objective: Choose what Ada puts her name to before Friday.

choices.label: Sign with a caveat
choices.outcome: Ada signs, adding a line that the figure is a target rather than a safety guarantee, and the committee accepts it without reading closely. The premium holds and the drying yard keeps its funding. At the renewal meeting the caveat is quoted once, in passing, before the brighter scheme is approved on the strength of her name.
choices.memoryHint: Sign the lighting figure as a target, not a guarantee.

choices.label: Publish the measurements
choices.outcome: Ada sends the survey and a note about the gate latch to the committee and the bulletin, and the insurer withdraws the reduction rather than argue with a light meter. The drying yard's funding returns to the general budget. Meret stops copying her on committee emails. The alley gate is repaired in March by nobody's campaign.
choices.memoryHint: Publish the survey and the broken gate-latch finding.

echoes.ada_c2_a: You developed the shielded lanterns, aiming warm light at the route and away from the windows, and recorded the checks still owed.
echoes.ada_c2_b: You tested reflected light on suitable surfaces and documented its limits before any specialist had agreed the approach was feasible.

chapters.title: The Concierge's Corner
chapters.setting: The lobby desk at Bellamy Court, half past eleven
chapters.intro: Ruth Vance has worked the night desk at Bellamy Court for nine years and has never asked Ada for anything until now. At half past eleven she walks Ada to the corner by the parcel shelf, where the design deliberately leaves a pool of shadow so the ground-floor window opposite can stay dark. Ruth does the late handovers alone, and since the clocks changed she has been walking residents to the gate rather than watching them cross. She asks for the nearest lantern to be turned fifteen degrees toward the desk. That fixture is on the reviewed schedule.
chapters.objective: Decide how far the design bends for one person.

choices.label: Aim the lantern over
choices.outcome: Ada authorizes a fifteen-degree turn and logs it as a temporary deviation, reviewable in April. Ruth's corner brightens. The ground-floor window takes a pale wash for two hours each evening, and its tenant, who never complained before, writes to the committee in the third week. Ada answers the letter herself and does not move the lantern back.
choices.memoryHint: Turn the lantern fifteen degrees toward Ruth's corner.

choices.label: Light the desk only
choices.outcome: Ada keeps the schedule and specifies a small shielded task light for the parcel shelf, wired to the lobby circuit at the operator's cost. Ruth's desk becomes legible and the window stays dark. Ruth thanks her and goes on walking people to the gate, which Ada notices in the nightly log and has nowhere to enter.
choices.memoryHint: Give Ruth a shielded shelf light, keeping the window dark.

echoes.ada_c3_a: You set a reviewed schedule with responsibilities and adjustment rules written openly, so residents would not assume the lights stayed fixed.
echoes.ada_c3_b: You proposed a reversible trial under supervision, defining which questions about spill light and route clarity would be reviewed.

chapters.title: What the Yard Becomes
chapters.setting: The drying yard at first light, April
chapters.intro: By April the contractor's price has expired twice and the drying yard is still dark. Meret Osei offers Ada the commission on her own terms: one shielded fixture over the lines, a schedule reviewed at three months, no public document, no photographs, and no argument with the committee in the bulletin. The laundrette's keyholder has already hung a work lamp of her own above the press, angled badly, and the flue throws its light straight at the windows. Ada can take the yard quietly, or she can write the method down and let someone else build it.
chapters.objective: Decide whether the yard is a commission or a published method.

choices.label: Take the yard quietly
choices.outcome: Ada accepts the terms and spends three evenings in the yard with a meter while the laundrette closes. The single fixture is aimed, shielded and logged, and the windows stay dark. Nothing is published. In June a contractor two districts over copies the Bellamy Court drawings for a yard of his own, and Ada hears about it from Meret, who thinks it is flattering.
choices.memoryHint: Take the commission and publish nothing about the method.

choices.label: Write the method down
choices.outcome: Ada writes four pages: how to read a yard at dusk, what to measure, when to refuse a drawing. She makes the note a condition of her involvement and sends it to the committee, the contractor and the bulletin. The contractor declines the condition. The yard waits until autumn, and the note is copied, argued over and used in two other buildings before the first fixture goes up.
choices.memoryHint: Make four written pages on reading a yard a condition.

echoes.ada_c4_a: You left a public design note showing where the light was aimed and where it deliberately stopped, dark areas included.
echoes.ada_c4_b: You handed the operator an approved record, the specialist specifications and the review responsibilities, so changes had to return through the agreed process.

title: The Mechanical Bird
tagline: Show the wonder without hiding the mechanism.
premise: A museum automaton is ready for restoration, but its proposed exhibit makes claims its records cannot support.

chapters.title: The Bird on the Bench
chapters.intro: Hugo inspects a mechanical bird with a documented history of repairs. An old exhibit caption calls its movements perfectly natural, but the mechanism’s limitations are part of what makes it interesting. The restoration brief needs to begin with evidence.
chapters.objective: Choose the first record to examine.

choices.label: Compare the drawings
choices.outcome: The surviving drawings show a deliberate sequence of simple motions rather than a copy of a living bird’s behavior. Hugo records the match and proposes an interpretation that credits the maker’s mechanical choices without exaggeration.
choices.memoryHint: The surviving drawings show a deliberate sequence of simple motions rather than a copy of a living bird’s behavior.

choices.label: Compare the demonstration record
choices.outcome: A dated demonstration recording shows pauses and resets omitted from the old caption. Hugo documents them as operating characteristics, giving the restoration team a realistic account instead of demanding a seamless performance the object never promised.
choices.memoryHint: A dated demonstration recording shows pauses and resets omitted from the old caption.

chapters.title: Original Parts, Daily Use
chapters.intro: The qualified team can preserve a worn original drive as a study object or retain it within a limited demonstration plan if specialists approve. Hugo explains the tradeoffs without treating constant movement as the only way an automaton can remain meaningful.
chapters.objective: Choose the proposal to assess.

choices.label: Preserve and use a dated replacement
choices.outcome: The team proposes conserving the original drive and evaluating a clearly dated replacement for demonstrations. Hugo makes the distinction visible in the records, so useful motion will not come at the price of disguising a new component as old.
choices.memoryHint: The team proposes conserving the original drive and evaluating a clearly dated replacement for demonstrations.

choices.label: Plan limited original demonstrations
choices.outcome: The team examines whether a limited specialist-approved demonstration schedule can retain the original drive. Hugo records that the proposal depends on condition and operating review, with a static display remaining a valid outcome.
choices.memoryHint: The team examines whether a limited specialist-approved demonstration schedule can retain the original drive.

echoes.hugo_c1_a: The surviving drawings show a deliberate sequence of simple motions rather than a copy of a living bird’s behavior.
echoes.hugo_c1_b: A dated demonstration recording shows pauses and resets omitted from the old caption.

chapters.title: Wonder in Plain Sight
chapters.intro: The proposed exhibit can reveal the bird’s motion through an explanatory model or show the original alongside a clearly labeled diagram. Hugo wants the audience to enjoy the mechanism without believing that it has feelings or independent intentions.
chapters.objective: Choose the explanatory approach.

choices.label: Use a visible mechanism model
choices.outcome: A clearly labeled teaching model shows the motion sequence without asking visitors to handle the historic object. Hugo distinguishes the modern model from the automaton, making the explanation part of the attraction rather than a correction hidden in small print.
choices.memoryHint: A clearly labeled teaching model shows the motion sequence without asking visitors to handle the historic object.

choices.label: Pair the bird with a motion diagram
choices.outcome: A readable diagram follows the object’s documented sequence and identifies the limits of the surviving evidence. Visitors can understand the planned pauses and resets. The bird gains a clearer story without being made into a pretend living creature.
choices.memoryHint: A readable diagram follows the object’s documented sequence and identifies the limits of the surviving evidence.

echoes.hugo_c2_a: The team proposes conserving the original drive and evaluating a clearly dated replacement for demonstrations.
echoes.hugo_c2_b: The team examines whether a limited specialist-approved demonstration schedule can retain the original drive.

chapters.title: A Demonstration with a Pause
chapters.intro: The museum has a responsible operating proposal and an honest interpretation. The last decision is whether visitors encounter a static explanatory display or scheduled demonstrations under the approved procedure. Both can leave room for wonder without demanding constant performance.
chapters.objective: Choose the exhibit’s main experience.

choices.label: Keep the explanatory display
choices.outcome: The museum opens with the conserved object, its documented parts and the approved explanatory material. Visitors can see how much thought went into a small set of movements. Hugo closes the workshop log on a bird that does not need to pretend to be alive.
choices.memoryHint: The museum opens with the conserved object, its documented parts and the approved explanatory material.

choices.label: Offer scheduled demonstrations
choices.outcome: Approved demonstrations are clearly timed and supervised, with the object’s pauses described in advance. The static interpretation stays available between sessions. Hugo leaves the mechanism with a schedule that respects its material limits and its audience’s time.
choices.memoryHint: Approved demonstrations are clearly timed and supervised, with the object’s pauses described in advance.

echoes.hugo_c3_a: A clearly labeled teaching model shows the motion sequence without asking visitors to handle the historic object.
echoes.hugo_c3_b: A readable diagram follows the object’s documented sequence and identifies the limits of the surviving evidence.

chapters.title: Six Runs in One Evening
chapters.setting: The gallery floor after closing, early spring
chapters.intro: The bird has drawn a crowd since the gallery reopened, and the late-opening queue now reaches the geology case. On a Tuesday after closing, Hugo winds it through one demonstration and hears something new on the return: a small double catch, two teeth where there should be one. The programming office wants six runs for the spring late opening, printed in the brochure already. The conservation note approved two a day with an inspection between. Delphine Karr, who signed that note, is on leave until Thursday. The brochure goes to print on Wednesday morning, and the bird is the only thing on it that moves.
chapters.objective: Decide how many times the bird runs on Thursday.

choices.label: Hold at two runs
choices.outcome: Hugo tells programming the bird runs twice and the brochure is corrected at the museum's cost. The queue at the gallery door is turned away twice that evening, and a family who came for the bird stands in front of the teaching model instead. The double catch is still there on Friday. Programming books the hall for a film night in June.
choices.memoryHint: Hold the bird at two runs and correct the brochure.

choices.label: Run the teaching model
choices.outcome: Hugo offers the modern model for the four extra sessions, with a label at the plinth saying so in the same size as the bird's own. The queue moves and the gallery keeps its late opening. Three visitors ask why they paid to see a copy, and one writes in the comment book that the copy was better, because it did not stop.
choices.memoryHint: Put the modern copy on the plinth with an honest label.

echoes.hugo_c1_a: You began with the surviving drawings, reading a deliberate sequence of simple motions rather than a copy of a living bird.
echoes.hugo_c1_b: You began with the dated demonstration record, finding pauses and resets the old caption had left out.

chapters.title: The Family's Gift
chapters.intro: The family who gave the bird to the museum has offered to fund the whole east gallery, which has needed a rehang since before Hugo arrived. The condition arrives as one sentence in a long letter: the panel headed “What the evidence cannot tell us” should come down, replaced with text describing the maker as a man ahead of his time. The development office has already drafted the new wording. Hugo's own post is funded to June, and the rehang is where the next contract gets written. The letter's last page lists the maker's patents, which are real, dated, and more interesting than the phrase.
chapters.objective: Decide what the gallery says about the maker.

choices.label: Rewrite for the maker
choices.outcome: Hugo accepts the gift and rewrites the panel to lead with the patents, the tool marks and the two documented repairs. The caveats move to a numbered catalogue entry and a folder at the desk. The gallery opens in September with the family in the front row, and the folder at the desk is taken twice in the first month.
choices.memoryHint: Lead the panel with patents, tool marks and repairs.

choices.label: Decline the condition
choices.outcome: Hugo writes back that the panel stays and the gift is welcome without it, and copies the exchange to the director. The family withdraws. The east gallery keeps its old cases and its peeling label rail, and Hugo's contract is extended to December on an unrelated grant. The panel stays up, unread, at the far end.
choices.memoryHint: Keep the panel and refuse the family's rewriting condition.

echoes.hugo_c2_a: You conserved the original drive and evaluated a dated replacement, keeping the distinction visible so useful motion would not disguise a new component.
echoes.hugo_c2_b: You examined a limited, specialist-approved demonstration schedule for the original drive, with static display left as a valid outcome.

chapters.title: One Run, No Audience
chapters.setting: The gallery after the alarms are set, 8pm
chapters.intro: Delphine Karr retires on Friday after thirty-one years, twenty-six of them in this building, and the leaving card is circulating in a manila folder. On Wednesday evening she finds Hugo at the bench and asks for one thing: the bird, once, after the alarms are set, with no audience and no clipboard. She wrote the supervision rule herself in 2011. She trained on the mechanism in the years when it ran every day, and she has spent four months explaining to visitors why it pauses. Hugo has the key in his pocket. The double catch is louder than it was in March.
chapters.objective: Decide what Hugo does with the key on Wednesday.

choices.label: Run it for her
choices.outcome: Hugo sets the alarms late and runs the bird once, standing at the fire door with the log open and the time written down. Delphine watches from the bench and does not touch it. The double catch sounds twice. Afterwards she signs the log herself, in the column for supervised runs, and writes her own name as supervisor.
choices.memoryHint: Run the bird once for Delphine and log the time.

choices.label: Play her the recording
choices.outcome: Hugo keeps the case closed and plays her the old demonstration recording through the gallery speakers, then the four minutes he taped in March. Delphine listens with her coat on. She says the recording is not the same, which is true, and signs the leaving card on Friday with the department pen and does not come back to the bench.
choices.memoryHint: Play Delphine the recording and keep the case shut.

echoes.hugo_c3_a: You built a clearly labeled teaching model so the motion could be shown without asking anyone to handle the historic object.
echoes.hugo_c3_b: You paired the bird with a readable diagram following its documented sequence and naming the limits of the evidence.

chapters.title: The Case and the Key
chapters.setting: The east gallery, an hour before opening
chapters.intro: By October the double catch happens on every third run, and the conservation report gives the drive a working life measured in months. The museum offers Hugo two ways to spend it. The bird can go into the case now, lit from below, with the interpretation doing the moving, and the label finished, accurate and permanent. Or it can run twice a week until December under a schedule with an end date printed on it, opened and inspected after every session, with the case prepared while it still moves. The key is in the lock. The gallery opens in an hour.
chapters.objective: Decide how the bird spends its last working months.

choices.label: Case it now
choices.outcome: Hugo builds the mount himself, cut to the three contact points the drawings show, and sets the drive on a felt bed with the access panel facing the glass. The last demonstration is a Tuesday in October with eleven people in the room. The case light comes on at ten, and the bird is still. Visitors lean in to find the seam where the wing meets the body.
choices.memoryHint: Build the mount on three contact points now.

choices.label: Run until December
choices.outcome: Hugo prints the end date on the schedule card and opens the case after every session, logging the catch each time. Attendance doubles in November. On the last Tuesday the bird runs its two minutes, pauses where it always pauses, and stops a tooth short of the end. Hugo writes down the time and leaves the case open for the mount.
choices.memoryHint: Print an end date and keep the bird running.

echoes.hugo_c4_a: You opened with the conserved object, its documented parts and explanatory material, closing the log on a bird that did not pretend to be alive.
echoes.hugo_c4_b: You chose timed, supervised demonstrations with the pauses described in advance, keeping the static interpretation available between sessions.

title: The Tea with No Name
tagline: Give a blend a name that tells the truth.
premise: A studio’s new blend needs a clear identity that respects ingredients, contributors and guests who do not want to taste.

chapters.title: A Tin Without a Label
chapters.intro: Sana sets a sample tin beside the draft description of a new blend. The description promises a feeling that no ingredient list can guarantee. She wants a name and explanation that help adult guests choose without turning ordinary tea into a remedy.
chapters.objective: Choose the first description source.

choices.label: Start with the ingredients
choices.outcome: Sana rewrites the description around the documented ingredients, caffeine information and ordinary flavor notes. The blend gains a useful starting point without promises about health, mood or what every guest will experience.
choices.memoryHint: Sana rewrites the description around the documented ingredients, caffeine information and ordinary flavor notes.

choices.label: Start with voluntary tasting notes
choices.outcome: Sana reviews consented notes from the adult tasting group and separates shared descriptions from personal associations. The draft credits the process without publishing private stories or pretending that a majority preference predicts everyone’s taste.
choices.memoryHint: Sana reviews consented notes from the adult tasting group and separates shared descriptions from personal associations.

chapters.title: An Option Beside the Main Blend
chapters.intro: The studio can offer the main blend alone with careful information or develop a separately reviewed alternative for guests avoiding caffeine. Sana keeps the choice practical, knowing that one additional option will not meet every dietary or medical need.
chapters.objective: Choose the next product proposal.

choices.label: Clarify the main blend first
choices.outcome: Sana concentrates on an accurate description of the main blend and makes its ingredients and caffeine status easy to find. Guests can decide whether to try it without being steered toward a claim that it suits everybody.
choices.memoryHint: Sana concentrates on an accurate description of the main blend and makes its ingredients and caffeine status easy to find.

choices.label: Develop a distinct alternative
choices.outcome: Sana prepares a clearly separate alternative for ingredient and labeling review. It is described on its own terms, with no promise that caffeine status makes it universally appropriate. The studio’s range grows by one honest option rather than a vague wellness claim.
choices.memoryHint: Sana prepares a clearly separate alternative for ingredient and labeling review.

echoes.sana_c1_a: Sana rewrites the description around the documented ingredients, caffeine information and ordinary flavor notes.
echoes.sana_c1_b: Sana reviews consented notes from the adult tasting group and separates shared descriptions from personal associations.

chapters.title: A Tasting You Can Decline
chapters.intro: Sana plans a small adult review session. Some guests may wish to discuss the label without drinking or smelling the samples. The session can prioritize written information or an optional tasting with a clearly available observation route.
chapters.objective: Choose the review format.

choices.label: Review the label first
choices.outcome: Guests can evaluate the ingredient list, caffeine description and proposed name without tasting. Sana gathers only voluntary product feedback, making participation useful even for people who choose not to consume the blend.
choices.memoryHint: Guests can evaluate the ingredient list, caffeine description and proposed name without tasting.

choices.label: Offer an optional tasting
choices.outcome: The session explains the ingredients and participation choices before any samples are offered. Guests can observe or leave feedback without drinking. Sana keeps the discussion about a product’s description rather than asking anyone to explain a medical or personal reason for declining.
choices.memoryHint: The session explains the ingredients and participation choices before any samples are offered.

echoes.sana_c2_a: Sana concentrates on an accurate description of the main blend and makes its ingredients and caffeine status easy to find.
echoes.sana_c2_b: Sana prepares a clearly separate alternative for ingredient and labeling review.

chapters.title: A Name Worth Printing
chapters.intro: The blend’s information has been reviewed, and the studio has a clear description of its limits. Sana can choose a simple sensory name or a project name that credits the documented design process. The label does not need to promise a transformed life to be inviting.
chapters.objective: Choose the final naming approach.

choices.label: Use a sensory name
choices.outcome: The printed name points to the blend’s documented ingredients and ordinary flavor character. Clear caffeine and ingredient information stays beside it. Sana closes the tin with a label that helps a guest choose instead of telling them what to feel.
choices.memoryHint: The printed name points to the blend’s documented ingredients and ordinary flavor character.

choices.label: Credit the shared process
