choices.outcome: The studio uses a modest project name with a brief, consented credit to the adult review process. The ingredient description remains primary. Sana leaves room for guests to have their own experience without turning their private associations into a product story.
choices.memoryHint: The studio uses a modest project name with a brief, consented credit to the adult review process.

echoes.sana_c3_a: Guests can evaluate the ingredient list, caffeine description and proposed name without tasting.
echoes.sana_c3_b: The session explains the ingredients and participation choices before any samples are offered.

chapters.title: Thirty Kilos a Month
chapters.setting: The studio bench, a Tuesday in March
chapters.intro: Three months after the label went to print, the blend is in the window and the tin is empty by Thursday most weeks. On a Tuesday in March, Rui Almeida from the hotel cafe across the street asks for thirty kilos a month as the house blend, with the studio's name on the menu. Sana works out what that means. The smoked leaf comes from one holding up the valley, which can send eight kilos a month and no more, and the honey note depends on it. The rest of the blend is ordinary and easy. Rui needs an answer by Friday, when the hotel prints its spring menus.
chapters.objective: Decide what the blend is when it has to be bigger.

choices.label: Cap it at eight
choices.outcome: Sana offers the hotel eight kilos a month and no more, and Rui takes it for the lobby trolley rather than the menu. The blend stays one thing, made one way, and the Thursday queue does not change. In April a second hotel asks. Sana sends the same letter with the same number in it.
choices.memoryHint: Offer the hotel eight kilos and keep one blend.

choices.label: Blend a second lot
choices.outcome: Sana builds a second lot with a smoked leaf from a broker, cups it nine times against the original and labels it Lot Two on the tin and the menu card. It is close and not the same. The hotel takes thirty kilos. Two regulars tell her, correctly, that it is different, and one of them stops buying it.
choices.memoryHint: Blend a second lot of smoked leaf as Lot Two.

echoes.sana_c1_a: You started from the documented ingredients, caffeine information and ordinary flavor notes, and wrote the description around what could be checked.
echoes.sana_c1_b: You started from the consented tasting notes, separating shared descriptions from private associations and crediting the process without publishing anyone's story.

chapters.title: The Calm Category
chapters.setting: The studio office, a shortlist email open on the desk
chapters.intro: The shortlist email arrives on a Monday and the whole studio reads it over the counter. The blend is one of six in a category called Calm and Comfort, for drinks that help people unwind, and the winner gets a listing in a grocery chain whose buyer has already asked about shelf space. The rent went up in January by more than the studio's margin on a good week. The organizers want forty words from Sana about what the blend does for a person at the end of a day, and a photograph of the tin with steam above it. The entry form has a box for the category and a box for comments.
chapters.objective: Decide what the studio enters, and in which category.

choices.label: Enter with plain words
choices.outcome: Sana writes forty words about smoke, honey and the second pot, and ticks the category. The judges call the quote restrained. The blend does not win, and the grocery buyer takes the winner's blend instead. The rent is paid in March by three wholesale accounts and a wedding order, all of them small.
choices.memoryHint: Write forty plain words about smoke, honey and the second pot.

choices.label: Ask for another category
choices.outcome: Sana writes to the organizers asking to be judged as a blended tea rather than a comfort drink, and sends the ingredient sheet with the entry. The request goes to a panel that meets in April. By then the shortlist is printed and the category stands, and the studio's name appears in the program under a heading Sana did not choose.
choices.memoryHint: Ask the judges for a blended-tea category instead.

echoes.sana_c2_a: You clarified the main blend first, making its ingredients and caffeine status easy to find so guests could decide for themselves.
echoes.sana_c2_b: You prepared a separate alternative for ingredient and labeling review, described on its own terms with no claim to suit everybody.

chapters.title: The Line on the Card
chapters.setting: The reading room next door, a week before opening
chapters.intro: Noor Haddad came to the autumn sessions and has spent the winter fitting out the reading room next door, which opens in nine days with borrowed chairs and a hand-painted sign. She asks Sana for twelve kilos of the blend and for one line on her shelf card: a sentence a customer said in October, that the tea was the only thing that got her through the winter. Sana remembers the sentence and the woman who said it, who asked that her words stay in the room. Noor has already set the card in type. She is nine days from opening and has nothing else for the shelf.
chapters.objective: Decide what happens to the sentence on Noor's card.

choices.label: Hold the room's agreement
choices.outcome: Sana supplies the tea and asks Noor to reset the card without the sentence, offering to write a new one that afternoon. Noor agrees and does not hide her face, which is worse. The card goes up with three words about smoke and honey. The opening is quiet. The taster from October comes in during the second week and does not mention it.
choices.memoryHint: Ask Noor to reset the card without her sentence.

choices.label: Ask the taster again
choices.outcome: Sana calls the taster, explains the card and the opening, and asks whether the sentence can be used, with her name or without it. The answer takes four days and comes back as no, kindly. Noor resets the card on the eighth day. The tea is on the shelf for the opening. The sentence is not, and both women know who asked.
choices.memoryHint: Call the taster and ask permission for the sentence.

echoes.sana_c3_a: You let guests review the ingredient list, the caffeine description and the proposed name without tasting anything.
echoes.sana_c3_b: You explained the ingredients and the participation choices before any samples were offered, so declining needed no reason.

chapters.title: The Kiosk Specification
chapters.setting: The hotel lobby kiosk, before the first service
chapters.intro: The kiosk is brass and glass and has stood empty since the hotel opened its lobby bar, and the manager now offers it to Sana on a two-year lease at a rent she can meet. The condition is a specification: gram weights, water temperature, a three-minute steep, a fixed leaf blend, so that any of the hotel's staff can make it identically on a Tuesday in August. The studio's bench cannot promise that and never has. Sana's alternative is to keep the bench and send dated lots, each with a card explaining what changed and why. The kiosk keys lie on the counter between them.
chapters.objective: Choose what the blend is in two years' time.

choices.label: Sign the specification
choices.outcome: Sana signs and spends six weeks at the bench reducing the blend to numbers a stranger can follow. The kiosk opens in June and the tea is the same every day, which is the point. In September the smoked leaf arrives lighter than the year before, and the specification has no line for that, so she writes one that nobody follows.
choices.memoryHint: Reduce the blend to numbers a stranger can follow.

choices.label: Keep the dated lots
choices.outcome: Sana declines the kiosk and sends the hotel a standing order of dated lots with a card for each. The first three are consistent. The fourth is not, and she says so on the card, in pencil, with the reason. The kiosk stays empty until a coffee company takes it. The hotel keeps the standing order through the winter, for the trolley.
choices.memoryHint: Send dated lots with honest cards, not a kiosk blend.

echoes.sana_c4_a: You printed a sensory name pointing to the documented ingredients, with caffeine and ingredient information kept beside it on the tin.
echoes.sana_c4_b: You chose a modest project name crediting the review process, keeping the ingredient description primary and private associations out of the product story.

title: The Quiet Watch
tagline: Listen long enough to notice what the silence contains.
premise: A forest station’s evening recording falls silent at the same minute for three nights, while the written observations continue.

chapters.title: Three Minutes Missing
chapters.intro: Vincent compares three evening recordings and hears the same short silence each night. His written log still describes wind and branches during those minutes. The mismatch is intriguing, but the notebook gives him a reason to begin with the equipment rather than an alarming story.
chapters.objective: Choose the first comparison.

choices.label: Read the written observations
choices.outcome: The handwritten entries mention a scheduled station check near each silent interval. Vincent aligns the dates and marks the connection as a lead. The forest’s missing sound now has a human routine worth examining before any stranger explanation.
choices.memoryHint: The handwritten entries mention a scheduled station check near each silent interval.

choices.label: Read the recorder’s service log
choices.outcome: The equipment log shows a recurring check window matching the gaps. Vincent keeps the recordings intact and asks the responsible technician to confirm the behavior, avoiding the temptation to edit silence into a more exciting discovery.
choices.memoryHint: The equipment log shows a recurring check window matching the gaps.

chapters.title: The Sound Between Checks
chapters.setting: A notebook beside the cabin window
chapters.intro: The technician confirms that the recorder pauses during its scheduled check. That explains the gap, but Vincent’s handwritten observations still contain details the machine missed. A light tapping on the roof appears several times, always after the evening wind changes.
chapters.objective: Choose how to investigate the ordinary sound.

choices.label: Compare the weather notes
choices.outcome: Vincent compares his notes about wind direction with the tapping entries. The pattern is consistent with loose natural material moving near the roof, and he records that modest explanation without presenting an unverified wildlife identification.
choices.memoryHint: Vincent compares his notes about wind direction with the tapping entries.

choices.label: Ask for a routine site inspection
choices.outcome: The station’s responsible team checks the permitted maintenance area and finds material resting near the roof edge. Vincent records the finding and leaves any work to the staff, preserving the distinction between listening and unsafe investigation.
choices.memoryHint: The station’s responsible team checks the permitted maintenance area and finds material resting near the roof edge.

echoes.vincent_c1_a: The handwritten entries mention a scheduled station check near each silent interval.
echoes.vincent_c1_b: The equipment log shows a recurring check window matching the gaps.

chapters.title: A Record with Room for Quiet
chapters.intro: The silence has a practical explanation, and the tapping has become a small documented observation. Vincent can organize a sound diary or a window-side observation sheet for visitors. He wants people to notice the forest without encouraging disturbance or promising rare encounters.
chapters.objective: Choose the quiet invitation.

choices.label: Build a sound diary
choices.outcome: Vincent pairs approved recordings with the written notes, labeling equipment gaps and uncertain sources. The diary shows that listening includes understanding the recorder’s limits. No rare animal is invented to make the ordinary evening worth keeping.
choices.memoryHint: Vincent pairs approved recordings with the written notes, labeling equipment gaps and uncertain sources.

choices.label: Create an observation sheet
choices.outcome: A simple sheet invites adult visitors to record general conditions from the approved viewing area. It asks for no personal details and makes no promise of wildlife sightings, leaving room for a worthwhile visit that remains uneventful.
choices.memoryHint: A simple sheet invites adult visitors to record general conditions from the approved viewing area.

echoes.vincent_c2_a: Vincent compares his notes about wind direction with the tapping entries.
echoes.vincent_c2_b: The station’s responsible team checks the permitted maintenance area and finds material resting near the roof edge.

chapters.title: The Last Entry at Dusk
chapters.setting: The cabin as the evening settles
chapters.intro: Vincent’s revised record contains the missing minutes, the equipment explanation and the small sounds his notebook caught. He can leave the project as a seasonal diary or help the responsible staff plan a limited quiet-viewing session under the station’s rules.
chapters.objective: Choose how the record meets its readers.

choices.label: Keep the seasonal diary
choices.outcome: The station files the diary with its sources and uncertainties. Its final page describes a clear evening without a remarkable event. Vincent closes the notebook knowing that an honest quiet entry is still an observation worth preserving.
choices.memoryHint: The station files the diary with its sources and uncertainties.

choices.label: Offer a supervised quiet session
choices.outcome: The responsible staff propose a limited session in the approved viewing space, with clear access and behavior rules. The sound diary remains available to anyone who prefers reading. Vincent leaves the window facing a forest that owes its visitors no performance.
choices.memoryHint: The responsible staff propose a limited session in the approved viewing space, with clear access and behavior rules.

echoes.vincent_c3_a: Vincent pairs approved recordings with the written notes, labeling equipment gaps and uncertain sources.
echoes.vincent_c3_b: A simple sheet invites adult visitors to record general conditions from the approved viewing area.

chapters.title: The Loan of a Microphone
chapters.setting: The lookout cabin, the first week of March
chapters.intro: The seasonal diary was read by more people than the station expected, and by February a research unit two valleys over has offered to lend an autonomous acoustic array for the spring: four microphones, a solar panel, a memory card that records every hour until June. Rona Sepp, the district's operations officer, is enthusiastic, because continuous data is what the funding forms ask for. Vincent thinks about the scheduled checks, which the array would record without a gap, and about the four visitors who came in January because the diary mentioned a silence. The crate sits on the porch with the loan papers on top.
chapters.objective: Decide whether the station listens by machine or by hand.

choices.label: Sign for the array
choices.outcome: Vincent signs, mounts the microphones on the approved brackets and keeps the notebook going alongside. The data is enormous and mostly wind. In April the array records a sound at twenty to four in the morning that nobody was awake to hear. Rona puts it in a funding report before Vincent has identified it, which takes him nine days and two calls to the unit.
choices.memoryHint: Sign for the microphone array and keep the notebook.

choices.label: Keep the notebook
choices.outcome: Vincent sends the crate back with a note about the check schedule and the visitors. Rona is disappointed and says so in the minutes. The station's application goes in without continuous data and is marked partial. Vincent walks the ridge on the last evening in March and writes four lines about ice leaving the ditch, which nobody will read until the diary is printed.
choices.memoryHint: Send the microphone crate back and keep writing by hand.

echoes.vincent_c1_a: You read the written observations first and found a scheduled station check beside each silent interval, marking the connection as a lead.
echoes.vincent_c1_b: You read the recorder's service log first, kept the recordings intact and asked the technician to confirm the recurring check window.

chapters.title: The Quiet Program
chapters.setting: The station office, a coach timetable on the desk
chapters.intro: The district's winter program has a page for places that are dark and quiet, and the station is on it. The tourism office proposes four coach visits in January and February, forty adults each, arriving at dusk and leaving after an hour, and the fee would cover the roof repair that has been deferred for two winters and now drips into a bucket beside the desk. Vincent's supervisor, Rona Sepp, has already accepted in principle. The approved viewing area holds twelve people comfortably. The coaches would park at the gate with their engines running for the heaters, and the walk to the window is four hundred meters of gravel.
chapters.objective: Decide what the station offers its visitors in January.

choices.label: Take the coach visits
choices.outcome: Vincent agrees, writes a route and a set of rules, and meets the first coach at the gate with a flashlight. Forty adults walk to the window and stand in the dark for an hour, and eleven of them talk. The roof is repaired in March. In the visitor book, one entry calls it the quietest hour of her year, and four say the walk was too long.
choices.memoryHint: Write a route and rules for forty adults in the dark.

choices.label: Sell the diary instead
choices.outcome: Vincent proposes that the station print the diary and sell it at the gate and by post, with a booked hour for eight people on Saturdays. The tourism office drops the station from the program. The diary sells sixty-one copies by April, the bucket stays under the drip, and the roof is patched in May from the station's own maintenance budget.
choices.memoryHint: Print the diary and book eight Saturday places.

echoes.vincent_c2_a: You compared the wind notes with the tapping entries, recording a modest explanation without claiming an unverified wildlife identification.
echoes.vincent_c2_b: You asked the responsible team for a routine site inspection and let staff handle the material resting near the roof edge.

chapters.title: The Writer's Question
chapters.setting: The interpretation desk, a wet Thursday
chapters.intro: Hanne Loew has come up the track every Thursday since October and has never asked for anything but the kettle. She is writing a piece for a regional magazine about places that keep a record of quiet, and the station is the middle of it. On a wet Thursday she asks Vincent to lend her the notebook: the pages from the three nights, the tapping entries, and whatever he recorded about the roof edge. Rona has already given her the station's name and a photograph of the window. The roof edge sits inside the maintenance area, behind a gate with a sign on it.
chapters.objective: Decide how much of the notebook leaves the desk.

choices.label: Lend her the pages
choices.outcome: Vincent photographs the relevant pages and sends them, including the roof entry with its bearings. The piece runs in April with the phrase “the place where the sound comes from”, and a map. In May two readers park at the gate and walk into the maintenance area. Rona has the gate rehung with a lock and asks Vincent to write the incident up.
choices.memoryHint: Send page photographs, including the roof entry's bearings.

choices.label: Read them together
choices.outcome: Vincent keeps the notebook on the desk and reads the entries aloud while Hanne takes notes, leaving out the bearings and saying why. She argues, then writes the piece around the gap, which makes the silence the subject rather than the roof. It runs in April without a map. She does not come on Thursdays in May, and the kettle stays on its shelf.
choices.memoryHint: Read entries aloud but withhold the roof bearings.

echoes.vincent_c3_a: You built a sound diary pairing approved recordings with written notes and labeling equipment gaps and uncertain sources.
echoes.vincent_c3_b: You made an observation sheet for the approved viewing area that asked for no personal details and promised no sightings.

chapters.title: A Page Dated April
chapters.setting: The window at dusk, the last of the light
chapters.intro: Spring closes the question. Rona wants the station to become a monitored site: the array bought outright on the district's budget, the data archived and published monthly, the window open to booked visitors on Saturdays, and Vincent's notebook running alongside. The alternative is the diary he already knows how to make, printed once a year, with the uncertainty left in and nothing published that would send anyone up the track. Both need a decision before the district's budget closes at the end of the month. The light is going. The window is open, and the ditch is loud with water.
chapters.objective: Decide what the station's record is for, and for whom.

choices.label: Take the monitored watch
choices.outcome: Vincent signs the station over to a monthly rhythm: downloads on the first Monday, a page of notes to go with them, the window open on Saturdays. The first published month is dull and accurate. In June a reader writes to ask about a gap on the fourteenth, and Vincent answers it in a sentence, because the schedule is published too.
choices.memoryHint: Commit to monthly downloads and a published notes page.

choices.label: Print the annual diary
choices.outcome: Vincent declines the purchase and spends April setting the year's diary in a cheap serif, gaps and all. The station prints a hundred and forty copies and sells most of them by August. Nothing on the ridge changes. On the last page he leaves a blank entry for the reader, with the date and the weather already written in.
choices.memoryHint: Set the year's diary in cheap serif, gaps included.

echoes.vincent_c4_a: You filed the seasonal diary with its sources and uncertainties, ending on a clear evening with no remarkable event.
echoes.vincent_c4_b: You offered a limited supervised session under the station's rules, with the diary available to anyone who preferred reading.

title: The Shard at Low Water
tagline: Follow the evidence without turning a shard into a treasure map.
premise: A legally documented coastal pottery fragment bears a workshop mark absent from its original catalog entry.

chapters.title: A Mark Under the Glaze
chapters.intro: Petra receives a legally documented pottery fragment from an existing collection. Its catalog entry lists a find location and material, but a small impressed mark was never described. The missing detail could improve the record without proving an exciting journey across the sea.
chapters.objective: Choose the first comparison.

choices.label: Compare workshop references
choices.outcome: A documented reference collection contains a similar mark with an uncertain attribution. Petra records the resemblance and its limits, adding a useful comparison without assigning the fragment to a maker the evidence cannot yet establish.
choices.memoryHint: A documented reference collection contains a similar mark with an uncertain attribution.

choices.label: Review the find documentation
choices.outcome: The original collection file confirms where and under what authority the fragment entered the archive. Petra adds the overlooked mark to the record and separates the object’s documented recovery from any theory about how it reached the coast.
choices.memoryHint: The original collection file confirms where and under what authority the fragment entered the archive.

chapters.title: A Route That Is Not a Wreck
chapters.setting: Historical cargo lists beside a map
chapters.intro: A trade archive mentions pottery moving between two fictional coastal towns during the relevant period. The connection is plausible but not specific to this fragment. Petra can compare material references or investigate the broader trade context while keeping the object’s story appropriately limited.
chapters.objective: Choose the next research direction.

choices.label: Compare the material references
choices.outcome: Approved non-invasive comparisons place the fragment within a broad group of similar wares. Petra records the range instead of an exact origin, giving the catalog a stronger description without making it sound more precise than the evidence allows.
choices.memoryHint: Approved non-invasive comparisons place the fragment within a broad group of similar wares.

choices.label: Trace the documented trade context
choices.outcome: Petra maps the documented cargo routes as background information, clearly labeling them as context rather than the fragment’s proven journey. The coast gains a richer history without a fictional shipwreck being passed off as an archaeological finding.
choices.memoryHint: Petra maps the documented cargo routes as background information, clearly labeling them as context rather than the fragment’s proven journey.

echoes.petra_c1_a: A documented reference collection contains a similar mark with an uncertain attribution.
echoes.petra_c1_b: The original collection file confirms where and under what authority the fragment entered the archive.

chapters.title: Small Enough to Overlook
chapters.intro: The improved record makes the fragment interesting, but the original needs controlled handling and display conditions. Petra can propose a clearly labeled replica for a public exhibit or an illustrated case study while the object remains protected.
chapters.objective: Choose how to make the research visible.

choices.label: Use a labeled replica
choices.outcome: The exhibit uses a documented replica beside photographs of the original and an explanation of the mark. Visitors can understand the research question without the replica being mistaken for an ancient object or the original being handled casually.
choices.memoryHint: The exhibit uses a documented replica beside photographs of the original and an explanation of the mark.

choices.label: Use an illustrated case study
choices.outcome: A concise case study follows the catalog entry from its first description to the new evidence. The original stays in protected collection storage, while the research remains accessible through clear images, sources and unanswered questions.
choices.memoryHint: A concise case study follows the catalog entry from its first description to the new evidence.

echoes.petra_c2_a: Approved non-invasive comparisons place the fragment within a broad group of similar wares.
echoes.petra_c2_b: Petra maps the documented cargo routes as background information, clearly labeling them as context rather than the fragment’s proven journey.

chapters.title: An Ordinary Object, Properly Seen
chapters.intro: Petra’s work has produced a better catalog entry, not a treasure hunt. The fragment can support a local loan proposal under collection rules or remain a documented study case in the archive. Both endings give the object attention without exaggerating what it proves.
chapters.objective: Choose the next home for the research.

choices.label: Propose a local museum loan
choices.outcome: The collection considers a properly documented loan with the necessary conservation and access conditions. The interpretation keeps the mark’s attribution uncertain. Petra leaves the fragment with a richer account that has not borrowed certainty from a dramatic setting.
choices.memoryHint: The collection considers a properly documented loan with the necessary conservation and access conditions.

choices.label: Keep an open research case
choices.outcome: The archive publishes the approved case study and invites relevant scholarly comparisons through its normal process. Petra files the original carefully. Its story ends, for now, with a useful question rather than an invented answer.
choices.memoryHint: The archive publishes the approved case study and invites relevant scholarly comparisons through its normal process.

echoes.petra_c3_a: The exhibit uses a documented replica beside photographs of the original and an explanation of the mark.
echoes.petra_c3_b: A concise case study follows the catalog entry from its first description to the new evidence.

chapters.title: The Caption Under the Photograph
chapters.setting: The district heritage office, a wet Tuesday
chapters.intro: Three weeks after the entry was signed off, a heritage-weekend leaflet arrives at the lab in a stack of post. On the second page is the fragment, photographed against grey card, and beneath it a caption calling it a trader's token from a wreck off Sallow Point. Petra's name appears in the credits as the researcher who identified the mark. She reads the caption twice. Nothing in her record says wreck; nothing says trader; the attribution is still open in her own file. The leaflet is due for a reprint in nine days, and the printer's number sits at the foot of the page.
chapters.objective: Decide how to answer a caption that borrows her name.

choices.label: Correct it through the trust
choices.outcome: Petra writes to the heritage board's press officer with the record attached and asks for a correction in the reprint and in the online listing. The reply takes four days and arrives copied to her head of collections, who adds a line about staff speaking to the press. The caption changes. So does the way her emails are read upstairs.
choices.memoryHint: Put the correction in writing through the press office.

choices.label: Ring the leaflet's editor
choices.outcome: Petra calls the editor directly, and by Thursday afternoon the caption reads "pottery fragment, workshop mark, attribution uncertain". It is fast, and it is a favour between two people. Nobody writes down why the change was made, and the editor asks her, pleasantly, whether she might draft a short piece for the next issue.
choices.memoryHint: Fix the caption by phone, leaving no record.

echoes.petra_c1_a: You compared the workshop references and kept the resemblance's limits, so the leaflet's confident attribution reads as something done to your name.
echoes.petra_c1_b: You reviewed the find documentation and kept the shard's recovery separate from theories of how it reached the coast, which the leaflet has undone.

chapters.title: A Post With Conditions
chapters.setting: The trust's grants room, upstairs, four o'clock
chapters.intro: The heritage trust offers the lab a two-year cataloguing post, which would make Petra's own contract permanent, and the offer letter ties it to a condition. The lab will supply public interpretation for the Sallow Point trail: object text for six panels, written to the trust's brief. The trail's designer has already sketched a wreck across the first one. Petra's director wants the post badly enough to have printed the letter twice. The decision is due on Friday, and the brief describes the interpretation as light-touch. Petra thinks about what light-touch means at four hundred millimetres.
chapters.objective: Decide whether to take the funded post and its clause.

choices.label: Sign and write the panels
choices.outcome: Petra signs, and spends the first month drafting six panels that say what the objects can support and no more. The designer accepts four and rewrites two. Her contract is renewed in the spring. The panels carry her initials in the project file and her caveats in smaller type than she wrote them.
choices.memoryHint: Trade six trail panels for a permanent contract.

choices.label: Refuse the condition
choices.outcome: Petra writes back declining the clause and asks the trust to fund cataloguing on its own terms. The post goes to a fixed-term assistant instead, and the trail's panels are written by a freelancer in the trust's office. Her contract runs to December. The fragment stays in the lab, where she can still answer for it.
choices.memoryHint: Decline the clause and keep the fragment in the lab.

echoes.petra_c2_a: You placed the shard in a broad group and recorded a range rather than an origin; the trail now wants that range narrowed.
echoes.petra_c2_b: You mapped the cargo routes as background, labelled as context rather than a proven journey; the trail has since flattened them into a wreck.

chapters.title: Her Father's Wreck
chapters.setting: The collections lab, after the volunteers leave
chapters.intro: Merce Aldon has volunteered at the lab on Thursdays for eleven years, and she was fourteen when she picked the shard off the strand at Sallow Quay and carried it to the museum in a shoe box. She has read the new entry twice. Now she sits on the stool by the sink with her coat still on and asks Petra to pass her father's account to whoever writes the trail panel: he told her the pottery came off a ship that broke on the point, and he had it from his own father. Merce does not want the wreck proved. She wants it written that this is what her family has always said.
chapters.objective: Decide where Merce's father's account belongs on the trail.

choices.label: Give it its own panel
choices.outcome: The panel goes in beside the case, headed What the Aldon family has always said, attributed to Merce and dated. It is set in a different type and the object label does not mention a wreck. Visitors read it aloud to each other. Two of them ask the front desk whether it is true, which is the question Petra wanted the label to leave open.
choices.memoryHint: Set the family's account beside the case, dated.

choices.label: Record it in the file
choices.outcome: Petra records the interview, dates it, and files it with the recovery documentation, where a researcher can find it and a visitor cannot. Merce listens, nods, and takes her coat off the hook. She comes the following Thursday and the one after. She does not mention the panel again, and Petra notices that she works with the radio on now.
choices.memoryHint: File the interview where only researchers can find it.

echoes.petra_c3_a: You used a labelled replica so visitors could follow the mark without handling the original; Merce now offers a story to set beside it.
echoes.petra_c3_b: You kept the original in storage and made a readable case study; Merce has read it and come to add what it left out.

chapters.title: What the Label Leaves Out
chapters.setting: The trail's first plinth, an hour before opening
chapters.intro: The trail opens on Saturday. The first plinth stands at the top of the slipway with a stainless plate screwed to its face, and the plate is blank because the text is still in dispute. The trust wants the fragment shown. The designer wants a ship. The panel currently reads "pottery fragment, workshop mark, attribution uncertain", and everyone has agreed to live with that sentence until Monday. Petra has the loan paperwork in her bag and the shard in a foam cut on the passenger seat of her car, forty metres down the hill.
chapters.objective: Decide what the fragment becomes when the trail opens.

choices.label: Lend it for the season
choices.outcome: Petra signs the loan, and the shard goes under glass at the top of the slipway with the plain sentence on the plate and Merce's panel six feet away. Walkers and ferry passengers stop at it. In October it comes back to the lab with a scratch on the case and a visitor book full of wrecks.
choices.memoryHint: Lend the shard under glass for one season.

choices.label: Keep it in the lab
choices.outcome: Petra withdraws the loan on the Friday, and the plinth shows a photograph at actual size instead, with a note that the original is held in the collection. The trail's first panel loses its relic and keeps its sentence. On Monday the lab opens as usual; the shard is in tray four, and the foam still smells of the cutter.
choices.memoryHint: Withdraw the loan and show a photograph instead.

echoes.petra_c4_a: You proposed a documented loan with conservation conditions and kept the attribution uncertain; the plinth is what that proposal looks like built.
echoes.petra_c4_b: You filed the original and published an open case ending in a question; the trail now wants that question turned into a caption.

title: The Shelf Between Us
tagline: Make space for both a conversation and a quiet page.
premise: Two anonymous suggestions ask the same small reading room to become both quieter and more conversational.

chapters.title: Two Cards in the Box
chapters.intro: Ellis finds two anonymous suggestions in the reading room’s box. One asks for fewer interruptions; the other asks for a place to discuss books with other adults. Neither writer has asked to be identified, and the room does not have space for every idea at once.
chapters.objective: Choose the first planning step.

choices.label: Read the room’s existing pattern
choices.outcome: Ellis reviews general room-use observations without consulting individual borrowing histories. The notes show different rhythms across the evening, giving him a way to consider both requests without guessing who wrote the cards.
choices.memoryHint: Ellis reviews general room-use observations without consulting individual borrowing histories.

choices.label: Offer a private preference survey
choices.outcome: Adults can voluntarily indicate whether quiet reading or scheduled discussion would help them use the room. Ellis collects no names or personal explanations, keeping the question about the space rather than its readers’ private lives.
choices.memoryHint: Adults can voluntarily indicate whether quiet reading or scheduled discussion would help them use the room.

chapters.title: A Shelf as a Boundary
chapters.intro: The room can support a clearer spatial boundary or a predictable discussion schedule. Ellis prepares two modest arrangements using the existing furniture and agreed venue rules. The aim is not to decide which kind of reader belongs more.
chapters.objective: Choose the first arrangement to try.

choices.label: Separate quiet and discussion areas
choices.outcome: A modest layout proposal uses an existing shelf to clarify two areas without pretending to soundproof the room. Ellis explains the limits and keeps a route between the areas, so the new boundary guides use rather than dividing people into fixed groups.
choices.memoryHint: A modest layout proposal uses an existing shelf to clarify two areas without pretending to soundproof the room.

choices.label: Set a predictable discussion time
choices.outcome: The room proposes a limited adult discussion period with clearly advertised quiet hours around it. Ellis makes participation optional and keeps ordinary borrowing available, giving visitors a predictable choice without asking them to join an activity.
choices.memoryHint: The room proposes a limited adult discussion period with clearly advertised quiet hours around it.

echoes.ellis_c1_a: Ellis reviews general room-use observations without consulting individual borrowing histories.
echoes.ellis_c1_b: Adults can voluntarily indicate whether quiet reading or scheduled discussion would help them use the room.

chapters.title: More Than One Way to Read
chapters.intro: The arrangement is ready for a trial. Ellis can support it with a multi-format selection or clear participation notes for the optional adult discussion. He wants the invitation to remain useful to someone who arrives alone and chooses to keep reading silently.
chapters.objective: Choose the supporting resource.

choices.label: Offer a multi-format selection
choices.outcome: The table includes clearly identified available formats under the library’s normal lending rules. Ellis describes the options without treating any format as a lesser version of reading. The selection supports different preferences without requiring an explanation.
choices.memoryHint: The table includes clearly identified available formats under the library’s normal lending rules.

choices.label: Make discussion expectations clear
choices.outcome: A short note explains the optional discussion’s format, time and respectful participation rules. Listening without speaking remains welcome. Ellis keeps it separate from personal disclosure, allowing the conversation to stay about the chosen book.
choices.memoryHint: A short note explains the optional discussion’s format, time and respectful participation rules.

echoes.ellis_c2_a: A modest layout proposal uses an existing shelf to clarify two areas without pretending to soundproof the room.
echoes.ellis_c2_b: The room proposes a limited adult discussion period with clearly advertised quiet hours around it.

chapters.title: The Room at Closing Time
chapters.setting: A review of the reading-room trial
chapters.intro: The trial gives Ellis enough feedback to recommend a continued arrangement or a smaller revised schedule. The anonymous cards remain anonymous. A useful outcome can make room for both kinds of evening without demanding that everyone use the room in the same way.
chapters.objective: Choose the recommendation.

choices.label: Keep the reviewed arrangement
choices.outcome: The reading room keeps the arrangement at its reviewed scale, with its limits clearly described. Ellis leaves a fresh suggestion card beside the box. Quiet and conversation now have a shared place without either becoming a condition of belonging.
choices.memoryHint: The reading room keeps the arrangement at its reviewed scale, with its limits clearly described.

choices.label: Revise the schedule gently
choices.outcome: Ellis proposes a smaller discussion schedule and a clearer quiet-reading notice before reviewing again. The room remains open under its ordinary rules. The project closes with two valid requests still in view, rather than one being treated as a problem to remove.
choices.memoryHint: Ellis proposes a smaller discussion schedule and a clearer quiet-reading notice before reviewing again.

echoes.ellis_c3_a: The table includes clearly identified available formats under the library’s normal lending rules.
echoes.ellis_c3_b: A short note explains the optional discussion’s format, time and respectful participation rules.

chapters.title: The Numbers and the Room
chapters.setting: The evening returns desk, monthly counts spread out
chapters.intro: The trial's counts land on Ellis's desk with the rest of the branch figures, and the room has done well. More adults come through the door on discussion evenings; fewer come on the quiet ones. On Tuesday the area manager brings the spreadsheet down, folded once, and says the obvious thing: that the quiet side is the smaller number now, that the second table could take four more chairs, and that engagement is what the service is measured on this year. She is not unkind about it. She has a printout and a date, and she asks Ellis to bring his view to Thursday's meeting.
chapters.objective: Decide what evidence to bring to Thursday's meeting.

choices.label: Bring the hour-by-hour counts
choices.outcome: Ellis builds a sheet that shows when the room is full and when it is quiet, and what the quiet hours hold: four people on a wet Tuesday, the same four, for years. The manager reads it, asks for a second sheet by month, and postpones the chairs. The room keeps its table until the next quarter, when the question comes back in a different shape.
choices.memoryHint: Show the manager which hours stay quiet.

choices.label: Ask for one evening shift
choices.outcome: Ellis invites her to work a Tuesday closing shift, and she does, shelving returns and saying nothing. At nine she sits at the quiet table with a magazine for twenty minutes because there is nowhere else to sit. On Thursday she does not mention the chairs. Ellis does not know whether the evening counted as evidence or as a favour.
choices.memoryHint: Ask the manager to work one Tuesday closing shift.

echoes.ellis_c1_a: You read the room's existing pattern rather than anyone's borrowing history, so the figures you bring are about hours and tables, not readers.
echoes.ellis_c1_b: You ran a voluntary survey with no names or explanations, so you can tell the manager what people chose without saying who chose it.

chapters.title: A Grant With a List
chapters.setting: The staff kitchen, grant papers on the table
chapters.intro: A small adult-education trust offers the branch money for the room: enough for six better chairs, a kettle that does not rattle, and a facilitator for a ten-week series on Tuesday evenings. The terms are ordinary and firm. A fixed programme, a sign-up sheet at the desk, and attendance reported back in numbers at the end. Ellis reads the sheet twice. A list by the door changes who walks in; it also buys the chairs, and the room has needed chairs since before the trial began. The trust's deadline is the end of the month, and the branch manager has already said yes in principle.
chapters.objective: Decide whether to accept the grant and its sign-up sheet.

choices.label: Take the grant as offered
choices.outcome: Ellis signs, and the sheet goes on a clipboard at the desk with a pencil on a string. The chairs arrive. Twenty-two people sign the first week, eleven the third, and the facilitator is good. The reported numbers are healthy. The quiet table is still there, and fewer people sit at it on Tuesdays than used to.
choices.memoryHint: Accept the clipboard sheet to buy the chairs.

choices.label: Ask for numbers only
choices.outcome: Ellis writes back asking whether attendance can be counted at the door rather than signed for, and offers the branch's own figures as the report. The trust takes three weeks to consider and returns a smaller sum, with no facilitator. Six chairs arrive in September. The series runs anyway, run by whoever turns up first, and the kettle is bought secondhand from the Friends.
choices.memoryHint: Count attendance at the door, not on a sheet.

echoes.ellis_c2_a: You used the shelf to clarify two areas without pretending to soundproof anything; the grant now wants one area with a programme in it.
echoes.ellis_c2_b: You set a limited discussion period with quiet hours advertised around it, and the trust now wants that period to become a ten-week course.

chapters.title: The Question Behind the Desk
chapters.setting: The reading room, ten minutes before closing
chapters.intro: Mara has come to the quiet table on Thursdays for six years and has never once asked Ellis for anything. Tonight she stands at the desk with her coat half on and says there is a man in the Tuesday discussion whom she thinks she recognises from a job she left badly, and she cannot be sure. She asks Ellis to look at what the man has been borrowing, just to see whether he reads the things she remembers him reading, and to say nothing to anyone. The returns are on the trolley. The terminal is still logged in, and the room is nearly empty.
chapters.objective: Decide how to answer Mara without using the borrowing record.

choices.label: Refuse and explain the limit
choices.outcome: Ellis tells her what the record is for and what it is not for, and that he will not look. He offers what he can do: sit in on Tuesday, keep the door propped, walk her to the corner. Mara listens, says she probably imagined it, and takes her book home. She comes back the following Thursday and sits at the quiet table with her back to the room.
choices.memoryHint: Refuse the record but offer to walk her out.

choices.label: Speak to the man directly
choices.outcome: Ellis does not open the record. On Tuesday he introduces himself to the new attendee, asks whether the room is working for him, and mentions the group's arrangements for keeping the conversation on the book. The man is polite and a little puzzled. He does not come back the following week. Mara does, and asks Ellis whether he found anything out.
choices.memoryHint: Speak to the man without opening his record.

echoes.ellis_c3_a: You offered formats under ordinary lending rules so no one had to explain a preference; Mara now asks you to explain another reader.
echoes.ellis_c3_b: You wrote participation rules that let listening count as taking part; Mara has listened for six years and now asks you a question.

chapters.title: A Room Without a Sign
chapters.setting: The empty room, an hour before opening
chapters.intro: The chairs are out, the kettle is on, and the room is arranged the way the review left it. Ellis has been asked to write the arrangement up for the branch's standing practice, which would put a short charter by the door and settle the matter for whoever runs the room after him. The alternative is to leave it as it is: nothing written, everything held in the shift handovers and in the fact that the shelf is heavy and nobody wants to move it. He has a blank sheet on the desk and forty minutes before the doors open.
chapters.objective: Decide whether the room needs a written charter.

choices.label: Write the charter
choices.outcome: Ellis writes four lines: quiet this side of the shelf, conversation that side, everyone may use both, nobody has to say why they came. He pins it by the door at eye height. Two regulars read it on the way in and say nothing. After that, two new staff run the room exactly as written, and the shelf is moved once for a heating repair and put back crooked.
choices.memoryHint: Pin four lines by the door at eye height.

choices.label: Leave it unwritten
choices.outcome: Ellis puts the blank sheet in the recycling and spends the forty minutes moving the good lamp to the quiet side, where the light has always been poor. He shows the new evening assistant where the cards live and how the shelf is meant to sit. Nothing is posted by the door. The room holds as long as the handovers do.
choices.memoryHint: Move the good lamp instead of writing rules.

echoes.ellis_c4_a: You kept the arrangement at its reviewed scale and left a fresh card by the box; the branch now wants it written down.
echoes.ellis_c4_b: You proposed a smaller schedule and a clearer quiet notice before reviewing again; the branch now wants something more permanent than a notice.

title: The City That Folds
tagline: A small fold can change how a whole city is read.
premise: A folding visitor-center model turns one district upside down whenever the final panel opens.

chapters.title: The Upside-Down Plaza
chapters.setting: A paper model on an indigo work mat
chapters.intro: Yara opens a prototype visitor model and watches its last panel pull a miniature plaza upside down. The paper buildings are harmless, but the mistake makes the district hard to understand. She sets aside the decorative pieces so the mechanism can be read clearly.
chapters.objective: Choose the first prototype comparison.

choices.label: Compare the hinge sequence
choices.outcome: Yara marks the order of the model’s folds and finds that the final panel reverses an earlier turn. A simplified prototype isolates the motion, giving her a specific paper mechanism to revise instead of rebuilding the entire miniature city.
choices.memoryHint: Yara marks the order of the model’s folds and finds that the final panel reverses an earlier turn.

choices.label: Compare the reading order
choices.outcome: Yara traces how an adult visitor encounters each district as the model opens. The plaza appears before its orientation is clear, suggesting that a change in presentation may work better than adding another decorative label.
choices.memoryHint: Yara traces how an adult visitor encounters each district as the model opens.

chapters.title: A City in Two Pieces
chapters.setting: Two paper prototypes beside the original
chapters.intro: Yara can revise the final hinge or divide the model into clearly connected modules. One keeps the single unfolding gesture; the other offers simpler handling at the cost of a less theatrical reveal. She prepares the two approaches without pretending there is one elegant answer for every user.
chapters.objective: Choose the next prototype.

choices.label: Revise the final hinge
choices.outcome: The revised prototype changes the last movement while keeping the city in one object. Yara records where it still needs handling tests, preserving the satisfying reveal without declaring that a clever fold has solved every usability question.
choices.memoryHint: The revised prototype changes the last movement while keeping the city in one object.

choices.label: Use connected modules
choices.outcome: The modular prototype lets each district open in a simpler sequence, with an obvious relationship between pieces. Yara trades one dramatic unfolding for more flexible handling and makes that design choice visible in the project notes.
choices.memoryHint: The modular prototype lets each district open in a simpler sequence, with an obvious relationship between pieces.

echoes.yara_c1_a: Yara marks the order of the model’s folds and finds that the final panel reverses an earlier turn.
echoes.yara_c1_b: Yara traces how an adult visitor encounters each district as the model opens.

chapters.title: Finding the Way by Touch
chapters.intro: The moving structure is clearer. The next review can focus on raised route cues or a high-contrast printed companion, with the appropriate specialists checking the design. Yara wants the model to offer useful information beyond its satisfying movement.
chapters.objective: Choose the next information layer.

choices.label: Review raised route cues
choices.outcome: A specialist review examines simple raised distinctions for the main route and landmarks. Yara keeps the model’s limits explicit and avoids representing an untested craft detail as a complete tactile navigation system.
choices.memoryHint: A specialist review examines simple raised distinctions for the main route and landmarks.

choices.label: Review the printed companion
choices.outcome: A clear printed companion uses strong contrast, plain labels and matching district order. Yara records how it relates to the model so visitors can choose an information format rather than being required to manipulate paper to understand the display.
choices.memoryHint: A clear printed companion uses strong contrast, plain labels and matching district order.

echoes.yara_c2_a: The revised prototype changes the last movement while keeping the city in one object.
echoes.yara_c2_b: The modular prototype lets each district open in a simpler sequence, with an obvious relationship between pieces.

chapters.title: A Fold Worth Sharing
chapters.intro: The prototype now opens coherently, and its information layers have a documented review path. Yara can prepare a supervised display model or publish a clearly credited paper pattern for an approved adult workshop. Neither needs to be mistaken for a real-world route guarantee.
chapters.objective: Choose the model’s final role.

choices.label: Keep a supervised display model
choices.outcome: The visitor center receives the approved model, companion information and clear handling guidance. Yara watches the plaza stay upright as the last fold opens. The small city has become easier to read without losing the pleasure of its movement.
choices.memoryHint: The visitor center receives the approved model, companion information and clear handling guidance.

choices.label: Prepare an adult workshop pattern
choices.outcome: A credited pattern supports an optional adult craft workshop with the venue’s normal supervision and materials rules. The visitor information remains separate from the craft activity. Yara leaves a design that people can explore without confusing a paper city with the real one.
choices.memoryHint: A credited pattern supports an optional adult craft workshop with the venue’s normal supervision and materials rules.

echoes.yara_c3_a: A specialist review examines simple raised distinctions for the main route and landmarks.
echoes.yara_c3_b: A clear printed companion uses strong contrast, plain labels and matching district order.

chapters.title: The Box Without Instructions
chapters.setting: The community hall, an hour before the evening talk
chapters.intro: The visitor centre has begun lending the model out, which Yara did not expect and did not forbid. Tonight it is at the harbour hall for an evening talk on the district's future, and the box has arrived ahead of her with the model inside and nothing else. No card, no cradle, just foam cut two years ago for a smaller version. The hall's steward has already opened it on a trestle table, and a queue of adults in waterproofs is forming. The last panel is the one people always reach for first, and the blue stop mark has worn to a smudge.
chapters.objective: Decide how the model survives an evening of strangers.

choices.label: Cut a new travel cradle
choices.outcome: Yara spends forty minutes at the hall's kitchen table with a scalpel and the box's own lid, cutting a stop that holds the last panel at eighty degrees. The talk starts late. The model comes home with every hinge intact and a lid that no longer closes flat, and she carries it to the car under her arm.
choices.memoryHint: Cut a new stop from the box lid.

choices.label: Write a handling card
choices.outcome: Yara writes six lines on the back of a talk programme and tapes it inside the lid: open left to right, stop at the blue mark, ask before lifting. Four people read it. The rest are careful anyway, and by nine the last panel has a soft crease where a thumb has pushed past the stop. She smooths it with her nail and says nothing.
choices.memoryHint: Tape six handling lines inside the lid.

echoes.yara_c1_a: You isolated the reversed turn in the hinge sequence instead of rebuilding the city; that hinge is what a stranger's thumb finds first.
echoes.yara_c1_b: You traced how a visitor meets each district as the model opens; tonight's queue meets the plaza before its orientation, exactly as you predicted.

chapters.title: The Word Accessible
chapters.setting: A council access meeting, fluorescent light
chapters.intro: The terminal project has asked whether the model can be listed in its access information as an orientation aid, and the committee has put the question to Yara in a room with no windows and a broken blind. The listing would mean the word accessible, in print, above her name, before any specialist has reviewed the raised cues at full size. The committee's own adviser is not in the room. The project opens in eleven weeks, and the alternative on the table is a standard tactile map bought from a catalogue, which nobody present has touched.
chapters.objective: Decide whether to allow the word accessible in print.

choices.label: Agree, with a review first
choices.outcome: Yara agrees to the listing on condition that the raised cues go to the committee's adviser before anything is printed, and that the wording says "model with raised route cues, reviewed by" and stops there. The review takes five weeks and asks for two changes. The opening slips a fortnight, and the printed line is longer than the designer wanted.
choices.memoryHint: Agree to the word only after a review.

choices.label: Decline the listing
choices.outcome: Yara says the model is a display you can touch and nothing more, and asks for that sentence in the terminal's information. The committee buys the catalogue map. It arrives in a plastic wallet, correct and lifeless, and is screwed to the wall by the ticket machine. Yara's model goes into the terminal anyway, on a plinth, four metres from the map.
choices.memoryHint: Call it a display you can touch, nothing more.

echoes.yara_c2_a: You kept the city in one object and changed the last movement; that object is what the terminal now wants to call a route.
echoes.yara_c2_b: You traded one dramatic unfolding for modules that open in a simpler order; the terminal now wants them to stand in for a route.

chapters.title: The Street That Isn't There
chapters.setting: The model table, after the last visitor
chapters.intro: Rennie has been opening the model for visitors since March and has a patter for every district. After the last visitor on Friday, Rennie stays behind and asks for one more thing. The terrace off Kiln Row, where Rennie was raised, comes down in the spring, and it is not on the model at all. Rennie wants it added before the centre's redisplay: six houses and the drying green, hand-drawn if it has to be. The model's survey dates from before the terrace was built. Yara can see exactly where it would go, and exactly how much it would claim.
chapters.objective: Decide how to answer Rennie's request about the terrace.

choices.label: Add a dated overlay
choices.outcome: Yara builds a hinged overlay the width of a hand, painted in a different key, dated this year and lettered with Rennie's name in small capitals at the corner. It sits over the survey like a note clipped to a page. Rennie opens it for the first visitors on Saturday and does not use the patter at all that day.
choices.memoryHint: Clip a dated overlay of six houses over the survey.

choices.label: Keep the survey intact
choices.outcome: Yara declines the paper and offers what she can do: a recording of Rennie on the terrace, played on the bench beside the model and credited in the companion notes. It runs four minutes. Rennie records it twice, uses the second take, and stops opening the model for visitors in the evenings.
choices.memoryHint: Record Rennie's terrace as four minutes of audio.

echoes.yara_c3_a: You had the raised cues reviewed and kept the model's limits explicit, and the limits are why a street can't simply be added.
echoes.yara_c3_b: You built a printed companion in district order so information needn't come from the paper; Rennie asks for a place only paper can hold.

chapters.title: What Travels and What Stays
chapters.setting: The visitor centre's stores, a cold morning
chapters.intro: The model has been out four times this year and has come back four times needing a Saturday. The centre offers Yara a choice, in writing, with a budget line attached: either a formal loan programme, with two staff trained on repairs, a spares box and the pattern drawings handed over, or a case in the stores and a fixed label, permanently in the building, no more journeys. The travel box is on the bench between them with its lid open. Somewhere in the last four returns, a visitor has written a question in pencil on the inside of that lid.
chapters.objective: Decide whether the city keeps travelling or stays.

choices.label: Train two staff, hand over
choices.outcome: Yara spends three Saturdays teaching the repairs, cutting two sets of spares and annotating the drawings in pencil where the paper has failed. The first loan she does not attend goes to a library two districts over and comes back with a repaired hinge that is not quite hers. The pencil question stays inside the lid.
choices.memoryHint: Hand over the drawings and train two staff.

choices.label: Case it, label it, stop
choices.outcome: Yara builds the case herself, with a clear lid and a foam bed cut to the model's open shape, and writes the label in six lines: what it shows, what it leaves out, who reviewed it, and the year. It goes into the stores beside the survey maps. She keeps one spare hinge in her coat pocket for a year, then loses it.
choices.memoryHint: Build a clear-lidded case and write six lines.

echoes.yara_c4_a: You handed over a supervised model with handling guidance and watched the plaza stay upright; four loans later, that guidance works without you.
echoes.yara_c4_b: You wrote a credited workshop pattern and kept visitor information separate; the model's next life is a question of who holds the drawings.

title: Letters for an Open Door
tagline: Paint a welcome that can be read from the pavement.
premise: A fictional neighborhood workshop commissions a new entrance sign based on a beautiful but difficult-to-read old design.

chapters.title: The Sign from the Pavement
chapters.intro: Noel studies a fictional workshop’s old sign beside its new brief. The decorative letters are elegant at arm’s length but difficult to read from the public approach. The client wants the place to feel familiar without leaving first-time visitors searching for the entrance.
chapters.objective: Choose the first design reference.

choices.label: Study the old letter shapes
choices.outcome: Noel identifies a few distinctive curves that can survive a simpler design. He records the original sign as its own work, keeping the new version clearly dated rather than passing a fresh commission off as an untouched historic object.
choices.memoryHint: Noel identifies a few distinctive curves that can survive a simpler design.

choices.label: Study the approach view
choices.outcome: Noel compares the sign’s proposed location with the approved public approach, using a mock-up instead of unsafe site work. The review identifies which details disappear at a distance, giving the new design a practical starting point.
choices.memoryHint: Noel compares the sign’s proposed location with the approved public approach, using a mock-up instead of unsafe site work.

chapters.title: A Flourish with a Purpose
chapters.setting: Two sign mock-ups on the bench
chapters.intro: The new sign can retain a restrained decorative border or carry one distinctive letter detail within a simpler word shape. Noel lays both mock-ups beside the client’s verified wording. Neither version will invent a service or an opening promise just to make the sign inviting.
chapters.objective: Choose the design to develop.

choices.label: Keep the border, simplify the words
choices.outcome: The mock-up moves the ornament to a quiet border and gives the verified wording a clearer shape. Noel preserves a trace of the old design while letting the sign’s main job remain readable from the approach.
choices.memoryHint: The mock-up moves the ornament to a quiet border and gives the verified wording a clearer shape.

choices.label: Keep one letter detail
choices.outcome: A single distinctive curve survives within otherwise straightforward lettering. Noel documents the adaptation and leaves the rest of the sign calm, making familiarity a detail to discover rather than a puzzle every visitor must solve.
choices.memoryHint: A single distinctive curve survives within otherwise straightforward lettering.

echoes.noel_c1_a: Noel identifies a few distinctive curves that can survive a simpler design.
echoes.noel_c1_b: Noel compares the sign’s proposed location with the approved public approach, using a mock-up instead of unsafe site work.

chapters.title: The Door, Not Just the Name
chapters.intro: The lettering is ready for the client’s review, but visitors also need to identify the correct entrance. Noel can develop a simple matching direction cue or a coordinated text panel, subject to the venue’s access and installation checks.
chapters.objective: Choose the supporting information.

choices.label: Use a simple direction cue
choices.outcome: A matching cue points toward the approved entrance using a reviewed symbol and clear placement proposal. Noel keeps it separate from decorative lettering, so finding the door does not depend on appreciating the sign’s style.
choices.memoryHint: A matching cue points toward the approved entrance using a reviewed symbol and clear placement proposal.

choices.label: Use a plain text companion
choices.outcome: A concise companion panel uses the client’s verified entrance wording in a simpler layout. Noel pairs it with the decorative sign rather than forcing one object to do every job, giving visitors another readable route to the same door.
choices.memoryHint: A concise companion panel uses the client’s verified entrance wording in a simpler layout.

echoes.noel_c2_a: The mock-up moves the ornament to a quiet border and gives the verified wording a clearer shape.
echoes.noel_c2_b: A single distinctive curve survives within otherwise straightforward lettering.

chapters.title: The First Person Who Finds It
chapters.intro: The approved sign and supporting information are ready for qualified installation. Noel can leave a documented care and repainting record or prepare a small display of the design’s development. The final welcome should belong to the fictional workshop, not to a fabricated claim about its reputation.
chapters.objective: Choose what stays with the sign.

choices.label: Keep the repainting record
choices.outcome: The client receives the verified wording, approved colors, design file and specialist care guidance. Noel signs the new work with its real project date. The door can be found, and a future repaint will not need to guess what was promised.
choices.memoryHint: The client receives the verified wording, approved colors, design file and specialist care guidance.

choices.label: Show the design’s evolution
choices.outcome: A small display pairs the old design record with the new mock-ups and their readable details. It credits the work without inventing an endorsement or rating. Noel leaves a familiar doorway with a clearer invitation written above it.
choices.memoryHint: A small display pairs the old design record with the new mock-ups and their readable details.

echoes.noel_c3_a: A matching cue points toward the approved entrance using a reviewed symbol and clear placement proposal.
echoes.noel_c3_b: A concise companion panel uses the client’s verified entrance wording in a simpler layout.

chapters.title: The Awning Under the Letters
chapters.setting: The pavement outside the workshop, mid-morning
chapters.intro: The sign has been up eleven weeks, and Noel has been avoiding Quarry Lane, which is a bad habit in a man who paints for a living. The workshop's owner has had an awning fitted: good canvas, sensible, bought secondhand from a café that closed. Its stripes run horizontally at exactly the height of the lower third of the lettering. From the pavement opposite, where a stranger stands, the words break into a row of pale blocks. From under the awning, at the door, they are perfect. Noel stands opposite for a while with his hands in his pockets, then crosses.
chapters.objective: Decide how to fix what the awning did.

choices.label: Re-cut the letters larger
choices.outcome: Noel redraws the word at a bigger weight that clears the stripes and quotes for a new fascia board. The owner signs it off with a sigh and a discount. The new board goes up in April. From opposite, the workshop's name reads clean; the fine spacing Noel liked is gone, and he notices it every time he passes.
choices.memoryHint: Redraw the word heavier to clear the stripes.

choices.label: Hang a blade sign
choices.outcome: Noel makes a small double-sided blade for the bracket by the door, at right angles to the street, where no awning can cross it. It reads at thirty metres. The fascia above stays as it was, half lost behind the stripes, and visitors find the door without ever looking up at the work he was commissioned to do.
choices.memoryHint: Hang a blade sign where the awning cannot reach.

echoes.noel_c1_a: You kept a few old curves in a simpler design and dated the work honestly; the awning cuts those curves at reading distance.
echoes.noel_c1_b: You studied the approach view with a mock-up and found which details vanish; the awning has done the same job faster and less kindly.

chapters.title: The Scheme's Approved Hand
chapters.setting: A regeneration office above the launderette
chapters.intro: The district's shopfront scheme has money this year and a list of approved painters, and Noel's name is on the list because the workshop's sign photographed well. The scheme's officer is friendly and specific: standard letter heights, a fixed palette of four, a small panel for the scheme's own mark, and eleven shopfronts on Quarry Lane and the streets behind it. It is four months of work. Two of the eleven signs are fine as they are, and one belongs to a woman who has painted her own window by hand for nineteen years and does not want him there.
chapters.objective: Decide whether to paint the street under the scheme's rules.

choices.label: Join and argue inside
choices.outcome: Noel signs the schedule and spends the first fortnight on letter heights, which he wins, and the palette, which he loses. Nine shopfronts get readable signs in four approved colours. The woman on the corner keeps her window and gets nothing. At the review, Noel asks for a variance clause and is told to put it in writing for next year.
choices.memoryHint: Join the scheme and argue letter heights inside.

choices.label: Stay off the list
choices.outcome: Noel declines and spends his evenings helping four shopkeepers apply individually, with measured drawings and their own wording. Two applications succeed. The scheme's own painter does the rest of the street in a fortnight, neatly, in the four colours, and the two signs Noel drew are the only ones that do not match.
choices.memoryHint: Help four shopkeepers apply on their own wording.

echoes.noel_c2_a: You moved the ornament to a quiet border so the wording could read; the scheme wants the border and the wording both standardised.
echoes.noel_c2_b: You let one distinctive curve survive in plain lettering as a detail to find; the scheme's four colours leave no room for it.

chapters.title: A Date Nobody Wrote Down
chapters.setting: The workshop's back room, kettle on
chapters.intro: Bram Tull has run the workshop since his father died and has never asked Noel for a favour, which is why the asking is awkward. He wants two words added under the name, Est. 1911, and a small painted laurel beside them, because customers ask how old the place is and a date answers them in one glance. The papers Bram gave Noel at the start say the Tulls took the premises in 1934. The 1911 on the old sign, where Noel cleaned the corner, belonged to a different firm with a different trade.
chapters.objective: Decide how to answer Bram's request for a founding date.

choices.label: Paint only what's documented
choices.outcome: Noel spends a wet week in the record office and finds the 1934 lease, a 1911 paint supplier's bill for a different firm, and nothing else. He paints Repairs since 1934 in the same hand and gives Bram the copies. Bram looks at it for a while, says it sounds like a bank, and hangs it anyway. The laurel stays in the drawer.
choices.memoryHint: Paint only the year with a lease behind it.

choices.label: Paint the laurel, no date
choices.outcome: Noel paints the laurel small and plain above the name, with no figure beside it, and tells Bram he will not put a year on a wall without a paper behind it. Bram likes the laurel. Customers still ask how old the place is, and Bram has started answering with a story instead of a number, which takes longer and, Noel notices, they listen to.
choices.memoryHint: Paint the laurel plain, with no year beside it.

echoes.noel_c3_a: You used a reviewed cue so finding the door didn't depend on style; Bram wants a date to do that work for the workshop.
echoes.noel_c3_b: You paired a plain companion with the decorative sign so the door had two readable routes; Bram wants one word to carry a century.

chapters.title: One Wall or the Whole Street
chapters.setting: The empty unit next door, shutters up
chapters.intro: The scheme's review comes back in February with a paid post attached: twelve months to write the district's shopfront lettering specification, with authority over every sign the scheme funds. The unit next door to the workshop is also empty, and the landlord has offered Noel first refusal on a lease he can just about afford. He has until the end of the month. Both offers want the same spring. He stands in the empty unit with a tin of undercoat at his feet and the specification draft in his coat, and the light through the dirty window falls in a long stripe across the floor.
chapters.objective: Decide where the next year of work happens.

choices.label: Take the specification post
choices.outcome: Noel takes the post and spends the year arguing about letter heights with contractors who have never held a brush. The specification is adopted in November, ninety pages long and dull as a timetable, and it will outlast him on eleven streets. He paints two signs that year, both for friends, both at weekends, both badly.
choices.memoryHint: Take the post that writes the street's rules.

choices.label: Take the unit next door
choices.outcome: Noel signs the lease, buys a second trestle and a used radiator, and paints what comes through the door: three shopfronts, a boat's name, a pub's back wall. The scheme adopts a specification written by a committee, with letter heights he would have argued about, and it is applied to the street outside his window in June. He watches it go up and goes back to work.
choices.memoryHint: Sign the lease and paint what comes through the door.

echoes.noel_c4_a: You left the client the wording, the colours and a repainting record; the district now wants that certainty for every door.
echoes.noel_c4_b: You put the old design beside the new mock-ups and credited the work without inventing an endorsement; the district wants it on eleven shopfronts.

title: The Platform Between Minutes
tagline: There is a platform between the printed departures.
premise: The clock says 17:09. The departure board goes from 17:08 to 17:10. Someone has been buying the missing minute every Thursday.

chapters.title: The Missing Minute
chapters.intro: A ticket arrives for a departure that appears on no public board. Its punched edge is old; its date is this Thursday. Vera finds the same missing minute in three editions of the timetable, each supposedly corrected by a different clerk. A railway employee has given her access to the closed records room, not the active tracks. She sets the ticket beside a station plan and asks where an honest mistake would leave a trace.
chapters.objective: Choose whether to compare the printed editions or examine the ticket punch.

choices.label: Compare the printed editions
choices.outcome: Vera finds that each edition inherits the same narrow strip of blank paper. It was not a fresh omission every year. Someone preserved it through several redesigns, and a small printer's mark points to a separate working timetable.
choices.memoryHint: Vera finds that each edition inherits the same narrow strip of blank paper.

choices.label: Examine the ticket punch
choices.outcome: The punch belongs to a staff shuttle rather than an ordinary passenger service. Vera records the distinction before interpreting it. The ticket could describe a real journey without promising that the journey is still available.
choices.memoryHint: The punch belongs to a staff shuttle rather than an ordinary passenger service.

chapters.title: The Door Behind the Board
chapters.intro: The working plan has a doorway where today's station has a sealed timetable cabinet. Behind the cabinet, an authorized maintenance inspection reveals the outline of an older passage. Ewan remembers carrying tea through it, but his account ends before the platform. Vera realizes that asking him to remember is not the same as giving him a reason to trust her.
chapters.objective: Choose whether to follow the maintenance plans or ask Ewan about the tea.

choices.label: Follow the maintenance plans
choices.outcome: An approved inspection leads to a narrow observation window overlooking a disconnected bay. No train can enter from the active line. Vera marks the difference between a surviving room and an operating route; the mystery becomes more interesting when she stops exaggerating it.
choices.memoryHint: An approved inspection leads to a narrow observation window overlooking a disconnected bay.

choices.label: Ask Ewan about the tea
